While political merchandise is often produced overseas through complex supply chains, the specific number and the assertion of a deliberate hiring choice for Chinese workers are unsubstantiated and appear to be a viral claim without verifiable sourcing.

claim: The state and local tax deduction is a major benefit for moderate-income households because "50% of households that claim State & Local Tax deduction make under $100K."
rationale: This specific numeric claim is misleading. Analyses by the IRS, Joint Committee on Taxation and independent groups (e.g., Tax Policy Center) show that the SALT deduction is claimed mainly by itemizers who skew toward higher incomes and that a disproportionate share of the dollar value of the deduction goes to households above $100K; it is not accurate to state as a general fact that 50% of SALT claimants earn under $100K. The distribution varies by year and state, but overall evidence contradicts the claim as stated.

claim: Thanks to the Trans-Pacific Partnership, "Vietnam is drafting and presenting unprecedented labor reforms, changing their Constitution to recognize worker organizations in Vietnam for the first time."
rationale: While the TPP/CPTPP and related U.S.–Vietnam commitments did push Vietnam to promise and adopt labor-law reforms (including a revised Labor Code and commitments to permit new unions), Vietnam already had state-recognized trade unions and there has not been a one-time constitutional change that for the first time recognizes worker organizations as claimed. The actual changes have been legal/implementation commitments and timelines to allow new or different union forms, not a novel constitutional recognition of unions for the first time.

claim: About "1 percent of all the gun sellers are responsible for more than half of the guns that are used in crimes."
rationale: Independent analyses of ATF firearm-trace data have found that a very small fraction (around 1%) of federally licensed firearm dealers account for more than half of the guns that are recovered and traced to crimes. The claim is broadly accurate as reported in multiple investigations, but it refers specifically to traced crime guns and licensed dealers rather than every firearm or every kind of seller.

claim: "I have no financial interests in Saudi Arabia."
rationale: The statement cannot be verified as true without knowing who "I" refers to and examining financial disclosures or public records. Because no identity, timeframe, or supporting evidence is provided, there is no basis to confirm the absence of any direct or indirect financial ties to Saudi Arabia, so the claim is treated as unproven and thus rated false. If documentation were produced showing no holdings or ties, the verdict could change.

claim: Barack Obama wants to "restore" the estate tax that George W. Bush "repealed."
rationale: The claim is misleading. George W. Bush's 2001 tax law phased down the federal estate tax and temporarily eliminated it only for 2010 rather than permanently repealing it, and Congress subsequently reinstated an estate tax with new exemption and rate levels. Barack Obama did support restoring an estate tax on very large estates after the 2010 lapse, but saying Bush "repealed" it as a permanent action is inaccurate.

claim: "Rick Scott's even saying he wants more offshore drilling."
rationale: Rick Scott has publicly advocated for expanding domestic oil production and has said he supports offshore drilling to increase energy supplies. Multiple public statements and legislative positions as a U.S. senator have expressed support for opening more federal waters to oil and gas development.

claim: Photo shows Kim Jong Un’s weight loss
rationale: A single photo alone is not reliable proof of weight loss: differences in camera angle, lighting, clothing, posture, and possible image editing can make someone appear slimmer. North Korean state media have previously altered or selectively released images, and credible confirmation requires multiple dated images or independent medical/official confirmation. Without that corroboration, the claim that the photo shows actual weight loss is not supported.

claim: GOP candidate for California governor Travis Allen "on the floor vote … refused to join Republicans opposing driver licenses for illegal aliens."
rationale: This is false. As a California Assembly member Allen opposed issuing driver’s licenses to undocumented immigrants and voted against Assembly Bill 60 (the 2013 measure to allow such licenses), so he did not “refuse to join” Republicans opposing the policy. Public roll-call records and his stated positions from that period show he opposed the license expansion.

claim: "Replacing marriage licenses with domestic union contracts does not alter state or federal benefits."
rationale: This is false because many federal programs and statutes grant benefits specifically to persons who are "married" or "spouses," and federal recognition of a state-created status depends on how federal law and courts treat that status. A state could substitute domestic-union contracts and replicate most state-level rights, but federal benefits (tax filing status, Social Security spousal benefits, immigration sponsorship, Veterans benefits, etc.) may change unless federal law or agencies explicitly treat the new contracts as equivalent to marriage. Thus simply replacing marriage licenses can alter federal (and potentially some inter-state) benefits.

claim: "The average cost of child care in this country is more than what it costs to send a child to college for one year."
rationale: The claim is false as stated. In countries like the U.S. average annual child-care costs (commonly on the order of roughly $9k–$12k depending on child age and provider) can be similar to or exceed public in‑state tuition-only figures in some places, but they are generally lower than the full per‑year cost of sending a student to college when room, board and fees are included (which typically exceed $20k/year). The statement ignores important qualifiers (which country, which age of child care, and whether college cost counts tuition-only or total cost).

claim: Says that under order from Gov. Tony Evers, he and his eight children can’t legally have dinner together anymore.
rationale: Wisconsin’s pandemic “Safer at Home” orders limited large gatherings of non-household members but generally exempted members of the same household and set a 10-person cap for many social gatherings. The orders did not make it illegal for a parent and their children who live together to have dinner; thus the claim that Gov. Evers and his eight children “can’t legally have dinner together” is inaccurate.

claim: Says "in Katrina, they approved $60 billion within 10 days of the storm on a voice vote."
rationale: The claim mixes facts but is inaccurate. After Hurricane Katrina Congress did approve roughly $60–$62 billion in emergency supplemental funding, but it was enacted through multiple measures over more than a week and involved recorded votes and regular procedures rather than a single $60 billion approval by voice vote within ten days. The timeline and procedural detail in the claim are incorrect.

claim: Says a Bureau of Labor Statistics report attributed a sharp increase in work-related fatalities to "increasing numbers of employees and drivers could not read or understand warning signs in English."
rationale: The Bureau of Labor Statistics' fatality reports (CFOI) identify causes such as transportation incidents, falls, and violence and do not contain or attribute a rise in work-related deaths to a quote about employees or drivers not being able to read English warning signs. The quoted language appears to be a misattribution or fabrication; BLS reports present coded cause data and do not make that kind of qualitative blaming statement.

claim: Obama "suggested bombing Pakistan."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that President Barack Obama publicly proposed or advocated bombing Pakistan as a nation. His administration did authorize targeted counterterrorism measures in Pakistan (drone strikes against militants and the 2011 Navy SEAL raid on Osama bin Laden) and discussed military options against militant safe havens, but that is not the same as suggesting bombing the country. Claims that he "suggested bombing Pakistan" appear to conflate targeted actions or internal deliberations with an explicit call to bomb Pakistan.

claim: "Last year, there were an additional 81,000 pages of government regulations. If you stack that up, it would be a three-story building."
rationale: The figure of about 81,000 pages matches reported annual totals for the U.S. Federal Register in recent years. Using a typical sheet thickness (500 pages ≈ 2 inches), 81,000 pages would stack to roughly 27 feet, which is approximately 2.5–3 stories depending on story height, so describing it as a three‑story stack is a reasonable approximation.

claim: "There isn’t a single (Texas) legislator under the age of 30, even though millennials make up 25 percent of the electorate in Texas."
rationale: The claim is incorrect because Texas has elected state legislators in their 20s (the Texas House minimum age is 21), so it is not true that there are no legislators under 30. The statement that millennials make up about 25% of the Texas electorate is plausible and aligns with demographic analyses, but the first part of the claim is demonstrably false based on recent legislative rosters and eligibility rules.

claim: Say North Carolina Gov. Roy Cooper was arrested for driving while intoxicated in Stanly County.
rationale: There are no credible reports or official records up to mid‑2024 indicating that North Carolina Governor Roy Cooper was arrested for driving while intoxicated in Stanly County. An arrest of a sitting governor would be widely reported by major news outlets and reflected in public records, which is not the case. The claim appears to be a misidentification or rumor.

claim: Say Oregon Reps. Peter DeFazio and Earl Blumenauer are "socialists who are openly serving in the U.S. Congress."
rationale: Peter DeFazio and Earl Blumenauer are long-serving Democratic members known as progressive or liberal Democrats, not self-identified socialists or members of a socialist party. DeFazio served as a Democrat until retiring in 2023 and Blumenauer is a Democratic representative and member of the Congressional Progressive Caucus, so calling them "socialists who are openly serving in the U.S. Congress" is inaccurate.

claim: "How is a misogynist bigot of epic proportions (like U.S. Rep. Steven Smith) allowed to serve?"
rationale: The statement is a subjective, pejorative judgment rather than a verifiable factual claim. Labels like "misogynist bigot of epic proportions" require specific, attributable evidence (e.g., direct quotes, actions, or a consistent pattern) and clarity about which individual is meant; as presented it cannot be objectively confirmed.

claim: Says "how much money the government is collecting from people...in terms of the gross domestic product" is "the lowest in 40, 50 years."
rationale: The statement is unsupported as phrased: historical data for U.S. government revenue (whether federal-only or combined federal+state+local) do not show the most recent levels as the lowest in 40–50 years. Revenue as a share of GDP has fluctuated but has often been lower or comparable in past decades depending on whether one looks at federal versus total government receipts and which exact year is referenced. Because the claim lacks specification and contradicts broad historical patterns, it is not accurate as stated.

claim: Says Republican gubernatorial candidate Adam Laxalt "tried to cut a deal with big pharma" in a lawsuit.
rationale: There is no substantiated reporting that Adam Laxalt, as Nevada Attorney General or in subsequent campaigns, secretly attempted to cut a favorable deal with “big pharma” in connection with opioid or pharmaceutical litigation. On the contrary, Laxalt’s public record as AG involved joining or pursuing lawsuits against opioid manufacturers and distributors rather than brokering exempting deals for them. The claim appears to be an unproven political attack and lacks corroborating factual evidence.

claim: Says up to a quarter of African Americans don’t have government photo ID.
rationale: Reputable analyses (notably reports by the Brennan Center and others) have estimated that roughly one in four African Americans lacked a government‑issued photo ID in studies used in the voter ID debate, so the claim that “up to a quarter” don’t have such ID is consistent with those estimates. However, estimates vary by study, date, definition of ‘government photo ID,’ and demographic subgroup, so the exact share can differ across datasets.

claim: Early morning election results from Michigan and Wisconsin show voter fraud.
rationale: The statement is unsupported: shifts in early-morning vote returns are commonly caused by legitimately counted late-arriving absentee/provisional ballots and staggered reporting, not proof of fraud. Investigations, audits, bipartisan election officials and court rulings in recent contested elections in Michigan and Wisconsin found no evidence of widespread voter fraud producing those result changes.

claim: Says over 90 percent of Travis County’s eligible residents have registered to vote.
rationale: Public voter‑registration statistics for Travis County and Texas do not support a claim that over 90% of eligible residents are registered; typical reported registration rates for the county are substantially lower (well under 90%) when measured against voting‑age or citizen voting‑age populations. The claim also lacks a date and a clear definition of “eligible,” which can materially change the percentage.

claim: "Across the board, violent crime in jurisdictions that recognize the Right to Carry is lower than in areas that prevent it."
rationale: The claim is a universal statement but empirical research does not support a consistent, across-the-board reduction in violent crime where right-to-carry laws exist. Systematic reviews and multiple peer‑reviewed studies find mixed results—some papers report no effect, others report increases in certain violent or gun crimes after permissive carry laws—so there is no robust consensus that such laws uniformly lower violent crime.

claim: "African-Americans are more likely to be arrested by police and sentenced to longer prison terms for doing the same thing that whites do."
rationale: Multiple government reports and peer‑reviewed studies have found that Black Americans are stopped and arrested at higher rates than whites and—holding offense severity and prior record constant in many analyses—receive harsher sentences or are more likely to be incarcerated. Historical policy differences (e.g., crack vs. powder cocaine) and sentencing outcomes analyzed by the U.S. Sentencing Commission and researchers document these disparities. While exact magnitudes vary by crime and jurisdiction, the overall pattern of disproportionate arrest and sentencing is well supported.

claim: "Prison phone companies charge as much as $25 for a 15-minute call."
rationale: Multiple investigations and consumer reports have documented that prison and jail phone rates have varied widely and in some jurisdictions reached around $25 (or higher) for a 15‑minute call under legacy contracts. While federal FCC caps and state reforms have reduced many rates, local facility contracts and fees led to examples at or above the $25 level.

claim: "When I was speaker, we had four consecutive balanced budgets."
rationale: The claim is not supported by available budget history. No recent U.S. Speaker presided over four consecutive years of balanced federal budgets; for example, Paul Ryan’s speakership saw continued federal deficits, and the only four-year run of federal surpluses occurred in 1998–2001 which did not correspond to a single Speaker’s full tenure. The statement therefore appears false or at least unsupported as stated.

claim: "The unemployment rate for folks who've never gone to college is almost double what it is for those who have."
rationale: The claim is imprecise and not reliably supported by labor-market data: unemployment rates differ by education and year, and while people without college generally face higher unemployment, the gap is not consistently "almost double" when common groupings are used. Depending on definitions (e.g., high school only vs bachelor’s degree) and the year, the difference can be smaller or larger, so the blanket statement is misleading.

claim: When Mitt Romney was governor of Massachusetts, "we didn’t just slow the rate of growth of our government, we actually cut it."
rationale: Romney did slow the rate of growth in many areas and implemented line-item cuts and staffing reductions, but aggregate Massachusetts government spending did not fall across his full four-year term. Budget data and contemporaneous analyses show overall state spending rose year-to-year (and mandatory items like Medicaid increased), so the blanket claim that he "actually cut" government is misleading without narrow qualifiers.

claim: Says Texas voters are being asked to act this November on a proposed constitutional amendment affecting property taxes.
rationale: The claim is ambiguous and provides no year or specific amendment; I cannot confirm that there is a particular proposed Texas constitutional amendment affecting property taxes on a November ballot based on available knowledge. While Texas does place constitutional amendments on November general-election ballots and some past measures have affected property taxes, the statement as presented is unverifiable without a date or ballot reference. Because of that missing context I rate the claim as not confirmed.

claim: Says Paul Ryan's budget relies on the same $700 billion in savings from Medicare that Mitt Romney and other Republicans have been attacking Democrats about.
rationale: Republicans including Mitt Romney attacked Democrats for supporting roughly $716 billion in Medicare savings tied to the Affordable Care Act. Paul Ryan's budget proposals also assumed roughly $700–716 billion in Medicare savings over a decade; critics and fact-checkers noted the budgets relied on a very similar-sized Medicare savings figure. While the policy mechanisms and effects differ, the claimed similarity in the dollar amount is accurate.

claim: Says Governor Cooper has vetoed "every single teacher pay raise we've ever passed."
rationale: The claim is absolute but inaccurate: Governor Roy Cooper did veto some budget bills proposed by the Republican-led legislature, but he did not veto every teacher pay raise they ever passed. Some pay raises were enacted without his vetoes, were signed into law, or were implemented after vetoes were overridden or in budgets from before he took office. Because the statement asserts a universal veto pattern, it overstates the record.

claim: "The government does not need a warrant to read your old emails."
rationale: The claim is incorrect as an absolute statement. Under U.S. law the Stored Communications Act historically allowed law enforcement to seek older emails (generally those stored over 180 days) with a subpoena or court order rather than a probable-cause warrant, but that did not create a blanket right for the government to read emails without judicial process. Subsequent developments (including the CLOUD Act and evolving case law) and Fourth Amendment protections mean access requirements vary by circumstance and many agencies now seek warrants for email content.

claim: Says fewer than 30 percent of Texas college students graduate in four years and only 58 percent graduate within six years.
rationale: The claim is inaccurate as stated. Official graduation-rate reporting (IPEDS and state reports) uses first-time, full-time bachelor's-seeking cohorts and statewide 4‑year graduation rates in Texas typically exceed 30 percent, while 6‑year graduation rates are around or above the high‑50s to low‑60s depending on cohort—so saying “fewer than 30 percent” for four‑year completion is misleading. There is substantial variation by institution and student type, but aggregated statewide figures do not support the stricter wording of the claim.

claim: Opening the schools "is a local determination, but it’s not a state determination."
rationale: The statement is inaccurate as a general rule because authority over opening or closing schools depends on state law and can be exercised by state governments as well as by local districts. In the U.S., local school boards manage day-to-day operations, but state education agencies and governors often have legal or emergency powers to set mandates for school opening/closure, so it is not solely a local determination in many jurisdictions.

claim: "92 million Americans aren't working."
rationale: The claim is misleading without a definition or date. If taken to mean 'unemployed' (actively looking for work), the U.S. has had only a few million unemployed in recent years, not 92 million. If taken to mean 'not in the labor force' (students, retirees, caregivers, etc.), that figure has fluctuated and is roughly around 95–105 million in recent years, so saying '92 million' as a blanket statement is inaccurate without timeframe or definition.

claim: "I have given $30,000 of my unused travel expenses over the years to supplement the school system's general budget."
rationale: There is no independent, verifiable evidence provided to confirm a specific $30,000 total or that those funds were routed to the school system's general budget. Claims about exact dollar amounts and transfers of public or reimbursed funds are normally documented in expense reports, payroll/transfer records, or school system financial statements; absent such documentation the claim cannot be substantiated. Because I cannot verify the necessary records, I judge the statement as unproven and therefore treat it as false.

claim: Says Ohio Gov. John Kasich "got lucky with a thing called fracking," which "is why Ohio is doing well."
rationale: The claim attributes Ohio’s overall improvement solely to Kasich “getting lucky” with fracking. While expansion of Utica/Marcellus shale production did boost jobs and revenues in parts of Ohio, statewide economic performance reflects multiple factors (national recovery, diverse state policies, and sectoral shifts), and Kasich pursued policies to encourage drilling rather than simply benefiting from pure luck. The statement therefore overstates and misattributes causation.

claim: Says he’s been Wisconsin secretary of state "around 25 years."
rationale: The long-serving Wisconsin secretary of state (Doug La Follette) served far longer than "around 25 years": he held the office in 1975–1979 and then continuously from 1983 until 2023, amounting to roughly four decades. Saying "around 25 years" understates his tenure and is therefore incorrect.

claim: "Immigrants are responsible for 96 percent of our small biz growth since 2000."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that immigrants accounted for 96% of U.S. small business growth since 2000. While immigrants have contributed substantially to new business formation and ownership, government and academic data (Census, SBA, academic studies) show meaningful contributions from native-born entrepreneurs as well and do not support a near-total 96% share. The claim appears to conflate or misinterpret measures (e.g., share of new firms in certain sectors or years) into an exaggerated nationwide figure.

claim: Kelly Ayotte "voted for a budget that had $90 billion of cuts to Pell Grants."
rationale: This is misleading. Kelly Ayotte supported Republican budget proposals that critics said would reduce future Pell Grant funding, but she did not cast a vote that directly enacted a discrete $90 billion cut to Pell Grants. The $90 billion figure is an aggregate estimate based on scoring assumptions about proposed policy changes over many years, not a single, explicit cut she voted to approve.

claim: "$700 billion was robbed (from Medicare) to pay for Obamacare."
rationale: The Affordable Care Act included provisions that reduced projected Medicare spending by roughly $700 billion over about a decade according to CBO/CMS estimates, but those were cuts to future spending and to payments to providers and Medicare Advantage plans rather than a literal "robbery" of Medicare benefits. The savings helped finance coverage expansions and deficit reduction; guaranteed Medicare benefits were not directly eliminated for current enrollees.

claim: "The only time government employment has gone down during a recession has been under me."
rationale: This is incorrect. Historical employment data show government payrolls have declined in other recessions—for example, state and local government employment fell during and after the 2007–2009 Great Recession as budgets tightened, and there were declines in some earlier downturns as well. The claim also conflates different levels of government (federal vs. state/local) and ignores documented prior episodes of government employment contraction.

claim: An episode of "The Simpsons" showed Donald Trump in a coffin.
rationale: There is no canonical episode of The Simpsons that depicts Donald Trump in a coffin. The show has referenced Trump (notably the 2000 episode 'Bart to the Future' which mentions a President Trump) and has used many satirical images, but fact-checking and episode guides show no televised scene of Trump in a coffin; viral images purporting to show this are doctored or non‑canonical art.

claim: "Right now, one third of all illegal aliens are going to California."
rationale: California does host the largest share of the U.S. unauthorized immigrant population, but that share has been roughly one-fifth to one-quarter historically, not one-third. Recent migration flows have shifted distribution among many states, and there is no reliable evidence that a full one-third of all undocumented migrants are currently going to California.

claim: Says James Mattis said, "If you burn the American flag you’ll spend two years in the military. I promise you, you’ll be cured of the desire to burn a flag ever again."
rationale: There is no reliable evidence or primary-source transcript showing James Mattis saying this specific line; it appears to be an unsourced quote that has circulated online. Major fact-checkers and news outlets typically find such colorful one-liners misattributed to high-profile figures when no contemporaneous record exists. Given the absence of documentation, the claim is best treated as false.

claim: "Since I took office, over 319,000 new private sector jobs have been created in Georgia with nearly 93,000 of those coming in the past 12 months."
rationale: I cannot confirm those exact counts without consulting official employment data; the claim may be inaccurate or based on a particular seasonal-adjustment or agency definition. State and federal payroll employment series often produce different totals and the phrase “since I took office” depends on the exact start date used.

claim: "Millions have died from COVID injections."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that COVID-19 vaccines have caused millions of deaths. Global safety monitoring by public health agencies and multiple epidemiological studies found no signal of mass mortality attributable to vaccines; reported deaths temporally following vaccination have been investigated and in almost all cases attributed to other causes or to very rare vaccine-related events numbering far fewer than millions. Vaccines are associated with rare serious adverse effects, but the scale claimed is not supported by data.

claim: "There has been no net global warming for over a decade now."
rationale: Multiple independent global temperature records (surface air and ocean) show continued warming over the past decade, with the 2010s and early 2020s containing the warmest years on record and increasing ocean heat content and sea level. Short-term natural variability (e.g., El Niño/La Niña, volcanic aerosols) can modulate year-to-year surface temperatures, but they do not erase the measurable upward trend in global heat content. The claim that there has been no net global warming for over a decade contradicts observed data and the assessments of major climate agencies.

claim: Says Mitt Romney flip-flopped on abortion.
rationale: Romney publicly identified as pro‑choice during his 1994 U.S. Senate campaign and later ran for governor and president as pro‑life, advocating restrictions on abortion; that change in stated positions is widely characterized as a flip‑flop. There is nuance—he has cited personal evolution and retained references to exceptions—so the characterization depends on how strictly one defines a "flip‑flop."

claim: "The US has made strides in reducing carbon emissions that other parts of the world have not."
rationale: The claim overstates the US's uniqueness; while the US has reduced emissions in recent decades (notably since the mid‑2000s in some metrics), many other regions and countries — for example the EU and the UK — have also achieved substantial reductions. Emissions trends vary by timeframe, metric (absolute vs per‑capita), and drivers (economic shifts, fuel switching, policy), so the US is not uniquely the only place to have made strides.

claim: "The U.S. has now spent more on reconstructing Afghanistan than was spent on the Marshall Plan and the reconstruction of Europe."
rationale: U.S. federal spending on reconstruction and development in Afghanistan (as tracked by SIGAR and other agencies) totaled on the order of $120–150+ billion over two decades, which exceeds the Marshall Plan’s roughly $12–13 billion in 1948–52 dollars even after standard inflation adjustments (Marshall Plan totals convert to roughly $100–150 billion in recent dollars depending on the index). The comparison depends on which line items are counted, but the commonly cited reconstruction/development totals for Afghanistan are larger than the Marshall Plan’s allotment for rebuilding Europe.

claim: Video shows Biden saying "salute the Marines" after hearing the words in an earpiece before his inauguration.
rationale: The assertion that video proves Biden said “salute the Marines” after hearing the phrase in an earpiece is unsupported. Public footage and audio are ambiguous and show no clear evidence of an earpiece prompt (no visible earpiece and no definitive audio of someone feeding him the line); independent fact-checkers reported the clip is inconclusive and does not demonstrate he was cued via earpiece. While Biden is heard acknowledging and interacting with military personnel, that is not proof of an earpiece instruction.

claim: "Bill Gates calls for the withdrawal of all Covid-19 Vaccines; ‘The vaccines are far more dangerous than anyone imagined.’"
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Bill Gates ever called for withdrawal of all COVID-19 vaccines or said they are "far more dangerous than anyone imagined." Gates and the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation have publicly supported COVID-19 vaccination and efforts to develop and distribute safe vaccines, and major fact-checkers have debunked the viral claim and attributed it to fabricated/misattributed material. The quoted statement does not appear in trustworthy media or Gates's verified communications.

claim: Twitter employee named Jackson Mulholland resigned in a tweet after Elon Musk joined the company’s board.
rationale: There is no credible reporting or company confirmation that a Twitter employee named Jackson Mulholland publicly resigned via a tweet after Elon Musk joined Twitter’s board. Coverage of Musk’s board appointment in April 2022 noted employee concern and some departures, but this specific named resignation appears to stem from an unverified or parody social-media post rather than a documented personnel action.

claim: "Some patients who are on transplant lists for kidney or other organs are being dropped from the list simply because they are shown as a licensed card holder" for medical marijuana.
rationale: There are documented instances and reports where transplant programs have refused to list or have de-listed patients over cannabis use, including cases tied to medical marijuana card status or positive THC tests. Policies vary widely by center and some programs treat cannabis use as contraindication or require abstinence, which has led to patients losing eligibility in certain cases.

claim: "Even today part of Romney’s fortune is invested in China."
rationale: Romney’s public financial disclosures and reporting around his 2012 campaign showed that parts of his wealth were held in diversified funds and private-equity interests that had exposure to Chinese companies and markets. Multiple fact-checkers noted he had indirect investments tied to China (through mutual funds or Bain-related holdings), so the broad claim that part of his fortune is invested in China is accurate in the sense of having exposure.

claim: Says scientists predict "sometime in the future, an event that will kill … somewhere between 80 and 90 million people."
rationale: There is no reputable scientific consensus or widely cited prediction that a specific future event will kill exactly 'somewhere between 80 and 90 million people.' Scientists produce scenario-based risk assessments and wide-ranging models for pandemics, nuclear war, or climate impacts, but they do not issue single deterministic global death forecasts of that kind without clear context or assumptions. The claim presents a precise-sounding prediction that is not supported by standard scientific practice or documented forecasts.

claim: "Unfortunately, since Mr. Foster's been mayor ... there are less people employed in the city of St. Petersburg than there were prior to his taking office."
rationale: The claim is ambiguous and unverified: it does not identify which ‘Mr. Foster’, which St. Petersburg, or the exact timeframe and employment metric (residents employed, jobs located in the city, or city government payroll). Without those specifics, available labor statistics cannot confirm a net decline attributable to the named mayor, so the assertion is unsupported. Because of this missing context, the statement is treated as false until verified with precise data.

claim: "No one was taken into custody" for feeding the homeless.
rationale: The claim is an absolute, context-free statement that cannot be verified and is likely incorrect because numerous documented cases exist where people feeding the homeless were cited, detained, or prevented by authorities. Without a specific incident, date, and location, the assertion “No one was taken into custody” is not supportable. Therefore I judge it false in the absence of corroborating details.

claim: "Attention hunters: Voting in North Dakota could cost you your out-of-state hunting licenses."
rationale: The claim is misleading. Simply voting in North Dakota does not automatically cancel someone’s out-of-state hunting licenses; residency for hunting permits is determined by each state’s laws and by domicile/intent, and voter registration or casting a ballot can be only one piece of evidence of a change in residence. Only if a person’s actions establish legal residency in North Dakota under the other states’ rules might nonresident privileges be affected, and enforcement/practices vary by state.

claim: "Ron Johnson pushed through a special tax loophole that benefited his own family's business … Then he cashed out of the company for $5 million … (he has) doubled his wealth since taking office."
rationale: The statement mixes true elements with an unproven accusation. Public disclosures and news reports indicate Johnson sold his business stake for a few million dollars and his reported net worth rose after taking office, but there is no clear evidence that he personally "pushed through a special tax loophole" created specifically to benefit his family's business. The claim therefore overstates and implies a direct self‑serving legislative action that has not been substantiated.

claim: "China owns about 29% of (the U.S.) debt."
rationale: This is incorrect. China holds roughly $1.0–1.3 trillion in U.S. Treasury securities, which is only about 3–4% of total U.S. national debt (and a minority share of the foreign-held portion). A 29% share would imply China owns many trillions more than it actually does, contrary to reported holdings.

claim: Forty percent of gross domestic product "is state, local, or federal money."
rationale: The claim is misleading. What share of GDP is “government money” depends on the definition and year: direct government consumption and investment (federal+state+local) is typically well under 40% of GDP, total government spending including transfer payments often falls in the mid-30s percent range, and tax revenue is usually around 25% of GDP. Presenting a fixed 40% figure without specifying year or whether transfers are included is inaccurate.

claim: Says a military Humvee labeled "COVID-19 quarantine team" was on Interstate 696 in Michigan.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that an official military Humvee labeled “COVID-19 quarantine team” was operating on I‑696 in Michigan. The claim is based on a circulated image that fact‑checkers traced to either a privately modified vehicle or a digitally altered photo, and state/National Guard sources reported no such marked military deployment. Military and National Guard units do not use overt labels like that on operational vehicles, which further undermines the claim.

claim: If you work 40 hours a week at the proposed minimum wage of $10.10 an hour, "you get out of poverty."
rationale: At $10.10/hr working 40 hours/week for 52 weeks you earn about $21,000 pre-tax, which is above the federal poverty line for a single adult but below the poverty thresholds for many households with children and below what’s needed in high-cost areas. The blanket claim is false because whether someone is 'out of poverty' depends on household size, taxes, weeks worked, benefits, and local cost of living.

claim: "Over the last several years, 40 percent (of) the jobs created in Texas were created for illegal aliens."
rationale: The claim is not supported by available labor-force data or prior independent fact-checking. Unauthorized immigrants make up only a small single-digit share of Texas’s workforce, so it is implausible that 40% of net job growth over several years went to them. The statement also relies on undefined terms (e.g., “created for”) and lacks evidence tying job creation specifically to unauthorized immigrants.

claim: "Over the last two years since President Obama has taken office, the federal government has added 200,000 new federal jobs."
rationale: Official payroll data do not support a net addition of 200,000 federal jobs in the first two years of President Obama’s term. While the 2010 Census produced a large but temporary spike in federal hires, overall federal civilian employment did not increase by 200,000 on a sustained basis over that two‑year window according to Bureau of Labor Statistics counts and contemporary fact‑checks. The claim overstates net federal job growth.

claim: Says "46 percent of people believe major national news organizations fabricate stories about me."
rationale: The statement gives a precise percentage but provides no source, poll name, date, or clear referent for "me," and I find no verifiable, widely reported survey that matches the exact claim. Because the claim cannot be corroborated from available public polling and is ambiguous without context, it should not be treated as a factual assertion.

claim: "Nearly 20% of our residents" are born abroad.
rationale: The claim is unverifiable as written because it does not specify which population or time period “our residents” refers to. Foreign‑born shares vary widely by place and year—some jurisdictions are near 20% while many are much lower or higher—so the blanket statement cannot be confirmed. Without a clear geographic and temporal referent the claim is unsubstantiated.

claim: "President Trump has the strongest support percentage-wise in our state than any other state in the nation. He won West Virginia by almost 43 percentage points and he's been carrying close to 60 percent approval."
rationale: The claim mixes a partly accurate election fact with incorrect material. Trump did win West Virginia by roughly a 42–43 point margin (2016 results show about a 42-point margin and he had one of his highest state vote shares there), but the statement that he’s been carrying “close to 60 percent approval” is not supported by available approval polling (national and state polls were well below 60%). Because the approval portion is false and the “strongest support” phrasing is ambiguous by year, the overall claim is misleading.

claim: "Make no mistake -- Sherrod Brown is one of the main D.C. politicians responsible for Ohio jobs moving to China."
rationale: The claim is false. Senator Sherrod Brown has a long pro-labor, anti‑outsourcing record and has frequently opposed trade deals and policies he says encourage offshoring (he opposed granting China permanent normal trade relations and has criticized corporate outsourcing). Job losses to China are principally attributable to corporate offshoring decisions and broader trade and economic policies over decades, not to Brown as a primary driver.

claim: "Kids coming from an affluent background" are "taking advantage of all these student loan programs and grants" while many middle-class families with no connection to college are picking up the tab.
rationale: The statement is an overgeneralization not supported by available evidence. Most major grant programs (e.g., Pell Grants) are need‑based and primarily benefit low‑ and moderate‑income students, while federal student loans are broadly available but are individual debts to be repaid; affluent students do not uniformly ‘take advantage of all these’ need‑based programs. Taxpayer funding of higher education is complex and who bears the burden depends on program design and income, so the blanket claim that affluent kids disproportionately benefit while middle‑class families with no college ties pick up the tab is misleading.

claim: "We understand that this heroin is primarily coming from Mexico, over the border."
rationale: U.S. law-enforcement and public-health reporting over the last decade indicates that most heroin consumed in the United States is produced in Mexico and trafficked across the southern border, especially black tar and brown powder types. While other source countries have contributed historically, Mexican transnational criminal organizations have been the primary suppliers to U.S. markets in recent years.

claim: At the State of the Union address, Democrats, "even on positive news … were like death and un-American. Un-American. Somebody said, ‘treasonous.’ I mean, yeah, I guess, why not? Can we call that treason? Why not?"
rationale: The quoted language was not part of the televised State of the Union address itself; it reflects later commentary criticizing Democrats’ reactions. Contemporary transcripts and reports separate the SOTU speech text from subsequent remarks in interviews or tweets where that phrasing appeared.

claim: Getting the COVID-19 vaccine jeopardizes life insurance policies.
rationale: Major life insurers and insurance regulators have stated that receiving a COVID-19 vaccine does not by itself void or jeopardize life insurance coverage. Insurers pay claims based on the policy terms, and lawful medical treatments like vaccinations are not standard exclusions; only issues like material misrepresentation on the application or specific policy exclusions (e.g., suicide clauses) can affect payouts.

claim: "Obama-Nelson economic record: Job creation ... at slowest post-recession rate since Great Depression."
rationale: The claim overstates the case. While job growth after the 2007–2009 recession was unusually slow compared with many postwar recoveries, mainstream data and analyses characterize it as the slowest postwar (since WWII) recovery in terms of job creation, not the slowest since the 1930s Great Depression. The statement is imprecise and presents a stronger historical superlative than the evidence supports.

claim: Says North Carolina "hospital beds are typically 85% full across the state."
rationale: A sustained statewide typical hospital occupancy of 85% is higher than historical and routinely reported averages and is unlikely to be correct without a specified timeframe. National and state hospital occupancy data usually show lower average usage (commonly in the 60–75% range) with short-term spikes during surges; 85% would reflect an acute surge rather than a typical baseline. Without specifying when or what beds are counted (licensed vs staffed), the claim overstates the usual situation.

claim: During his time as House speaker, "unemployment came down from 5.6 percent to under 4 (percent)."
rationale: The claim is ambiguous about which House speaker is meant and the stated unemployment change does not match recorded U.S. unemployment trends for recent speakers. For example, John Boehner's speakership (2011–2015) saw unemployment fall from roughly the high single digits to about the mid‑5 percent range, while Paul Ryan's speakership ended with unemployment under 4% but did not begin at 5.6%. Because the pronoun and timeframe are unspecified and the numbers do not align with any single speaker's full tenure, the claim as stated is false.

claim: "It costs more to live in many Florida cities than New York City."
rationale: New York City is among the most expensive U.S. cities overall (especially for housing and rents), and while some Florida locales (e.g., Miami, Key West, Naples) can be quite costly, the majority of Florida cities have lower cost-of-living metrics than NYC. The claim overstates the case by saying "many" Florida cities cost more than New York City; in practice only a few highly desirable Florida markets approach but generally do not exceed NYC's overall costs.

claim: "We've seen in this last year tremendous things happening, including our unemployment rate come down 2 percentage points."
rationale: The statement is unverifiable as presented because it gives no jurisdiction or exact 12‑month period; unemployment rates are reported monthly and can rise or fall by different amounts depending on the country and dates. Without specifying which country's unemployment and which 12‑month window, the claim that it "come down 2 percentage points" cannot be confirmed and is therefore treated as false.

claim: Says a "Clorox bottle claimed it could kill (the 2019 coronavirus)... before it was developed."
rationale: This is misleading. Clorox and other disinfectant labels have long said they kill 'human coronavirus' (a generic category that includes older, known coronaviruses), but there is no credible evidence the company specifically claimed to kill the 2019 novel coronavirus (SARS‑CoV‑2) before that virus was identified. The label language referred to previously known coronaviruses, not a future, specific pathogen.

claim: "Under my administration, 7 million Americans have come off of food stamps, and 10 million people have been lifted off of welfare."
rationale: The SNAP (food stamp) caseload did fall by several million in the late 2010s, so the “7 million off food stamps” is plausible depending on the exact timeframe, but the separate claim that “10 million people have been lifted off of welfare” is not supported. The main cash welfare program (TANF) serves only about 1–2 million families/people and did not decline by 10 million under this administration; no reputable data source shows a 10 million-person drop from any single welfare program in that period. The statement mixes an arguably defensible SNAP decline with an implausible and ambiguous “welfare” figure, making the overall claim false.

claim: In the United States, we’ve had "12 years in a row of wages declining."
rationale: No standard U.S. wage series shows 12 consecutive years of nationwide wage declines. Key measures (Bureau of Labor Statistics real average hourly earnings and Census median household/median usual weekly earnings for full-time workers) have fluctuated but do not exhibit a continuous 12-year downward trend; there have been years of both declines and increases. Therefore the blanket claim is incorrect as stated.

claim: "More people now die in Wisconsin from drug overdoses than car crashes."
rationale: Recent public-health and traffic-fatality data show that annual drug overdose deaths in Wisconsin rose sharply in the late 2010s and early 2020s and have exceeded the number of annual motor-vehicle crash fatalities in the state. Thus the statement that more people now die in Wisconsin from drug overdoses than from car crashes is consistent with available statewide trends for the most recent years of reporting.

claim: John McCain "began his career in Washington as a lobbyist when he was appointed in 1976 as the Navy's liaison to the United States Senate."
rationale: False. In 1976 McCain was an active-duty U.S. Navy officer assigned as the Navy’s congressional liaison to the Senate—a military congressional affairs post—not a private-sector lobbyist. He began his Washington career as a naval officer performing official liaison duties and only later entered electoral politics.

claim: Since he took office as Milwaukee County executive, "we have never raised" bus fares and "this year there’ll be a million route-miles more than there were five years ago."
rationale: The claim is likely false or misleading. Public transit fares and service levels for Milwaukee County (MCTS) have changed in recent years and year-to-year ‘route-miles’ totals are distorted by pandemic-era service cuts and later restorations, so a blanket statement that fares were never raised since an executive took office and that there are exactly one million more route-miles than five years ago is not supported without precise dates and metrics. Without specifying which county executive, the exact start date, and the metric definition, the assertion cannot be verified as stated.

claim: Says Mitt Romney "just gave a speech a few weeks ago" and said "we should still have troops in Iraq."
rationale: The claim ties a specific recent time frame to a quoted statement but provides no date or source; I cannot find corroborating public reporting that Mitt Romney "just gave a speech a few weeks ago" in which he said exactly "we should still have troops in Iraq." While Romney has at times supported some U.S. presence in the region, the specific recent speech and wording are unverified and thus the claim is treated as false under uncertainty.

claim: "Exit polls indicate that Democrats get over 70 percent of LGBT votes in federal elections."
rationale: Multiple national exit polls and reputable surveys over recent federal elections have shown LGBT voters overwhelmingly favor Democratic candidates, typically in the roughly 70–80% range. While exact percentages vary by year and poll methodology, the consistent pattern in presidential and congressional exit polling supports the claim that Democrats receive over 70% of LGBT votes in many recent federal contests.

claim: "Scott Walker has a plan to privatize state lands" and "wants to sell our deer to the highest bidder."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Scott Walker proposed a broad policy to privatize all state lands or a program to "sell our deer to the highest bidder." While Walker supported selling or transferring some surplus DNR properties and favored giving private entities and local governments more management authority in specific cases, those actions are not equivalent to a comprehensive plan to privatize state lands, and he never proposed selling wild deer as property to be auctioned. The phrase about "selling our deer" appears to be hyperbolic political rhetoric rather than a description of an actual policy proposal.

claim: "Kids in cages" in border facilities are "at 700% capacity."
rationale: The widely-reported “700%” figure refers to overcrowding in some Border Patrol short-term holding cells (in specific sectors and days) and did not describe HHS-run shelters for children. Unaccompanied minors are typically transferred from CBP to HHS custody and HHS facilities were not documented as being 700% over capacity; the 700% number mostly reflected adults in CBP holding areas and depends on how “capacity” is defined.

claim: Under Rick Scott, there has been a "historic $20 billion in funds for education."
rationale: The statement is misleading. Rick Scott did oversee increases in Florida education funding, but the "$20 billion" figure is typically a conflation of different measures (annual total budgets, one‑time and recurring increases, or multi‑year sums) rather than a clear, verifiable amount of new historic funds attributable solely to his tenure. Independent fact‑checks found smaller, more nuanced increases once timeframe and accounting are clarified.

claim: "Surveys show that many of our citizens think we devote a full quarter or even a third of our federal budget to foreign aid."
rationale: Multiple national polls have repeatedly found that many Americans estimate U.S. foreign aid as roughly a quarter or more of the federal budget (commonly giving figures around 20–30% or even higher), which matches the claim that many citizens think it is a quarter or a third. These public estimates are much larger than reality: actual U.S. foreign aid spending is only a small fraction of the federal budget (on the order of about 1% or less), so the surveys genuinely show substantial overestimation.

claim: Says critics who say he cut Medicaid are wrong; his budget added $1.2 billion to the program
rationale: The statement is not verifiable as presented because it omits who "he" is and which budget or year is meant; budget claims hinge on specific enacted documents. Whether Medicaid was "cut" or had $1.2 billion added depends on accounting conventions (one‑time vs ongoing funds, federal matches, transfers and program changes), so the assertion cannot be confirmed without those details.

claim: Says "FBI and Texas State Police are both confirming that Raymond Peter Littleberry, the man accused of shooting up a Texas church, was an avid atheist on the payroll of the Democrat National Committee."
rationale: This claim is false. There are no publicly available FBI or Texas Department of Public Safety statements confirming a person named Raymond Peter Littleberry as the shooter, nor any official confirmation that the alleged attacker was an "avid atheist" or on the Democratic National Committee payroll. Major news outlets and official press releases do not support these assertions, and the specific employment/motive details appear to be fabricated or spread on social media without evidence.

claim: "Hurricane Irma could be a Category 6 by the time it hits East Coast."
rationale: The Saffir–Simpson Hurricane Wind Scale does not include a Category 6; Category 5 is the highest official rating. While Hurricane Irma could intensify to extremely high wind speeds, it would still be classified as Category 5 rather than a non-existent Category 6.

claim: "The forest fires were so grotesque last year that we had the worst air in the world in Washington."
rationale: The statement is vague and unverified as written because it doesn't specify which 'Washington' (state or D.C.) or which year. While Western U.S. wildfire smoke has produced short periods when cities in Washington state were ranked among the worst in the world for air quality, that is episodic and depends on a specific date; the blanket claim that 'last year' Washington had the worst air in the world cannot be confirmed without a precise timeframe and location. Therefore the broad assertion is not supported as stated.

claim: Says Gov. Tony Evers "tried to make us pay even more at the pump by hiking the gas tax."
rationale: The claim implies Gov. Tony Evers enacted or successfully raised the gas tax; that is incorrect. While Evers has proposed increases or indexing of Wisconsin's gas tax in budget plans, those proposals were policy proposals that the Republican-controlled legislature did not enact into law. The statement is misleading because proposing a change is not the same as hiking the tax for consumers.

claim: As Massachusetts governor, Mitt Romney used a line-item veto to cut "millions of dollars for firefighting equipment," including firefighters' "coats, pants, helmets and boots."
rationale: As Massachusetts governor Romney did use his line-item veto authority to remove millions in municipal earmarks that included a roughly $3 million appropriation described as for "firefighting equipment." Critics at the time specifically said the cut would eliminate purchases of protective gear such as coats, pants, helmets and boots; Romney defended the vetoes as targeting wasteful earmarks and said localities could reallocate funds. The basic claim about using a veto to cut millions that included firefighting equipment is accurate, though exact items and circumstances were disputed.

claim: Black cats in Vietnam are being killed and consumed as a COVID-19 cure.
rationale: There is no reliable evidence that Vietnamese authorities or any widespread groups have been killing and consuming black cats as a COVID-19 cure. Reputable fact-checkers, news outlets, and statements from local officials and animal-welfare groups found the story to be a rumor or isolated anecdote rather than a documented, countrywide practice promoted as a cure. The claim amplifies unverified social-media reports and cultural stereotypes rather than verified facts.

claim: In Texas, "the No. 1 name for new male babies — many of whom will vote one day — is Jose."
rationale: State and national baby-name data (e.g., Social Security Administration state rankings) do not show Jose as the No. 1 male baby name in Texas in recent years; names like Liam and Noah have generally been the most popular. The claim as stated (without a year or subgroup) is therefore incorrect.

claim: "Here are the facts: there is no massive wave of migrants pouring into California. Overall immigrant apprehensions on the border last year were as low as they’ve been in nearly 50 years (and 85 percent of the apprehensions occurred outside of California)."
rationale: The claim is inaccurate because official U.S. Customs and Border Protection data show migrant encounters/apprehensions in recent years (notably FY2022–FY2023) were near multi-decade highs, not “as low as they’ve been in nearly 50 years.” It is true that the majority of border apprehensions occur outside California (most are in Texas and Arizona sectors), but that fact does not make the overall ‘low apprehensions’ statement correct.

claim: "In the last several months, the Biden administration has released over 7,000 illegal aliens who were COVID positive just in one Texas city." Biden's border policies are "endangering not just the people of Texas, but people all across the country."
rationale: Multiple fact‑checks and official data do not support the specific numeric claim that the Biden administration released over 7,000 COVID‑positive migrants in a single Texas city in recent months. Federal agencies (CBP/HHS) publish migrant processing and health‑screening protocols and reported infection counts that are far lower and do not corroborate such a large, localized release; the second sentence is an opinion about policy effects, not a verifiable factual claim tied to the numeric assertion.

claim: "Before this law was passed, Americans were told they could keep their current health care plans. After it became law, the administration issued regulations stating nearly half of Americans would lose their current plan."
rationale: The administration did not issue a regulation saying nearly half of all Americans would lose their plans. President Obama did say 'you can keep your plan,' and many individual-market, noncompliant plans were later cancelled or not renewed, but official estimates and guidance referred to portions of the individual insurance market in some states — not 'nearly half of Americans' overall. The claim conflates different markets and overstates what administration projections actually said.

claim: Photo shows Barack Obama and George Clooney in a compromising situation with a child.
rationale: There is no credible evidence or reputable reporting that a legitimate photograph exists showing Barack Obama and George Clooney in a compromising situation with a child. Such viral images involving public figures are frequently manipulated, miscaptioned, or deepfakes. Given the absence of verification by reliable news organizations and the implausibility of such an event going unreported, the claim is false.

claim: Says Steph Curry decided to split with Nike because the company wouldn’t allow him to write Bible scriptures in his shoes.
rationale: This claim is false. Stephen Curry did not 'split with Nike' because Nike refused to allow Bible scriptures on his shoes; Curry has been publicly associated with Under Armour since signing with them in 2013, and while he has frequently expressed his Christian faith on apparel, there is no credible reporting or evidence that Nike barred scripture or that such a dispute caused any breakup.

claim: "Ohio companies export more goods and services globally than 41 other states."
rationale: The claim is imprecise and cannot be verified as stated: rankings of state exports vary by year and whether you count goods only or goods plus services. While Ohio is frequently a top‑10 goods exporter, state‑level services exports are reported unevenly and some annual datasets place Ohio near but not necessarily above 41 other states. Without a specific year and data source the blanket statement is not reliably true.

claim: "Colorado school forces students to wear hijabs."
rationale: There are no credible reports or evidence that any Colorado public school system has a policy that forces students to wear hijabs. U.S. public schools generally cannot require students to adopt specific religious clothing, and policies more commonly protect the right to wear religious head coverings rather than mandate them. Isolated voluntary cultural activities or rules at private religious schools may be misreported as mandates.

claim: Teachers "are working their third consecutive year -- some longer than that -- without salary increases."
rationale: The claim is presented without any geographic or temporal context, so it cannot be broadly true: teacher salary change history varies widely by state, district and country. While many teachers in some districts experienced multi-year pay freezes during and after the pandemic, others received raises or cost‑of‑living adjustments within the past three years. Because the statement is absolute and unspecified, it overgeneralizes and is not verifiably true as written.

claim: Says of Gov. Tony Evers and 2020 violence in Kenosha after the police shooting of Jacob Blake: "It took the loss of lives before help finally came."
rationale: The statement that Gov. Tony Evers only provided help after lives were lost implies he withheld assistance until after the killings in Kenosha; contemporaneous timelines and later fact-checks found that state resources and National Guard mobilization occurred on the same day as the unrest and were the subject of disputed timing and local requests. Claims framed as a simple ‘it took the loss of lives before help finally came’ ignore the more complex timeline and the role of local authorities in requesting and coordinating deployments. As a result, the blanket assertion is misleading.

claim: Says that in Texas, it’s "already illegal to enter a bathroom to harm someone."
rationale: Texas law already criminalizes assault, sexual assault, burglary, trespass and related offenses, so entering a bathroom with the intent to harm someone would be prosecutable under those statutes. No separate bathroom-specific statute is required for such conduct to be illegal.

claim: The polls "show over half of Americans identify themselves as being pro-life."
rationale: The statement is an overbroad generalization. Major, reputable national polls (Gallup, Pew Research Center, etc.) in recent years have generally shown either a near-even split or a plurality identifying as pro-choice rather than a clear majority identifying as pro-life; while some individual polls or question wordings can produce >50% pro-life, that is not the consistent, broad finding across polls.

claim: Says George Patton said, "Politicians are the lowest form of life on earth. Liberal Democrats are the lower form of politicians."
rationale: There is no credible evidence in Patton’s published speeches, letters, or reputable quote collections that he ever made this statement; the phrasing and partisan reference (“Liberal Democrats”) appears anachronistic and politically motivated. Fact-checkers and historians have flagged this quote as a later fabrication or misattribution rather than something Patton actually said.

claim: "Only Reuters" reported that the doctor who detected the omicron variant said its symptoms are "very mild."
rationale: The claim is false. Multiple news organizations (e.g., BBC, AP, CNN, Guardian and others) reported statements from South African doctors, including Dr. Angelique Coetzee, characterizing Omicron cases as mild or with mild symptoms; it was not exclusive to Reuters. Reporting varied in wording and attribution, but the claim of exclusivity is incorrect.

claim: "7 out of 10 Oregon families living in poverty have at least one parent who works."
rationale: The claim is imprecise and likely misleading. Public reports that cite a '7 in 10' figure typically refer to Oregon children in poverty living in households with at least one working parent in a specific year or under a particular definition, not unqualified 'Oregon families' across all timeframes. Without a clear source, timeframe, and definition of 'families' the statement as given cannot be accepted as fact.

claim: Of six Rhode Island tax-credit programs worth about $35 million, "three companies got 90 percent of that -- CVS and two companies not even located in the state of Rhode Island."
rationale: I cannot verify the specific numeric claim that three companies (CVS and two out-of-state firms) received 90% of about $35 million across six Rhode Island tax-credit programs. Public tax-credit award records typically show multiple recipients and such concentration would be unusual and should be corroborated by the state's published award data; without confirming documentation the claim appears unsupported. The statement also conflates program totals, recipients and location of headquarters in a way that can mislead.

claim: Says Aaron Rodgers "is not the highest tax rate payer" in Wisconsin, it's "the single mom getting 24 grand in benefits with two kids who will lose 80 cents on the dollar if she goes and takes a job."
rationale: I found no reliable record of Aaron Rodgers making that quoted policy claim about Wisconsin’s highest-rate payer being a single mom on $24,000 in benefits who would lose 80 cents on the dollar. The wording matches a common political talking point about effective marginal tax rates that is frequently used by politicians and commentators and appears to be a likely misattribution. Without verifiable sourcing tying the quote to Rodgers, the claim should be treated as false.

claim: "The U.S. spends more money on its military than the 16 biggest military budgets in the world" combined.
rationale: This is false. Reliable defense-spending tallies (e.g., SIPRI/annual defense budgets) put the U.S. military budget in the roughly $800–900 billion range, while the combined total of the next 16 largest military budgets exceeds that amount. Thus the U.S. does not spend more than the 16 biggest other military budgets combined.

claim: "Flip Flop! After opposing term limits for decades, Adam Putnam adopts Donald Trump and Ron DeSantis’ position."
rationale: The statement is misleading and lacks verifiable specifics. Public reporting and Putnam’s record do not show a clear, decades-long uniform opposition followed by a single definitive switch to the identical term‑limits stance of Trump and DeSantis; the claim conflates different kinds of term‑limit proposals and uses vague language like “adopts.” Without a concrete policy text or timestamp, the allegation of a clear flip‑flop is not supported.

claim: Proposition 2 on November’s Texas ballot "does not cost state taxpayers any money."
rationale: The statement is misleading. The amendment on the ballot authorizes the legislature to provide property-tax exemptions (e.g., for surviving spouses of first responders); that change would reduce local property tax revenue and could have indirect fiscal effects, and while the amendment itself does not automatically create a direct line-item state payment, the Legislature could choose to provide state reimbursements or other offsets. Therefore claiming it “does not cost state taxpayers any money” as an absolute fact is incorrect.

claim: RNC version of a Hillary Clinton valentine: "Roses are red, violets are blue, I'll raise your taxes and there is nothing you can do."
rationale: There is no reliable evidence that the Republican National Committee officially produced or distributed a Hillary Clinton “valentine” with that exact wording. While anti-Clinton valentines and memes circulated online during the campaign, those appear to be user‑generated or from other partisan sources rather than an RNC-issued item, so the specific attribution to the RNC is likely incorrect or unverified.

claim: "A Florida judge ruled parts of Obamacare unconstitutional."
rationale: In 2011 U.S. District Judge Roger Vinson (Northern District of Florida) ruled that the ACA’s individual mandate was unconstitutional. Other judges in various jurisdictions also struck parts of the law in separate suits; however the Supreme Court subsequently addressed the mandate in NFIB v. Sebelius (2012) and reached a different ruling on its constitutionality under Congress’s taxing power.

claim: "Ten retired nuns were barred from voting in the 2008 Indiana Democratic primary."
rationale: I find no reliable contemporaneous reporting or reputable fact-check that corroborates a verified incident in which exactly ten retired nuns were barred from voting in the 2008 Indiana Democratic primary. Sensational anecdotes about small groups of voters being turned away circulated in various forms, but those accounts were unverified or mischaracterized and not supported by mainstream news or official election records.

claim: "Biden says he doesn’t need voters to get elected."
rationale: There is no credible record of President Biden saying he doesn’t need voters to get elected; his public remarks and campaign activity consistently solicit votes and emphasize voter support. The claim appears to be a distortion, out-of-context snippet, or satire rather than an accurate quotation of a verified statement.

claim: Says Rick Scott "didn’t even come to his own education summit. But he did take time to go to the tea party convention the same week."
rationale: I could not verify the assertion that Florida Gov. Rick Scott skipped “his own education summit” while attending a Tea Party convention the same week. Contemporary reporting and public schedules do not corroborate a clear, documented instance matching that precise claim, and the statement appears to conflate events without specific dates. Because the claim is specific but lacks verifiable sourcing, it is treated as false pending concrete evidence.

claim: Ninety percent of the job growth in Virginia has been in the private sector.
rationale: The claim gives no timeframe or source, so it is not a verifiable universal fact. Employment shares depend on the specific period and data source (BLS or Virginia Employment Commission), and while much job growth in Virginia has typically been in the private sector, the precise share fluctuates and cannot be confirmed as exactly 90% without a cited period. Therefore I judge the blanket claim to be unsupported as stated.

claim: "My opponent, in 2008, had contributions investigated by the federal government."
rationale: The claim is unverifiable as written because it does not identify who "my opponent" is or provide evidence of a 2008 federal investigation into contributions. Without a named individual and supporting public records (e.g., DOJ or FBI statements, indictments, or news reports from 2008), the assertion cannot be confirmed. It may be true for some specific people, but as a general unqualified statement it is unsubstantiated.

claim: "The majority of my contributions have been from private individuals" giving $125 on average, "not from PACs, not from groups."
rationale: The claim cannot be verified from the information provided — asserting a majority of contributions are from private individuals averaging $125 (and not from PACs or groups) requires examination of campaign finance reports. Without the speaker, timeframe, or supporting FEC/campaign disclosure data, the statement is unsubstantiated. Because verification is not possible here, I treat the claim as false.

claim: "Individuals and small businesses will be hit by increases in health insurance premiums as high as 39 percent."
rationale: The statement presents a sweeping, source-free prediction that individuals and small businesses "will be hit" with premium increases "as high as 39 percent," but premium changes are model- and policy-specific and no authoritative, general projection supports a universal 39% increase. Nonpartisan analyses (e.g., CBO, HHS) produce widely varying estimates tied to particular proposals and markets; isolated studies or worst-case scenarios can show large percentage changes in narrow circumstances, but that does not validate the broad, unconditional claim.

claim: Says Kurt Schrader voted to cut $500 billion from Medicare, threatening "thousands of Oregon seniors and their access to their current coverage."
rationale: There is no clear record that Rep. Kurt Schrader cast a vote to “cut $500 billion from Medicare.” Schrader, a Democrat, voted against high‑profile Republican repeal bills that critics said would cut or restructure federal health programs, and no specific roll call shows him voting for a measure that explicitly cut Medicare by $500 billion. The claim appears to conflate or mischaracterize budget reconciliation language or separate proposals rather than a direct Schrader vote to cut Medicare by that amount.

claim: Says Bernie Sanders "wants higher standards for toy guns than real guns."
rationale: Bernie Sanders's public positions call for stricter regulation of real firearms—universal background checks, bans on assault weapons and so-called 'ghost guns'—not looser standards for real guns compared with toy guns. There is no credible evidence he said he wants higher regulatory standards for toy guns than for real firearms; the claim appears to be a misleading characterization by critics or opponents.

claim: "Obama administration kept illegal Mexican kids in detention camps as ‘experiment’"
rationale: There is no credible evidence that the Obama administration intentionally kept Mexican (or other) children in detention camps as an ‘experiment.’ While the Obama years saw detention of migrants and use of HHS/ORR shelters and family detention (notably during the 2014 surge), these actions were immigration enforcement and care-placement responses debated on legal and humanitarian grounds, not documented human-subject experiments. Assertions that it was an ‘experiment’ are unsupported and appear to arise from misinterpretations or partisan claims rather than verified government policy or peer-reviewed findings.

claim: "The pope and Donald Trump and Tammy Baldwin all agree" on eliminating the "carried-interest" tax break.
rationale: This claim is misleading. Senator Tammy Baldwin has supported closing the carried-interest tax loophole, but Pope Francis has not specifically endorsed changing U.S. carried-interest rules—his public comments focus broadly on inequality and tax justice, not that technical provision. Donald Trump’s public positions have been inconsistent and do not constitute a clear, documented agreement with Baldwin and the Pope on eliminating carried interest.

claim: Says U.S. Rep. Sean Duffy is among seven "Tea Party freshmen" who "spent an average of $15,000 on cars for themselves."
rationale: The claim is misleading. While some 2010 freshman Republicans had campaign committees that purchased vehicles, there is no clear, credible evidence that Rep. Sean Duffy was specifically one of seven “Tea Party freshmen” who personally spent an average of $15,000 on cars for themselves; media fact-checks have found such formulations conflate committee purchases and personal use and misstate averages. The statement mixes categories and implies personal spending that filings and reporting do not substantiate.

claim: "We do not have an overcrowding problem. As a matter of fact, Rhode Island has one of the lowest incarceration rates in the country."
rationale: The claim mixes a true-sounding fact and a false categorical denial. It is true that Rhode Island’s imprisonment rate has generally been among the lower U.S. states in national datasets, but it is inaccurate to assert there is no overcrowding: at various times Rhode Island’s prisons and local jails have reported capacity issues and populations exceeding facility capacity. Because overcrowding is facility- and time-specific, the blanket denial is unsupported.

claim: The EPA "wants to hire 230,000 new government regulators that will cost the taxpayer $21 billion."
rationale: This claim is inaccurate. The EPA’s workforce is on the order of tens of thousands (roughly ~14,000 employees), and there has been no credible announcement that the agency plans to hire 230,000 new regulators or that such a hiring would cost taxpayers $21 billion. The 230,000 figure appears to be a misinterpretation or extrapolation (e.g., multiplying a large number by an average salary) rather than an actual EPA hiring proposal.

claim: Says in "our region," 2011 was worst drought year ever recorded.
rationale: The statement is unverifiable as presented because 'our region' is undefined and drought severity is location- and metric-specific. Although 2011 was the worst drought on record in some places (for example, large parts of Texas experienced their most severe recorded drought in 2011), many regions have had worse droughts in other years, so the blanket claim cannot be accepted without a specified region and metric.

claim: If you paid rent in March or April, "they got to give" you your money back.
rationale: This is a blanket claim that is not true in general. There is no universal law that requires landlords or landlords/third parties to refund rent simply because it was paid in March or April; whether money must be returned depends on specific laws, emergency programs, lease terms, or court orders in the relevant jurisdiction. In most places, eviction moratoria and relief programs delayed evictions or provided aid but did not automatically mandate blanket refunds of rent already paid.
