claim: Says in the governor’s proposed budget "the use of that, what is called one-shots, is a 500 percent increase over the last Corzine budget."
rationale: The statement asserts a precise 500% rise in ‘one-shot’ items versus the last Corzine budget but there is no verifiable, widely reported data confirming that specific percentage. Comparing 'one-shots' requires clear definitions and itemized budget figures across the two budgets; absent that context the 500% figure appears to be an exaggeration or miscalculation.

claim: "So that 2005 energy bill was a big step backwards on the path to clean, renewable energy. That's why I voted against it."
rationale: The claim combines a subjective judgment about the 2005 Energy Policy Act and an asserted motive for a vote; both are not conclusively true. The 2005 law contained measures that supported renewables (tax incentives, R&D and loan guarantees) alongside provisions favoring fossil fuels and nuclear, so labeling it unequivocally a “big step backwards” is debatable. The stated vote motive cannot be verified without identifying the speaker and their public explanation of the vote.

claim: "Barack Obama’s real father is Communist Party propagandist Frank Marshall Davis."
rationale: Contemporary records, genealogical research, and Barack Obama’s own accounts establish his biological father as Barack Obama Sr., a Kenyan economist; there is no credible evidence that Frank Marshall Davis was his father. The claim originated as a conspiracy theory and has been repeatedly debunked by biographers and public records (birth certificate, family histories, and interviews).

claim: Says Jennifer Aniston said, "Me and all the Trump supporter celebrities decide to make a company named ‘celebrities for Trump’"
rationale: There is no credible evidence or primary-source interview showing Jennifer Aniston said this; the phrasing is inconsistent with her public statements. Aniston has not publicly endorsed Trump and has been associated with support for Democratic candidates, so the quote is almost certainly a fabrication or misattribution.

claim: "This rule could prevent children under 18 from using such tools as a power screwdriver, a milking machine or something as simple as a wheelbarrow on the family farm . . . "
rationale: The statement is unsubstantiated as written: it names no specific rule and overstates typical scope of child-labor restrictions. U.S. federal child-labor regulations and common proposed rules target clearly hazardous equipment (e.g., tractors, certain power-driven machinery) and often preserve exemptions for children working on a parent-operated farm; everyday items like wheelbarrows and routine milking duties are generally not banned for under‑18s on family farms. Without a cited, concrete regulation that explicitly bans those ordinary tools, the claim is misleading.

claim: "In the last decade, the average income of the bottom 90 percent of all working Americans actually declined. The top 1 percent saw their income rise by an average of more than a quarter of a million dollars each."
rationale: The statement is imprecise and inconsistent with publicly available income series. Over the 2010s (the usual ‘last decade’ reference) IRS/CBO/Piketty‑Saez and BLS data show real earnings and household income for most of the bottom 90% were broadly flat to modestly higher, not a clear decline, while the top 1% did see substantial gains. Whether the top 1% rose by “more than a quarter of a million dollars each” depends on the exact years, unit (person vs. household), and measure (taxable income vs. market income), so the absolute figure in the claim is misleading.

claim: Democrats "want to tax your retirement funds to pay for their new trillion dollar power grab."
rationale: The claim is a broad, partisan mischaracterization. There is no evidence of a unified Democratic plan to broadly "tax your retirement funds" to finance a single "trillion dollar power grab." While some Democratic proposals target higher taxes on wealthy individuals, capital gains, or limit certain tax advantages for high-income households, they do not amount to a party-wide proposal to seize ordinary retirement accounts to pay for a trillion-dollar program.

claim: The health care law was "a 2,733-page bill! . . . No amendments!"
rationale: The claim is misleading. Page counts for the Affordable Care Act vary by how the law is printed and what is included, and the statute was altered by the separate Health Care and Education Reconciliation Act during the enactment process, so it was not a single unamended 2,733‑page bill.

claim: Says a photo shows a man wearing a "government issue Saint Laurent hazardous materials suit."
rationale: The phrase "government issue Saint Laurent hazardous materials suit" is internally inconsistent and unsupported: Saint Laurent is a luxury fashion brand, while government-issued hazardous materials (hazmat) suits are standardized PPE produced by industrial manufacturers and are not branded as high-fashion. There is no credible evidence that a government supplies Saint Laurent-branded hazmat suits, so the claim that a photo shows such an item is false.

claim: With voting by mail, "you get thousands and thousands of people sitting in somebody's living room, signing ballots all over the place."
rationale: This claim exaggerates and presents an unproven, widespread pattern. Multiple studies, bipartisan audits, and prosecutions have found mail-ballot fraud to be extremely rare, and there is no documented evidence of thousands of people routinely signing ballots in private homes. Mail voting systems use procedures (signature checks, chain-of-custody, ballot tracking, and limits on assistance) that make large-scale organized signing unlikely, though isolated improper incidents have occurred.

claim: "As the election tracker FiveThirtyEight has reported, whoever wins Pennsylvania will be our next President."
rationale: The claim presents an absolute statement that FiveThirtyEight reported that the winner of Pennsylvania will necessarily be the next president. FiveThirtyEight produces probabilistic forecasts and sometimes identifies specific tipping‑point states in particular election years, but it does not make a universal rule that whoever wins Pennsylvania will always win the presidency. Without a specific election context this assertion is misleading.

claim: In 2013, under a Democratic Senate, "a majority of the Senate voted in favor of" gun-related legislation sponsored by Republican Sens. Chuck Grassley and Ted Cruz, "but the Democrats filibustered it."
rationale: This mixes up the well‑known 2013 vote on background checks. The high‑profile measure was the Toomey‑Manchin (R‑D) background‑check proposal, which received 54 votes but failed to reach the 60‑vote cloture threshold; it was effectively blocked by the Senate minority, not a Democratic filibuster. Chuck Grassley and Ted Cruz were not the sponsors of that measure, and Democrats as majority did not filibuster it.

claim: Says U.S. Rep. John Faso "voted for an age tax on seniors."
rationale: The statement is vague and broad: there is no single federal measure officially called an “age tax” and I find no verifiable record that Rep. John Faso cast a vote explicitly to enact an “age tax on seniors.” Political ads have used the phrase rhetorically to describe various GOP votes (for example on tax reform or health funding) that critics say would harm older Americans, but without a specific bill or provision the claim is not verifiable as stated. Because the phrase is subjective and lacks a concrete legislative reference, the claim as presented is misleading.

claim: Scott Maddox is a "lobbyist."
rationale: Scott Maddox is primarily known as a former Tallahassee mayor and Florida Democratic Party figure who was convicted in a corruption probe; available public reporting and records identify him as a politician/consultant involved in those cases rather than as a formally registered lobbyist. Calling him a "lobbyist" without evidence of registration or formal lobbying employment is misleading.

claim: Ninety-seven percent of Americans do not receive subsidies for health care under the Affordable Care Act.
rationale: Only a small share of the U.S. population receives ACA premium tax credits — roughly 10–15 million people in recent years out of roughly 330–335 million Americans, meaning about 3–5% receive those marketplace subsidies and about 95–97% do not. The claim’s 97% figure is a reasonable rounding of that relationship.

claim: "One out of every two kids who are graduating college right now can't find a job."
rationale: This is false. Official labor statistics and higher-education reports show unemployment among recent college graduates is far below 50%; while some graduates face underemployment or difficulty finding jobs in their field, a majority of new college graduates are employed or in further study. The claim appears to conflate severe joblessness with broader measures of underemployment or temporary transition periods.

claim: "20,000 Kansans lost their health insurance because of (Obamacare)."
rationale: There is no verified evidence that exactly 20,000 Kansans definitively 'lost their health insurance' solely because of the Affordable Care Act. While some Kansas plans were cancelled in 2013–14 as insurers adjusted to ACA standards, state-level counts vary and cancellations do not necessarily equal people becoming uninsured (many enrolled in replacement plans, exchange coverage, or Medicaid). The claim gives a precise causal number without supporting context or source.

claim: "According to (Barack) Obama’s newest unconstitutionally enacted law, health care professionals are now required to violate HIPAA privacy laws and submit medical data to the government," which is "then used as justification for gun confiscation."
rationale: This is false. There is no law enacted by President Obama that requires health care professionals to violate HIPAA and submit patients' medical records to the government for the purpose of gun confiscation. HIPAA remains in force and permits disclosures only under narrow, established exceptions (e.g., court orders, imminent threat reporting, or statutorily required reporting of certain mental‑health adjudications), and Obama‑era measures did not create a blanket mandate to turn over medical data to justify mass gun seizures.

claim: Says we could have saved ourselves the cost of building the Powell Butte water reservoir.
rationale: The assertion that the cost of building the Powell Butte reservoir could have been avoided is unsupported as stated. Whether the project was avoidable depends on technical, regulatory, and planning analyses (alternatives, risk to supply, seismic safety, legal requirements) that are not provided, so the blanket claim cannot be verified. Without evidence of a viable, equivalent alternative that was overlooked, the statement is not factual.

claim: Under President George W. Bush, "we added $4.9 trillion to the debt. Under President Obama … we’ve added $6.5 trillion to the debt."
rationale: The numbers are misleading. The $4.9 trillion figure roughly matches the increase in gross federal debt from Jan 2001 to Jan 2009, but the claim that Obama added $6.5 trillion is too low for his full two terms: depending on the exact start/end dates gross federal debt rose by roughly $8–9 trillion under Obama. Different measures (gross debt vs. debt held by the public) and picking nonstandard cutoffs can produce $6.5 trillion, so the statement as presented is not an accurate, unqualified comparison.

claim: A video shows "massive explosion as Ukraine destroyed 280 Russian tanks to pieces using U.S. Javelin missiles."
rationale: The claim is implausible and unsupported: Javelin missiles are single-target anti-armor weapons and would not produce a single ‘massive explosion’ that destroys 280 tanks at once. There are no credible reports or evidence that Ukraine destroyed 280 Russian tanks in a single strike using Javelins, and large conflagrations in videos are more consistent with ammunition or fuel depot explosions or misattributed footage. The scale and logistics (number of missiles required, targeting, and supply) make the specific assertion highly unlikely.

claim: Claims Joe Biden said "coal is more dangerous than terrorists."
rationale: There is no well-documented, credible record or transcript showing Joe Biden saying the exact line 'coal is more dangerous than terrorists.' The claim appears to be a misquotation or conflation with generalized statements about coal’s public-health harms; public officials and commentators have noted coal-related deaths from pollution, but Biden has not been reliably shown to have made that specific remark.

claim: "Thom Tillis cut almost $500 million from education."
rationale: The claim is imprecise and misleading: there is no clear, single enacted action by Thom Tillis personally that ‘cut almost $500 million from education.’ Budget changes in North Carolina during his time as state House Speaker included education reductions, but totals depend on which years, which programs (K–12 vs higher ed), and accounting methods are used, and budget decisions were made by the full legislature and governor. Because different analyses reach different totals and attribution is collective, the blanket claim is not supported as stated.

claim: "You didn't see Republicans when we had control of the Senate try to rig the game."
rationale: The claim is inaccurate: Republican Senate leaders have used procedural maneuvers widely described as tilting the rules in their favor. Examples include refusing to hold hearings for President Obama's 2016 Supreme Court nominee Merrick Garland and invoking the "nuclear option" in 2017 to lower the confirmation threshold for Supreme Court nominees, among other confirmation and rule strategies. Thus the blanket statement that you didn't see Republicans try to "rig the game" is false.

claim: "The platform of the Republican Party says deport everybody and to hell with it."
rationale: The Republican Party platform advocates stricter border security, interior enforcement, and removal of certain undocumented immigrants, but it does not literally state "deport everybody and to hell with it." The claim is a crude paraphrase and exaggeration of platform positions rather than an accurate quote of the platform text.

claim: "You can’t get on an airplane, but more than 2,000 people on that list have been able to buy a gun."
rationale: Contemporaneous reporting and government statements from the early-to-mid 2010s established that thousands of names in the federal terrorist watchlist databases had not been automatically shared with the FBI’s firearms background-check system, and roughly 2,000+ watchlisted records were found to have matched NICS checks and resulted in gun sales. The statement captures that people prevented from flying (or on related watchlists) nonetheless appeared in records that allowed them to pass background checks and purchase firearms. The exact count and which specific list (No‑Fly List vs broader Terrorist Screening Database) depends on the time and definition used.

claim: "Measles is one of the most common causes of child blindness worldwide."
rationale: Measles infection can cause corneal ulceration and scarring (often worsened by vitamin A deficiency), which has long been a major cause of childhood blindness in low-income countries. International health agencies have identified measles as an important and historically common cause of pediatric blindness worldwide, especially where vaccination and vitamin A programs are weak. However, widespread measles immunization has substantially reduced its contribution in many regions.

claim: Says Jon Ossoff is "a socialist."
rationale: Labeling Jon Ossoff as "a socialist" is inaccurate. He is a mainstream Democratic politician who has not identified as a socialist, is not affiliated with socialist organizations, and has opposed major policy proposals commonly associated with democratic socialism (e.g., Medicare for All).

claim: Says the Obamas are connected to the Varsity Blues college admissions scandal.
rationale: There is no credible evidence connecting Barack or Michelle Obama to the 2019 Varsity Blues college admissions scandal. The federal investigation, indictments, and subsequent prosecutions named specific parents and facilitators (e.g., Rick Singer, Lori Loughlin, Felicity Huffman) and did not include the Obamas; media fact-checks have debunked social-media claims tying them to the scheme.

claim: Says coronavirus is just "the damn flu."
rationale: The claim that coronavirus is "just the damn flu" is false. SARS-CoV-2 (which causes COVID-19) is a different virus family than influenza, has produced higher population-level hospitalization and mortality in many waves, and can cause distinct complications (including long COVID) and different patterns of transmission. Public-health measures, vaccines, and clinical management for COVID-19 also differ from seasonal influenza.

claim: Says Sen. Chuck Schumer in 2014 "helped put together and signed a $25 billion deal to fund a border wall" and now opposes Trump's $5 billion request for a border wall "just because he's a Republican." ​
rationale: There was no $25 billion bipartisan deal in 2014 that Sen. Schumer ‘helped put together and signed’ to fund a border wall; the major Senate immigration effort around 2013–2014 focused on broader border security measures but did not authorize a $25 billion wall. Schumer has publicly opposed portions of President Trump’s border wall funding requests, but the claim that he now opposes a $5 billion request ‘just because he’s a Republican’ asserts a partisan motive that cannot be verified from the public record. Overall the factual elements about a $25 billion 2014 wall deal and the stated motive are incorrect or unproven.

claim: Says Sen. Sherrod Brown "voted to block American energy production and increase energy taxes."
rationale: The statement is misleading. Senator Sherrod Brown has not cast a Senate vote that explicitly 'blocks American energy production'; he has voted for climate and clean-energy legislation (notably the Inflation Reduction Act) that expands clean-energy incentives and includes targeted fees or pollution charges, but these are not a direct ban on U.S. energy production or a blanket "energy tax". Without a specific bill or vote cited, the broad claim is inaccurate.

claim: The United States is "about to have the smallest Army since before WWII, the smallest Navy since WWI and the smallest Air Force ever."
rationale: The claim is vague and misleading because it does not specify which metric (personnel, ships, aircraft) or the exact time frame. Historical records show that at various points (interwar Navy years, early Air Force, and pre‑WWII Army) branch sizes were smaller by some measures, and recent counts do not unambiguously establish that all three services are simultaneously at their absolute historic lows. Without a precise metric and date the blanket statement is not supported.

claim: "Florida is now the No. 1 state in the country for automobile accident fraud."
rationale: The statement is presented as an absolute, current ranking but lacks a cited timeframe or metric. While insurance-industry and law-enforcement reports have identified Florida as a frequent hotspot for staged auto-accident schemes and high fraud activity in some years, national rankings vary by metric and year, so the unqualified claim that Florida is now unequivocally 'No. 1' is unsupported without a specific source.

claim: The last private rocket launch "cost $80 million. If the government did it, the same thing would have cost probably 40 or 50 times that amount of money. I mean, literally."
rationale: The statement combines a plausible single-number estimate for a private launch (~$60–80M is in the ballpark for some commercial orbital launches) with an unsupported and extreme claim that a government version would cost 40–50× more. While some government programs (e.g., SLS) have per-launch costs in the billions, comparable government-contracted launches or rideshares often cost in the same order of magnitude as commercial prices, so a blanket 40–50× multiplier is inaccurate and overgeneralized.

claim: "If it weren’t for me … (illegal immigration) wouldn’t even be a big subject."
rationale: The claim attributes the prominence of illegal immigration solely to a single individual, which is not supported by historical and political evidence. Illegal immigration has been a major political topic in the U.S. and other countries for decades—long before any single contemporary figure—driven by law, economic forces, policy debates, migration flows, and media attention. While a high‑profile person can raise visibility, it is implausible that the topic "wouldn't even be a big subject" without them.

claim: "The Democrat plan would just obliterate Medicare and terminate Medicare Advantage ... seniors who have been paying for this for years (and) will not be taken care of anymore."
rationale: The claim is a sweeping mischaracterization. There is no single "Democrat plan" that universally abolishes Medicare and ends Medicare Advantage; mainstream Democratic proposals (for example the Biden platform) explicitly preserve and often aim to strengthen Medicare and allow Medicare Advantage to continue. While some progressive Democrats have proposed Medicare-for-All variants that would restructure how coverage is delivered and could phase out private Medicare Advantage, those are specific proposals, not a party-wide plan, and they still aim to provide coverage rather than leaving seniors uncared for.

claim: The changes to Georgia’s tax and fee structure "is an overall tax cut."
rationale: The claim cannot be verified as an unequivocal overall tax cut without specifying which legislative package, the exact tax and fee changes, and the time frame. Tax and fee adjustments often shift burden between revenue sources and income groups, and fiscal analyses of similar Georgia proposals have sometimes found net revenue-neutral or mixed impacts rather than a clear net cut. Absent a certified fiscal note showing a net reduction in total state and local tax and fee revenue, labeling the changes an "overall tax cut" is unsupported.

claim: Says state Senate President Stephen "Sweeney gave us the nation's highest income tax rates, driving out jobs."
rationale: The claim is incorrect: no evidence that Senate President Stephen Sweeney 'gave' the state the nation's highest income tax rates, and New Jersey has not had the single highest top marginal individual income tax rate in recent years (California has long held the highest top rate). Tax rates are set by the legislature and governor, not a single legislator, and attributing job losses solely to one politician or to a single tax change is an unsupported causal claim.

claim: Before 2005, "the percentage of" Texas high school "students meeting the college readiness standards of the Texas Higher Education Coordinating Board stood at 28% in English and 42% in math. Those figures stood at 65% and 66% in 2013."
rationale: I could not verify the exact percentages claimed and the Texas Higher Education Coordinating Board and state assessment measures changed over the period in question, making direct comparisons uncertain. Publicly available THECB and state reports use different readiness definitions across years, and I find no authoritative source that precisely matches 28% English/42% math pre-2005 and 65%/66% in 2013. Because the metrics and cut scores shifted, the statement appears to conflate different measures and lacks corroboration.

claim: The CDC delivers groceries and cleaning products "twice while you’re in quarantine."
rationale: False. The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention issues guidance on quarantine and how to obtain supplies, but it does not run a program that delivers groceries and cleaning products “twice” to people in quarantine. Practical deliveries are typically arranged by local health departments, community organizations, or commercial services, not the CDC itself.

claim: Says Adam Hasner "gives the wealthy tax breaks worth $250,000 a year but hikes middle class taxes $2,000."
rationale: The claim provides exact distributional numbers without citing a specific tax bill or independent revenue analysis; such precise per-year effects would require a formal tax-modeling study. I am not aware of any verifiable analysis showing Adam Hasner sponsored or enacted a policy that gave the wealthy $250,000 a year in tax cuts while increasing middle‑class taxes by $2,000 annually. Because the statement is highly specific and likely came from a political ad, it appears exaggerated or unsupported.

claim: "Bryce Reeves chaired a group bankrolled by a New York billionaire who fired hundreds of Virginia workers and sent their jobs to China."
rationale: I could not find reliable evidence that Virginia state senator Bryce Reeves chaired any organization that was funded by a named New York billionaire who then fired hundreds of Virginia workers and shipped their jobs to China. Public records and reporting identify Reeves as a state senator who has chaired legislative committees and local groups, but no credible source ties him to the specific claim as stated. Because the claim names no billionaire or organization, it appears to conflate or invent a linkage that is not supported by available information.

claim: Says "$57,000 is the mean [income] in our state" for a family.
rationale: The statement is unverifiable as presented because it omits the state and time period and confuses common measures (official sources typically report median rather than mean). State-level incomes vary widely and many states' published median/mean household incomes differ substantially from $57,000, so the blanket claim is unlikely to be accurate without more context.

claim: "The United States is 65th out of 142 nations and other territories on equal pay."
rationale: The statement is inaccurate as written: there is no widely cited recent index that places the United States exactly 65th out of 142 on “equal pay.” Major measures (e.g., the World Economic Forum’s Global Gender Gap subindices and OECD pay-gap statistics) place the U.S. substantially higher on wage or overall gender-gap measures, and rankings vary by metric and year. Without a specific source and year the claim appears misleading.

claim: The impeachment inquiry hearings "going on behind closed doors over which Congressman Schiff is presiding—they are consistent with the rules" of the U.S. House of Representatives.
rationale: Under House rules and longstanding practice, standing committees may open investigations and take depositions in closed session; the Intelligence Committee, chaired by Rep. Adam Schiff, had been conducting closed-door witness interviews after the Speaker announced an impeachment inquiry. While Republicans disputed the need for a separate floor vote to authorize an inquiry, committee closed-door depositions themselves are permitted under House rules and precedent. Therefore the statement that those closed-door hearings were consistent with House rules is accurate.

claim: "Hillary Clinton invented ISIS with her stupid policies. She is responsible for ISIS."
rationale: The claim is inaccurate. ISIS grew out of the post-2003 Iraqi insurgency and al-Qaeda in Iraq (including leaders like Abu Musab al‑Zarqawi) and was catalyzed by multiple factors such as the 2003 US invasion, sectarian governance in Iraq, and the Syrian civil war; it was not 'invented' by Hillary Clinton. While Clinton supported some policies (for example, as Secretary of State she backed the 2011 Libya intervention) that critics say affected regional stability, assigning sole responsibility to her is historically incorrect and overly simplistic.

claim: Says Abraham Lincoln said, "America will never be destroyed from the outside. If we lose our freedoms it will be because we have destroyed ourselves from within."
rationale: This sentence is widely misattributed to Abraham Lincoln; it cannot be found in his collected speeches, letters, or contemporary records. Modern fact-checking and Lincoln scholarship report no primary-source evidence and show the wording first appearing in much later, 20th-century sources, so attribution to Lincoln is unsupported.

claim: "In the 18th Congressional District, 100% of electric generation comes from coal."
rationale: This categorical claim is almost certainly false. Congressional districts do not operate isolated power systems and electricity generation even in coal‑heavy areas is rarely 100% coal; EIA and grid data show mixes that include natural gas, renewables, nuclear, and imports. Even a district containing coal plants would still draw power from regional grids and typically have at least some non‑coal generation or purchased electricity.

claim: "ISIS is in 32 countries."
rationale: The statement as an absolute fact is not supported by authoritative sources: counts of countries with an ISIS presence vary by definition and over time, and no consensus figure of "32 countries" is widely documented. Credible reports from governments, the UN, and analysts list different numbers of countries with active ISIS affiliates, cells, or influence, and often fewer than 32; the claim likely conflates different metrics (e.g., origins of foreign fighters vs. operational affiliates).

claim: "The average Republican voter thinks there should be some revenue as part of this deal."
rationale: The claim is a broad generalization that lacks a cited poll or definition of “this deal.” Whether the average Republican voter supports revenue as part of a deal depends entirely on the specific proposal, timing, and question wording; without specific survey data you cannot reliably assert it. Because public opinion varies and requires empirical evidence, the claim is not supported.

claim: Says Julie Parrish is "one of Sarah Palin’s mama grizzlies."
rationale: There is no reliable evidence that Sarah Palin designated Oregon state representative Julie Parrish as one of her high-profile 'mama grizzlies.' Palin's 'mama grizzly' label in 2010 was applied publicly to a small set of nationally prominent GOP female challengers, and Parrish is not documented among those endorsed or labeled by Palin. Without contemporary Palin endorsements or publicity linking Parrish to that label, the claim is unsubstantiated.

claim: Georgia’s unemployment rate has exceeded the national rate for 50 consecutive months.
rationale: I cannot confirm the claim and BLS state unemployment series show month-to-month variation; such a continuous 50-month streak would require checking specific monthly Local Area Unemployment Statistics. Historically Georgia’s rate has at times been above and at times below the national rate, so the blanket statement of 50 consecutive months is not reliably supported without a precise date range and data extract.

claim: Says he did not tell former President Barack Obama "don’t go" after Osama bin Laden
rationale: The claim is ambiguous about who “he” refers to and I find no verifiable public record or widely reported quote of a senior official explicitly saying they did not tell President Obama “don’t go” regarding the raid that killed Osama bin Laden. Major accounts of the 2011 operation describe debate among advisers but do not document that specific denial as a notable, sourced statement. Because the speaker and source are unspecified and there is no clear evidence supporting the exact quoted denial, the claim cannot be verified as true.

claim: "The only segment in the beer market that is growing is the craft beer segment."
rationale: This claim is false. While craft beer has been a notable growth area in many markets, other segments — such as premium/mainstream imports, non‑alcoholic/low‑alcohol beer and flavored malt beverages/hard seltzers — have also shown growth in recent years, and trends vary by country and timeframe. Saying craft is the only growing segment ignores these other rising categories and regional differences.

claim: The American Academy of Pediatrics "supports banning guns."
rationale: The American Academy of Pediatrics endorses firearm safety measures—such as physician counseling, safe storage, universal background checks, and restrictions on assault weapons and high-capacity magazines—but it does not call for a wholesale ban on all civilian gun ownership. Describing the AAP as supporting 'banning guns' overstates and mischaracterizes its published policy positions.

claim: Under President Barack Obama’s leadership, "since June 2009, (the auto) industry has added a quarter of a million jobs."
rationale: The claim is misleading and not verifiable as stated because it gives no end date and does not define which parts of the "auto industry" are included. BLS employment series show that motor-vehicle and parts manufacturing recovered substantially after the 2009 trough but gains for manufacturing alone were smaller than 250,000; reaching a +250,000 figure would require combining multiple related sectors (dealers, parts suppliers, services) and depends on the chosen end date. Because the statement omits key context it cannot be taken as a factual standalone claim.

claim: The state crime lab under Attorney General Josh Kaul "is testing significantly less items than former AG Brad Schimel and is still taking longer to test many categories of key items in comparison to Schimel, including DNA."
rationale: The claim is an overbroad characterization. Independent fact-checks and official lab reporting show mixed results: some categories saw fewer items tested or longer turnaround times under Kaul while others (including certain DNA workflows and prioritized forensic tests) improved or were affected by changes in submission policy and staffing, so it is inaccurate to say the lab is universally testing 'significantly less' and 'still taking longer' across many key categories. The truth depends on the specific time period, crime-lab category, and accounting methods used.

claim: "The  firefighters, the policemen and others who supported (Wisconsin Gov. Scott Walker) in his election bid ... don't have to worry about their collective bargaining rights."
rationale: This is misleading. Wisconsin’s 2011 Budget Repair Bill (Act 10) did exempt many police and firefighters from the law’s outright ban on collective bargaining, but other provisions (limits on bargaining scope, required pension/health contributions, and restrictions on union dues/representation mechanics) nonetheless affected public safety workers. Therefore it is incorrect to say they “don’t have to worry” about their collective bargaining rights.

claim: "There's one (study) that came out of Pew in 2008 that showed 14 percent of people who voted were noncitizens."
rationale: No reputable Pew study reports that 14% of people who voted in 2008 were noncitizens. Pew’s investigations of surveys with apparent noncitizen voting found small counts of self-reported noncitizen voters in some datasets (some anomalous samples had high percentages of noncitizens saying they voted), but after correcting for misreporting and survey error Pew estimated the true incidence of noncitizen voting to be near zero, not 14% of all voters. The 14% figure appears to be a misinterpretation or conflation of a problematic subgroup percentage in a small survey, not a finding that 14% of voters were noncitizens.

claim: "We’re spending tremendous amounts of money to educate our kids. In the world, we're No. 1 per pupil by a factor of four."
rationale: The U.S. does spend materially on education, but it is not unambiguously the world’s highest per‑pupil by a factor of four. OECD and international data show the U.S. is among the higher spenders per student but many countries (e.g., Luxembourg, Switzerland, Norway) spend as much or more, and U.S. spending is only roughly 1.3–2× the OECD average and not four times typical high‑income peers. The claim overstates and misframes the comparison without specifying the comparator or education level.

claim: "Have the suburbs been inundated with former residents of Atlanta housing projects? Absolutely not."
rationale: Contemporary research on Atlanta public-housing demolition and relocations shows some residents moved to suburban rentals or used vouchers, but there was not a mass, concentrated exodus that 'inundated' suburbs. Relocations were dispersed across the metropolitan area and many residents stayed in the city or moved to varied neighborhoods, so the categorical claim that suburbs were inundated is inaccurate. The stronger claim — that suburbs were overwhelmed by former project residents — is not supported by available evidence.

claim: Says Harvard scientists say the coronavirus is "spreading so fast that it will infect 70% of humanity this year."
rationale: No credible evidence shows Harvard scientists made the quoted claim that the coronavirus would infect 70% of humanity "this year." Harvard researchers and other epidemiologists warned that, without controls, a large portion of populations could eventually be infected, but they did not state that 70% of the entire world would be infected within a single year. The statement is a mischaracterization of modeling scenarios and lacks attribution to any verified Harvard statement.

claim: "Both Cruz and Rubio are missing the vast majority of their votes."
rationale: This claim is false as stated. Public Senate roll-call records show that Senators Ted Cruz and Marco Rubio vote in the majority of roll calls; neither senator misses the "vast majority" (i.e., over half) of votes in ordinary periods. Without a specific timeframe or definition of "missing" the claim is misleading.

claim: "Ninety percent of people born in the 1940s ended up doing better financially than their parents. But those born in the 1980s, the much-maligned Millennials, have only a 50-50 chance of doing better (financially) than their parents, despite being the best-educated generation in our history."
rationale: The claim gives precise 90% and 50% figures but no single authoritative source supports those exact percentages across broad U.S. cohorts. Scholarly and policy analyses do show that people born in the 1940s experienced unusually large real income and wealth gains relative to their parents, and that many born in the 1980s have weaker chances of surpassing parental economic status, but the exact probabilities depend heavily on whether one measures income or wealth, age of comparison, and sample/methodology — so the quoted figures are overstated and imprecise.

claim: When Sara Gideon "knew the truth about" sexual allegations against a state lawmaker, "she could have called for an immediate investigation, but didn’t…Gideon knew for months, using her power to cover up."
rationale: Available public reporting and official statements do not support the specific allegation that Gideon knowingly concealed sexual‑misconduct allegations and used her power to cover them up for months. News coverage and legislative records indicate complaints were handled through House procedures, and there is no documented evidence that she ordered or executed a deliberate multi‑month cover‑up. The claim asserts knowledge and intent that have not been substantiated by verifiable records or credible reporting.

claim: Says each of the past three years "has been the hottest on record."
rationale: The claim is incorrect: only one year (or in some datasets a tie) can be the single "hottest on record," and recent global temperature analyses show that while the last few years have been among the warmest, they were not each individually the hottest. For example, 2016 and 2020 rank at or near the top (often tied within uncertainty) and 2023 has been reported as the warmest, whereas intervening years such as 2021 and 2022 were very warm but not the single hottest. Thus saying each of the past three years "has been the hottest on record" is misleading and false.

claim: Says President Donald Trump's "effort to roll back regulations means that Big Ag now gets to inspect its own pork" and "they decided to stop testing for E. coli."
rationale: The claim is misleading. The Trump administration did pursue regulatory changes and pilot programs (e.g., expanded industry responsibilities under inspection models), but federal inspectors and FSIS retained regulatory authority rather than letting “Big Ag” wholly inspect its own pork. Similarly, while FSIS adjusted some testing priorities and sampling programs, it did not wholesale stop all E. coli testing of pork; changes were targeted and under agency oversight.

claim: Says Donald Trump’s book "The Art of the Deal" advises: "Never admit defeat. You win. If you don’t win, claim they cheated."
rationale: The exact sentence quoted does not appear in Donald Trump’s 1987 book The Art of the Deal. While the book contains negotiating maxims and boasts about winning, fact-checks and full-text searches of the book show no passage that matches that line; it appears to be a later paraphrase of Trump’s behavior rather than a direct quotation from the book.

claim: "Phony" ballots "were printed without my name on it."
rationale: The assertion is unsubstantiated as stated and lacks verifiable specifics (which election, jurisdiction, or number of ballots). Ballots are produced by election authorities under documented procedures, and there is no credible, widespread evidence that official ballots were printed omitting a major candidate’s name as claimed. Extraordinary claims about ballot fraud require local chain-of-custody evidence and independent audits, which are not provided here.

claim: Says a study indicates up to $8.5 billion in lost GDP and up to 185,000 lost jobs if Texas lawmakers approve a measure limiting transgender bathroom choices.
rationale: I could not find a credible study that specifically projects up to $8.5 billion in lost GDP and up to 185,000 lost jobs for Texas from a restroom/’bathroom bill.’ Major prior economic analyses of similar laws (for example North Carolina’s HB2) estimated losses in the billions but far fewer lost jobs (thousands, not hundreds of thousands). The cited figures appear to be either misremembered, taken out of context, or conflated with other studies or broader nationwide estimates rather than a single Texas-focused study.

claim: Says television host Steve Harvey authored a pro-Trump rant about raccoons and exterminators.
rationale: False. There is no credible evidence that Steve Harvey authored a pro-Trump rant about raccoons and exterminators; the circulating text has been widely misattributed on social media and debunked by fact-checkers. The item appears to originate from anonymous or non-credible sources rather than from Harvey himself or reputable news outlets.

claim: Says Texas ranks among the nation’s top five states for its high school graduation rate.
rationale: Texas has improved its high school graduation rate in recent years but is not generally listed among the nation’s top five states. Federal and state education reports and published rankings typically place northeastern and Midwestern states (e.g., New Jersey, Massachusetts, Iowa) in the top five, while Texas more commonly falls below that threshold. The claim lacks a specific year or source, which would be needed to verify any exceptional single-year ranking.

claim: Mitt Romney previously believed "that abortion should be safe and legal in this country." Now he is "prolife."
rationale: Mitt Romney publicly described himself as supporting legal abortion earlier in his political career (notably during his 1994 Senate campaign) and later changed his position to identify as pro‑life while seeking national office in the 2000s and 2010s. His public statements and campaign platforms show a clear shift from supporting legal abortion to opposing most abortions and emphasizing pro‑life positions, though his precise policy positions include some qualifications and exceptions.

claim: State Rep. Elena Parent "supported Governor Nathan Deal’s plan to slash the HOPE scholarship."
rationale: Contemporaneous reporting and legislative records indicate Elena Parent, a Democratic state lawmaker, publicly opposed proposals by Governor Nathan Deal to reduce HOPE scholarship benefits and voted against rollback measures. She advocated preserving HOPE eligibility and funding rather than supporting Deal’s cuts, so the statement that she “supported” his plan is inaccurate.

claim: "If they made no changes whatsoever, the [state employees pension] plan still had enough money to go forward for approximately the next 16 years."
rationale: The claim is not verifiable as stated because it omits which state's plan and which valuation year or assumptions are meant. Whether a public employees' pension plan could pay benefits for 'approximately the next 16 years' depends on actuarial valuation assumptions, funded ratio, contribution policy, and investment returns; without those specifics the statement cannot be confirmed. Absent a cited official actuarial report showing a 16-year projected solvency under a no-change scenario, the assertion is unreliable.

claim: "Actually, on some procedures, you're more likely to die if you're on Medicaid than if you're uninsured."
rationale: Multiple peer-reviewed health services studies have reported that for certain operations and acute conditions, adjusted in-hospital mortality has been higher for patients insured by Medicaid than for uninsured patients. These findings are procedure- and context-specific and come from observational analyses that control for some but not all differences in patient risk and hospital characteristics.

claim: "Torture is illegal by our laws. It's illegal by international laws."
rationale: The claim is overbroad and ambiguous. While international law (e.g., the UN Convention Against Torture, ICCPR and the Geneva Conventions) expressly prohibits torture, whether torture is illegal under "our laws" depends on which country or jurisdiction is meant — many countries do criminalize torture, but some states have laws or practices that allow or tolerate abusive interrogation, and legal exceptions or immunity claims have been asserted. Without specifying the jurisdiction the domestic-legality assertion is not reliably true.

claim: Says U.S. Rep. Michael McCaul is "the sixth-richest person in Congress."
rationale: The claim is a specific, time‑insensitive ranking that is not supported by available public financial‑disclosure rankings; Michael McCaul has been listed among the wealthier members of Congress but is not consistently identified as the sixth‑richest. Wealth rankings of members fluctuate by year and by the valuation method used, and multiple reputable lists do not place him definitively at #6. Because rankings change and estimates vary, the precise assertion that he is the sixth‑richest is not reliable.

claim: Says Burisma admitted in a Ukrainian court to paying Joe Biden $900,000.
rationale: There is no credible evidence or court record showing Burisma admitted in any Ukrainian court to paying Joe Biden $900,000. Independent fact-checkers and reporting on public court filings have found no admission or judgment to that effect, and Burisma and court documents do not support the claim. Hunter Biden’s role with Burisma and various business payments have been reported, but those do not constitute a documented $900,000 payment to Joe Biden admitted in court.

claim: Says Donald Trump offered his hotel "to our troops to sleep in after they were put in a car garage."
rationale: There is no credible contemporaneous reporting or official record that President Trump offered his hotel as lodging for troops who were housed in a parking garage. While National Guard members were documented sleeping in austere locations (e.g., garages or temporary billets) after certain events, offers of private commercial lodging would have been arranged through Defense or local authorities and no verified sources attribute such an offer to Trump.

claim: Says in regard to providing "more tax cuts for the rich," Bill Pascrell said, "Republicans had great ideas. I liked some of their ideas."
rationale: There is no reliable evidence or contemporaneous news reporting that Rep. Bill Pascrell praised GOP proposals by saying “Republicans had great ideas. I liked some of their ideas” in the context of providing “more tax cuts for the rich.” Pascrell is a vocal critic of large tax cuts for high earners, and this positive-sounding quote does not match his known public statements; it appears to be a misattribution or out-of-context paraphrase.

claim: The shooting in Boulder, Colo., was a "false flag like most of the others."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that the Boulder, Colorado, shooting was a "false flag." Law enforcement investigations identified a named suspect who was arrested and charged, and reporting from multiple independent outlets found no signs the event was staged. Claims that it was a false flag are conspiratorial and contradict official findings and available evidence.

claim: "Covid-19 means ‘certificate of identification of vaccination with artificial intelligence.’"
rationale: COVID-19 is an acronym meaning 'coronavirus disease 2019' (CO=corona, VI=virus, D=disease, 19=2019). The proposed expansion 'certificate of identification of vaccination with artificial intelligence' is fabricated and does not match WHO or virology terminology.

claim: "We’ve saved over $100 million of (health care) costs" in Milwaukee County. "I did that."
rationale: There is no clear, independently verified public record showing Milwaukee County realized over $100 million in health care cost savings attributable to a single individual. Large county savings claims typically appear in audited budgets or independent evaluations; without a specific timeframe, program, or audit citation the claim is not verifiable. Because the statement mixes a broad numeric claim about county savings with personal attribution, it fails verification here.

claim: The Democratic Party "is the oldest continuous political party in the world."
rationale: The U.S. Democratic Party traces its formal founding to the late 1820s (often 1828) and is one of the oldest U.S. parties, but the claim it is the single "oldest continuous political party in the world" is disputed and not clearly true. Other parties (notably the British Conservative/Tory tradition and various European parties) have rival claims of continuous existence predating or comparable to the Democrats depending on how one defines "continuous" and "party." Because continuity and organizational lineage are interpreted differently by historians, the blanket claim is inaccurate.

claim: "If you earn $100 and pay $33 income tax you’re left with $67. You then buy $67 worth of fuel and in doing so pay a 48% fuel tax (fuel tax = $32.16 + $6.70 GST). This means that the government just got $71.86 tax from your hard earned $100."
rationale: The claim misapplies and double-counts taxes. It treats an assumed 48% “fuel tax” (the excise) and then adds a separate 10% GST on the same $67 as if both were independent percentages of that $67; in most VAT/GST systems the GST is calculated on the final price (which includes excise) so you cannot simply add 48% of $67 plus 10% of $67. Also the quoted income-tax and fuel-tax percentages depend on country, exact rates and price composition, so the specific $71.86 figure is arithmetically and contextually incorrect.

claim: "Hillary replaces Kamala Harris."
rationale: There is no evidence that any 'Hillary' has replaced Vice President Kamala Harris. Kamala Harris remains the sitting U.S. Vice President, and Hillary Clinton is a private citizen and former Secretary of State who has not been appointed or elected to replace Harris.

claim: "Twenty-five percent of our kids in foster care are there because their parents are involved in drugs."
rationale: The claim is presented without a defined population, timeframe, or data source, so it cannot be verified as a universal fact. While parental substance use is commonly reported as a major reason for child removal and foster placement, the reported share varies by state and year and is not uniformly 25% everywhere. Because the statement is absolute and lacks context, it is not reliably factual as stated.

claim: "Congressman Renacci is under FBI investigation."
rationale: There is no credible public reporting or official DOJ/FBI announcement indicating that Congressman (former Rep.) Jim Renacci is under FBI investigation. Claims of FBI probes of public officials are typically reported by major news outlets, and I found no evidence or reputable reporting supporting this statement as phrased. The claim also lacks a timeframe or source, which undermines its credibility.

claim: The IAEA, or the International Atomic Energy Agency, "last month said the Iranians are not currently living up to their obligations."
rationale: The claim cannot be verified as stated because the phrase "last month" has no reference date and my training data ends in June 2024. The IAEA has on multiple occasions expressed concerns about Iran’s cooperation with safeguards, but I do not have a record of that exact quoted sentence tied to a specific recent month. Without a precise date and source, the attribution is unverified and thus judged false under the instructions to prefer false when uncertain.

claim: "On issue after issue that really were hard to explain or understand, you voted present . . . And anytime anyone raises that, there's always some kind of explanation."
rationale: The statement is vague and asserts a recurring pattern of voting 'present' and always having explanations without naming who, when, or which votes are meant. Such a claim requires checking specific roll-call records and public statements to verify a pattern; in the absence of that evidence it cannot be confirmed and is therefore treated as false for fact-checking.

claim: "Only in the Third World do you see this habitual use of prosecutions of former leaders."
rationale: The claim that prosecutions of former leaders occur only in the 'Third World' is false. Numerous established democracies have prosecuted or indicted former leaders (for example Silvio Berlusconi in Italy, Nicolas Sarkozy in France, Park Geun‑hye in South Korea, and Benjamin Netanyahu in Israel), so such prosecutions are not limited to developing countries. Frequency and legal norms vary by country and period, but prosecutions are a global phenomenon.

claim: "Mexico’s Next President Calls for An Invasion Of The US"
rationale: There is no credible evidence that any incoming Mexican president has called for invading the United States; such a provocative declaration would have been widely reported by mainstream international media. The claim is inconsistent with Mexico's longstanding diplomatic norms and appears to be fabricated, satirical, or a misattribution.

claim: The U.S. Supreme Court is "five guys who start determining what contraceptions are legal."
rationale: The claim is inaccurate as stated. The U.S. Supreme Court is a nine‑justice body (not literally "five guys") and while a 5–4 majority can decide cases that affect access to contraception, the Court rules on specific legal disputes and interprets statutes and the Constitution rather than unilaterally creating regulatory approvals. Contraceptive legality also depends on statutes, regulations (e.g., FDA), and state laws, not solely on five justices.

claim: "We confer more PhDs each year than any other university in America except Berkeley."
rationale: The statement claims a specific university awards the second-most PhDs in the U.S. after Berkeley, but national doctorate counts vary year-to-year and several institutions (e.g., Michigan, Harvard, UCLA, Illinois) frequently award numbers comparable to or exceeding any single non‑Berkeley campus. Without naming the university or year and given variability in NSF/NCSES doctorate-conferral data and differing degree definitions, the blanket claim is unsupported.

claim: "449,000 Californians turned down jury duty because they were not citizens… but they were registered voters."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that 449,000 Californians both refused jury duty on the basis of noncitizenship and were simultaneously documented as registered voters. Public audits and fact-checks show that instances of noncitizen voter registration are rare and the number cited appears to be a misinterpretation or conflation of different datasets (e.g., excused jurors, voter-roll anomalies, or provisional matches). Court and election records do not support a statewide total that large of people explicitly turning down jury duty as noncitizens while remaining registered voters.

claim: "AIG insures the pension trust of the United States Congress!"
rationale: There is no evidence that AIG underwrites or 'insures' a U.S. Congress pension trust. Congressional retirement benefits are administered through federal retirement systems and statutory/taxpayer-backed mechanisms rather than being insured by a private company like AIG.

claim: Says Jon Ossoff "wants total, blanket amnesty and he wants a total lockdown."
rationale: The statement bundles two exaggerated claims that do not match Ossoff’s public positions. Ossoff has advocated for comprehensive immigration reform and pathways to citizenship for certain groups (such as Dreamers) and legalization with conditions, not an immediate, unconditional "total, blanket amnesty." Likewise, he supported public-health measures during the COVID pandemic (masks, vaccines, targeted restrictions) but did not call for an indefinite or absolute "total lockdown."

claim: "The average student will be spending $1,700 to $1,800 more during the life of their loan because of this surcharge."
rationale: The statement cannot be verified as a general fact because it omits which surcharge, which loans, and which population are being measured. Whether a surcharge increases lifetime loan costs by $1,700–$1,800 depends on principal, interest rate change, and repayment term, so the blanket claim is unsupported without those inputs. In the absence of specific data or a cited calculation, the claim should not be treated as established fact.

claim: Says "47 additional counties used the same software that caused a ‘glitch’ in Antrim County (that switched 6,000 votes from Trump to Biden in that county)" and votes in the state are "potentially fraudulent."
rationale: State election officials and independent reviews found the Antrim County discrepancy was a reporting/clerical error in unofficial canvassing results, not software that ‘switched’ 6,000 votes, and subsequent investigations found no evidence of widespread vote flipping. There is no credible evidence that 47 other counties experienced the same software-caused error or that statewide results are therefore ‘potentially fraudulent.’

claim: "Withheld union dues fund half of Dem (Democratic) campaigns in Florida."
rationale: There is no evidence that “withheld union dues” supply half of Democratic campaign funding in Florida. Public campaign finance records and reporting show unions are a significant donor category but do not comprise 50% of Democratic campaign dollars statewide, and much union political spending comes from separate voluntary political accounts rather than mandatory dues. The claim conflates vague terms and overstates union share of funding.

claim: "Kasich’s trade deals cost Ohio thousands of jobs - 49,000 jobs to Mexico, 91,000 to China."
rationale: The claim misattributes specific statewide job losses to “Kasich’s trade deals.” Kasich was a congressman and later governor but did not unilaterally negotiate or enact trade deals; trade-related job-loss estimates are produced by researchers and vary by timeframe and methodology, and the precise figures (49,000 to Mexico, 91,000 to China) are not reliably attributable to Kasich’s actions alone. At best the claim mixes real trade-related job-loss estimates with a misleading causal attribution to one politician.

claim: "An economic impact study found that for every $1 invested in pre-K in Pennsylvania, a total of $1.79 is generated in total spending within the state."
rationale: I cannot verify a specific, reputable Pennsylvania economic impact study that reports exactly $1.79 in total in‑state spending for every $1 invested in pre‑K. Studies of pre‑K often report different metrics (short‑term economic multipliers vs. long‑term benefit‑cost ratios) and results vary by methodology, so the precise $1.79 claim appears unsubstantiated without a cited study. Because the claim lacks a clear source and could conflate different types of returns, it should not be accepted as factual as stated.

claim: Democrats plan to keep student loan interest rates low  "by raising taxes on small businesses, very small businesses … the kinds of small businesses that give jobs to graduates."
rationale: There is no broad, endorsed Democratic plan to keep student loan interest rates low specifically by raising taxes on 'small businesses, very small businesses' as claimed. Democratic proposals to pay for student-debt relief or lower rates have typically focused on higher taxes on wealthy individuals, corporations, or closing tax loopholes, not blanket tax hikes on small employers that hire graduates. The statement mischaracterizes mainstream Democratic tax proposals and overgeneralizes potential effects on pass-through businesses.

claim: "The average age of the minimum wage worker is 35 years old."
rationale: This claim is not supported by authoritative analyses: U.S. data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics, Pew Research Center and Census-based studies show the average/median age of workers earning minimum or low hourly wages is typically younger than 35 (commonly in the late 20s to early 30s) and a substantial share are under 25. The “35 years old” figure appears to come from selective definitions or misinterpretation and is not the accepted national average for minimum-wage workers.

claim: Says Nancy Pelosi passed a bill awarding a $9 billion contract to her husband’s company.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Nancy Pelosi 'passed a bill' that directly awarded a $9 billion contract to her husband’s company. Individual members of Congress do not unilaterally award federal contracts, which are issued through competitive procurement or agency action, and fact-checkers and public records show no such $9 billion contract to Paul Pelosi's firms.

claim: "There has never been an alderman who has defeated an incumbent mayor in the history of this great city."
rationale: The claim is an absolute statement about an unspecified city and timeframe, which is implausible and unproven. In many cities, members of city councils or aldermen have run for mayor and in numerous cases have defeated incumbents, so asserting that it never happened requires strong historical evidence for a specific place. Without a named city and period, the claim cannot be accepted as true.

claim: Says Rob Portman was a registered foreign agent whose "client was Haiti, at a time when the Baby Doc, Duvalier, who was a despot, was killing people."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Senator Rob Portman ever registered under the Foreign Agents Registration Act as an agent for Haiti or the Duvalier regime. His public biography documents U.S. government service and private-sector legal/lobbying work, but FARA records and contemporary reporting do not show Portman representing Baby Doc Duvalier or Haiti during the Duvalier era (1971–1986).

claim: "Over-vaccination causes faster mutation of the (COVID-19) virus, which causes a super virus we may not have the ability to fight off."
rationale: The claim is false: vaccines do not cause faster mutation of SARS-CoV-2 in a way that produces an inevitable 'super virus.' Viruses mutate when they replicate, and widespread vaccination typically reduces infections and thus opportunities for mutation; although immune pressure can select for escape variants in some contexts (e.g., prolonged infections), there is no evidence that 'over-vaccination' creates uncontrollable superbugs.

claim: "Lindsey Graham threatens to convert to Democrat if Republicans don’t Dump Trump."
rationale: There is no credible record through mid‑2024 of Senator Lindsey Graham publicly threatening to switch his party registration to Democrat if Republican leaders did not abandon Donald Trump. Graham has at times criticized Trump and at other times defended or supported him, but mainstream news coverage does not substantiate a conditional threat to 'convert to Democrat.' The claim appears to be a mischaracterization or viral distortion of his comments or frustrations.

claim: "If Biden wins the election, there are people out there planning on mass murdering poc and lbgtq+ people. Please stay inside during the election and a few days after."
rationale: The claim that there are organized plans by unspecified people to mass-murder POC and LGBTQ+ individuals if Biden wins is not supported by credible public evidence. While there have been isolated threats and extremist rhetoric around elections, there is no verified proof of widespread, coordinated plans of mass murder tied to that specific election outcome. The broad, definitive nature of the claim exceeds available verified intelligence and reporting.

claim: Regarding her State Department email practices, "my predecessors did the same thing."
rationale: The claim is misleading. While some predecessors occasionally used personal email accounts for work (for example Colin Powell used an AOL account for some correspondence), none of Clinton’s predecessors operated a private, non-State Department server that routed all official email the way Clinton did. Thus the blanket statement that “my predecessors did the same thing” is inaccurate without that crucial distinction.

claim: Fox News changed its accreditation to "entertainment."
rationale: There is no reliable evidence that Fox News as an organization formally ‘‘changed its accreditation to ‘entertainment.’’’ Claims like this conflate different credentialing systems (e.g., event badges, website tags, or social‑platform classifications) or misinterpret labeling of opinion shows, but no official press‑gallery or government reclassification of Fox News to an ‘‘entertainment’’ accreditation has been documented. Fact‑checking organizations have debunked similar blanket assertions as inaccurate or misleading.

claim: Says Vice President Kamala Harris called the unvaccinated "dirty Trump people."
rationale: There is no credible record, transcript, or reputable news report showing Vice President Kamala Harris used the phrase "dirty Trump people." While Harris has criticized vaccine refusal and sometimes linked resistance to partisan messaging, fact-checkers and media coverage do not corroborate this specific quote and have debunked similar social-media misattributions.

claim: "The only people in this town that have voted to cut Medicare spending are the people who voted in favor of Obamacare. That’s a fact."
rationale: The statement is an unverified, overly specific claim about an unnamed town and asserts an exclusivity that is unlikely and unsupported. Votes that reduce Medicare spending occur in many legislative contexts and have been cast by officials with different positions on the Affordable Care Act; furthermore the ACA vote was a 2010 congressional vote, not a municipal one. Because the claim lacks evidence and is ambiguous about who ‘‘voted’’ and what counts as a ‘‘cut,’’ it cannot be accepted as fact.

claim: "There is no reason for these massive, deadly and costly forest fires in California except that forest management is so poor."
rationale: The claim asserts a single cause (poor forest management) for California’s large, deadly fires, but the scientific consensus and observed evidence identify multiple major drivers. Warmer temperatures and prolonged drought tied to climate change, extended fire seasons, insect outbreaks, accumulation of fuels, expansion of the wildland–urban interface, and human ignitions and failing utility infrastructure all contribute alongside forest-management issues. While forest management can reduce some risk, it is not the sole reason for massive California fires.

claim: Superdelegates "have never been a determining factor in who our nominee is since they've been in place since 1984."
rationale: The claim is incorrect. While superdelegates have not usually been the sole margin in every contested primary, their endorsements and potential convention votes were pivotal in close Democratic contests (notably 2008 and 2016) and prompted the Democratic Party in 2018 to restrict their role on the first ballot—an institutional response that contradicts the claim that they 'never' could determine a nominee.

claim: The Biden administration "gifted the Taliban with $80 billion-plus" in military-grade weapons but now "wants your 9mm pistols."
rationale: The claim misstates facts and conflates different figures. Pentagon and independent estimates put the value of U.S.-origin equipment left in Afghanistan after the withdrawal in the low billions (commonly cited ~$7–9 billion), not “$80 billion+,” and that equipment was previously provided to Afghan forces over two decades rather than being a deliberate Biden “gift” to the Taliban. Separately, regulatory actions discussed under the administration (e.g., rules on ‘‘ghost gun’’ parts or pistol braces) are about regulating certain unserialized parts and accessories, not a blanket effort to seize legally owned 9mm pistols from citizens.

claim: Says FEMA is giving essential workers $1,000.
rationale: There is no known FEMA program that issued a universal $1,000 payment to 'essential workers.' FEMA's authorities focus on disaster survivors, emergency assistance, and grants for response and recovery, not blanket bonus payments to essential workers; claims of $1,000 payments usually stem from misattributions of state/local hazard pay, employer bonuses, or other federal programs. Without a specific program name or official announcement from FEMA, the claim is not supported.

claim: A video shows a nurse pretending to vaccinate actor Anthony Hopkins before squirting fluid in the syringe on the floor.
rationale: Independent fact-checking and available fuller footage show the viral clip was an edited/zoomed segment that misrepresents the sequence; there is no reliable evidence that the nurse pretended to vaccinate Hopkins and then deliberately squirted vaccine onto the floor. The apparent “squirting” in the short clip is explainable by camera angle/cropping and normal syringe handling rather than a staged act. Multiple reputable checks concluded the claim is misleading or false.

claim: "Workers have begun removing spires of Cinderella Castle at Magic Kingdom ahead of Hurricane Dorian."
rationale: There is no contemporaneous, credible evidence that Disney began removing the Cinderella Castle spires specifically because of Hurricane Dorian. Major news outlets and official Disney communications noted park closures and precautionary measures, but images circulating online were either misdated, misattributed, or showed routine maintenance/scaffolding rather than spire removal. Therefore the claim as stated is not supported.

claim: "When you look at the nearly 150 men and women who have served us on the Texas Supreme Court, more than half of them had zero prior judicial experience."
rationale: I cannot verify the specific tally and the claim appears unlikely based on available biographical patterns: many Texas Supreme Court justices historically previously served as county or district judges, in elected local judicial posts, or on appellate benches. While a substantial number came from private practice or elected office, asserting that 'more than half' of nearly 150 had zero prior judicial experience is not supported by accessible summaries and likely overstates the share without systematic evidence. Without a compiled count from authoritative biographical records the claim is unproven and probably incorrect.

claim: Says Cory Booker "supports late-term and partial-birth abortion and opposes safety regulations."
rationale: The claim is misleading. Cory Booker is a pro‑choice politician who has defended access to abortion, including in some later‑term cases for health reasons, but he has not explicitly advocated for a policy called 'partial‑birth abortion' as a standalone advocacy point; moreover, he has opposed certain Republican bills framed as 'safety' measures (e.g., born‑alive/targeted restrictions) on grounds they were unnecessary or harmful rather than opposing all safety regulations. The statement compresses and distorts his nuanced record into a categorical assertion that is not supported by his public positions and votes.

claim: Even high estimates for an early draft of the health care plan are "less than the $1.8 trillion cost of the Bush tax cuts."
rationale: The statement is misleading because both figures depend on time frame and accounting rules. Budget experts (CBO and others) produced a range of 10‑year estimates for early health‑care drafts that, depending on whether gross costs or net federal costs and what offsets are counted, could approach or exceed $1.8 trillion; similarly, estimates of the Bush tax‑cut “cost” vary around $1.6–2.0 trillion. Without specifying which draft, which estimates, and whether costs are gross or net, the blanket claim is false.

claim: Says, "Carl proposed a 'windfall' tax on real estate development when he was a Metro Councilor."
rationale: The claim is ambiguous and unverifiable as written because it gives only the first name “Carl” and no jurisdiction or date. I am not aware of a widely reported instance up to mid‑2024 in which a Metro councilor named only “Carl” formally proposed a specific “windfall” tax on real estate development; without a full name or city, this cannot be confirmed. Because the statement lacks identifying details and supporting reporting, I treat it as not established.

claim: "Youth unemployment in minority communities is about 40 to 45 percent."
rationale: The statement is an unqualified, broad claim that is not supported by standard labor statistics. U.S. and comparable national data show youth unemployment varies widely by age bracket, race/ethnicity, location and year; national rates for Black or Hispanic youth are generally well below 40–45% except for brief spikes or specific local subgroups (and some teen cohorts sometimes approach but do not consistently reach 40–45%). Because the claim gives no timeframe, age definition, or geography and contradicts typical aggregate data, it is false as stated.

claim: Donald Trump "cancelled Bill Gates project known as ID2020."
rationale: False. ID2020 is an independent public–private alliance (not a sole "Bill Gates project") supported by multiple organizations including some Gates Foundation involvement, and there is no record of President Trump issuing an order or taking action that "cancelled" the ID2020 initiative. Reporting and the organization's own materials show the initiative continued through its partners and was not terminated by a U.S. presidential action.

claim: "John Cornyn has voted to increase the debt, raise taxes, bail out Wall Street banks and fund Obamacare."
rationale: The claim bundles multiple assertions that are not all true. Cornyn has voted for large spending measures (e.g., COVID relief) that increased the federal debt and supported some emergency financial rescue measures, but he voted against the Affordable Care Act and has not voted to “fund Obamacare” as a supporter; he has also generally opposed tax increases and supported the 2017 Republican tax cuts. Because the statement treats all four points as true for him, it is inaccurate without additional specificity.

claim: "More people die from hands, fists, feet, than rifles."
rationale: The claim is presented without time or place and therefore overgeneralizes. In typical crime statistics (for example the U.S. FBI and other national datasets), firearms account for the majority of homicide deaths and rifles—while a subset of firearms—are responsible for a meaningful share of lethal violence; deaths from unarmed assault (hands, fists, feet) are a much smaller category. Without a specific country and timeframe this blanket statement is not supported.

claim: "2 million rounds of ammo that ‘went missing’ under Obama turns up in enemy hands"
rationale: While U.S. audits and reporting have documented large quantities of ammunition that were unaccounted for in Afghanistan during the Obama years and instances of U.S.-origin weapons appearing with insurgents, there is no verified evidence that a specific stock of "2 million rounds" that "went missing" under Obama was later confirmed to have "turned up in enemy hands." The claim conflates documented inventory discrepancies and isolated captures of weapons into a precise, proven transfer which has not been substantiated by public DoD/GAO findings or reliable reporting.

claim: Ebola is "incredibly contagious," "very transmissible" and "easy to catch."
rationale: This is inaccurate: Ebola is not airborne and is not typically “incredibly contagious” in casual-contact settings. Transmission requires direct contact with blood or other bodily fluids of a symptomatic person (or contaminated surfaces), so it spreads mainly through close contact and is not easy to catch casually, though it can spread rapidly in unprotected healthcare or funeral contexts.

claim: "Nationwide tuition at public universities is up almost 300 percent ... in the last 20 years."
rationale: This overstates the change. National data from sources that track college costs show tuition and fees at public four‑year institutions rose substantially over the past two decades but not by “almost 300%” under typical measures; depending on the exact series (in‑state vs out‑of‑state, nominal vs inflation‑adjusted) the increase is much smaller. The claim also fails to specify which tuition measure or exact 20‑year window is used, which affects the percent change.

claim: Schools are putting litter boxes in bathrooms to accommodate kids who identify as furries.
rationale: This claim is false. Multiple reputable fact-checkers and school districts investigated viral reports and found no verified instances of schools installing litter boxes to accommodate students who identify as furries; the stories originated from social media hoaxes, mistaken photos, and misinterpretations. School communications and local officials consistently denied such practices and there is no credible evidence supporting the claim.

claim: "94 percent of winning candidates in 2010 had more money than their opponents."
rationale: The claim is not supported by readily available analyses of the 2010 U.S. elections. While winners commonly raised and spent more than their opponents, published summaries (e.g., by nonpartisan election money trackers) show lower rates—typically in the roughly 70–85% range depending on office—rather than a blanket 94% figure. The statement is therefore misleading or incorrect as a general claim without specifying office or metric.

claim: More than one-quarter of America’s young adults are too fat to serve in the U.S. military
