Without a cited source and precise definition/timeframe this exact claim is not supported by the established national data series I know.

claim: "The Katy Freeway, or Interstate 10 west of Houston, is the widest freeway in the world, with up to 26 lanes, including frontage road lanes."
rationale: The Katy Freeway (I‑10 west of Houston) was widened in the 2000s and commonly cited as having up to 26 lanes across in places when main lanes, managed lanes, and parallel frontage/collector roads are all counted. The "world's widest" label is widely used in reporting and engineering descriptions, though such rankings depend on how lanes and adjacent frontage/collector lanes are counted.

claim: "We paid down the debt for four years -- paid down $600 billion on the national debt."
rationale: This is not accurate as stated. In recent decades there was not a four-year stretch where the federal debt was paid down by $600 billion; the only multi-year declines occurred in the late 1990s and were smaller and depend on whether one cites 'debt held by the public' or total gross debt. In the administrations commonly discussed around this claim (Obama/Trump), the national debt rose rather than fell.

claim: "As governor, Kasich delivered the largest tax cut in the nation."
rationale: Kasich did sign significant tax reforms in Ohio that reduced income taxes and changed sales taxes, but independent fact-checkers found his package was not the largest tax cut in the nation. The claim mixes metrics and timeframes; other states enacted larger tax reductions by dollar amount or percentage, and Kasich’s team often framed the measure as largest in Ohio history or by a particular metric rather than nationwide.

claim: President Joe Biden cut "$30 billion to Black colleges and universities."
rationale: There is no evidence that President Biden cut $30 billion to Historically Black Colleges and Universities (HBCUs). Federal support for HBCUs is typically in the hundreds of millions to low billions annually, and a $30 billion cut would be widely documented and require Congressional action; reported Biden-era actions have included grants and proposed increases rather than a unilateral $30B reduction.

claim: Says his office "has already recovered over $2 billion from Wall Street for the workers, retirees, and investors who were harmed."
rationale: The claim cannot be verified as stated because it lacks the identity of “his office,” a timeframe, and the basis for the $2 billion figure. While state attorneys general and similar offices have recovered large sums from Wall Street in various settlements, the specific assertion as quoted is unsubstantiated without supporting documentation or a named office. Absent those details, the statement is not reliably provable.

claim: "We’re now spending 42 percent of our economy on government."
rationale: The claim is misleading because it lacks a time frame and measure; U.S. government spending as a share of GDP varies by year and by whether you count federal-only or total (federal+state+local) spending. In typical recent years total government spending has been in the mid-30s percent of GDP, while federal spending alone is lower; only during the COVID-19 spike (around 2020) did some measures approach ~41–42%. Without specifying country and year the blanket statement that “we’re now spending 42% of our economy on government” is not reliably true.

claim: The Redskins Training Camp deal "generated $40 million in new private investment in the city."
rationale: I could not find reliable, verifiable evidence that the Redskins training-camp agreement produced $40 million in actual new private investment in the city; public statements that cite such a figure relied on projected or pledged development and include pre-existing or planned spending rather than documented new private capital. Without clear documentation of completed private investments tied directly to the deal, the claim appears to overstate what was realized.

claim: Photo shows Joe Biden’s license plate says "THEBIGGUY."
rationale: There are no authenticated, credible photos showing President Biden’s personal or official vehicle bearing a license plate reading “THEBIGGUY.” Viral images claiming this have been debunked or shown to be edited or misattributed, and official presidential vehicles use government plates and registration protocols rather than novelty phrases. Therefore the claim that a photo shows Biden’s license plate saying “THEBIGGUY” is false.

claim: "Last year," Obama "administration officials released into our neighborhoods more than 36,000 criminal immigrants who had nearly 88,000 convictions. The crimes included hundreds of convictions for murder, rape and kidnapping and thousands of drug-related crimes."
rationale: The claim mixes and misrepresents immigration enforcement data. Publicly available ICE and DHS figures that have been cited in similar claims are based on a specific dataset and definitions (e.g., arrests, charges, prior convictions, or multiple charges per person) and do not support the sweeping statement that the Obama administration ‘released into our neighborhoods’ 36,000 criminal immigrants with nearly 88,000 convictions in the simplistic way presented. Independent fact-checkers have found the numbers are taken out of context, include many minor or old convictions and multiple counts per individual, and the characterization of where and why people were released is misleading.

claim: Says the Clintons "burst through their own self-pronounced guidelines" by accepting foreign donations. "There is a clip of Bill Clinton saying we're not going to take foreign donations."
rationale: The claim bundles two assertions but the specific, verifiable part — that there is a clip of Bill Clinton saying “we're not going to take foreign donations” — is not substantiated by a known, verified recording of him using that exact pledge. It is true that the Clinton Foundation accepted donations from foreign governments while Hillary Clinton was Secretary of State and that critics said this conflicted with public ethics assurances, but there is no clear public record of an unequivocal, time-stamped clip in which Bill Clinton declares a categorical ban on all foreign donations that was subsequently violated.

claim: "Republicans in the General Assembly cut teacher pay so much when they took over in 2011 that even with recent pay raises, we are still below pre-Recession pay levels."
rationale: The statement is presented as a universal fact but is underspecified and not verifiable as written. Teacher pay trends after the Great Recession varied by state and district—some Republican-led legislatures did enact pay freezes or cuts around 2011 and in some places later raises have not restored inflation‑adjusted pre‑recession levels, but that pattern is not uniform nationwide. Without a specific state and whether pay is measured in nominal or inflation‑adjusted dollars the claim overgeneralizes and cannot be confirmed.

claim: Milwaukee "incarcerates 1.2% of white men" and has "incarcerated over 50% of black men in their 30s."
rationale: The claim is misleading. Milwaukee’s jail and prison populations are far too small to mean that over 50% of Black men in their 30s are currently incarcerated, and published research on "ever incarcerated" rates for Black men and local county statistics do not support a 50% current-incarceration figure; the 1.2% figure for white men may refer to a specific prevalence measure (and lacks clear age/area context) but taken together the two-statements as presented are inaccurate or unsupported. The numbers conflate different measures (current incarceration versus lifetime prevalence) and lack a clear geographic/timeframe.

claim: Says police unions have it "written into a contract that (officers) are not going to be accountable" for misconduct.
rationale: The claim is an overbroad generalization. While many police collective bargaining agreements contain procedural protections (e.g., limits on interrogation, requirements for notice, timelines, grievance/arbitration, and record-expungement provisions) that can make disciplining officers harder, contracts do not uniformly or literally state that officers “are not going to be accountable” for misconduct. Whether and how accountability is impeded depends on the specific contract language and local policies.

claim: "The 90 percent statistic of supporting background checks, that's been debunked."
rationale: Multiple reputable national polls (Pew Research Center, Gallup, Quinnipiac and others) have repeatedly measured roughly 85–95% public support for background checks, so the core statistic is supported rather than debunked. Critics note wording and scenario effects can change exact percentages, but those methodological caveats do not nullify the general finding of overwhelming support.

claim: Ivermectin is an effective treatment for COVID-19.
rationale: Multiple high-quality randomized controlled trials and systematic reviews have found no consistent benefit of ivermectin for reducing COVID-19 mortality, hospitalization, or viral clearance, and several early positive studies were low-quality or retracted. Major health agencies (WHO, FDA, NIH) recommend against using ivermectin to treat COVID-19 outside clinical trials.

claim: Brookhaven homeowners pay hundreds of dollars less in property taxes compared with owners of the same-value homes in unincorporated DeKalb County.
rationale: The statement is an overbroad generalization. Whether a Brookhaven homeowner pays "hundreds of dollars less" than an owner of an identical-value home in unincorporated DeKalb County depends on the specific tax year, the applicable millage rates, exemptions, special service districts and the assessed value; comparisons have varied over time and are not uniformly in Brookhaven's favor. Without specifying year and exact tax components the claim cannot be treated as universally true.

claim: During the past four years, "average wages have barely budged."
rationale: The claim is misleading or false as stated: U.S. average hourly wages (nominal) have risen noticeably over the past four years according to labor-market data, even though high inflation in 2021–2022 reduced real purchasing power. Saying wages have "barely budged" ignores the distinction between nominal increases (which were significant) and inflation‑adjusted (real) changes, which varied by year and measure.

claim: The Benghazi probe is "the longest-running congressional investigation ever."
rationale: This is inaccurate. The various Benghazi investigations ran for a few years after the 2012 attack (roughly 2012–2016) but many congressional investigations have run longer in U.S. history. For example, the House Un-American Activities Committee and other long-standing oversight efforts spanned decades, so calling Benghazi the "longest-running congressional investigation ever" is incorrect.

claim: "NFL attendance and ratings are WAY DOWN. Boring games yes, but many stay away because they love our country."
rationale: The claim is misleading: while NFL TV ratings and some game attendance have fluctuated and declined in certain seasons, they have not been universally or consistently "WAY DOWN" across recent years and attendance has remained near historical norms. The assertion that "many" people avoid the NFL primarily because they "love our country" (i.e., as a patriotic protest) is unsupported — evidence shows a variety of reasons for viewership changes and no clear data that patriotism is a major, primary driver for a large share of fans.

claim: The Super Bowl has "one of the highest levels of human sex trafficking activity of any event in the country."
rationale: There is no reliable, empirical evidence showing the Super Bowl produces "one of the highest levels" of human sex trafficking among U.S. events. Multiple fact-checkers, researchers, and law-enforcement statements conclude trafficking occurs year-round and that claimed spikes tied to the Super Bowl are unsupported; observed increases in online ads or arrests are inconsistent and do not prove trafficking. The claim therefore overstates the evidence.

claim: Says there is proof Democrats hired actors to plan violence in Charlottesville.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Democratic Party operatives hired actors to plan the Charlottesville violence. Investigations and mainstream reporting show the Unite the Right rally was organized by white supremacist and far-right groups, and arrests were of participants linked to those movements; claims about hired 'actors' have been debunked as misinformation. The allegation appears to be a partisan conspiracy theory without substantiation.

claim: "U.S. government reports record tax haul after Trump tax cuts spur economic growth."
rationale: The claim mixes two misleading ideas: that federal receipts became a “record tax haul” specifically because of the 2017 Trump tax cuts, and that those cuts meaningfully spurred growth. While nominal receipts rose in some years after 2017, corporate receipts fell initially and overall deficits grew; independent analyses (CBO, Treasury and academic studies) found only modest, short‑run GDP gains and a large increase in the deficit rather than a revenue windfall caused by the cuts. Thus the causal claim is not supported and the ‘‘record haul’’ framing is misleading.

claim: "No one beta-tested" healthcare.gov.
rationale: Government reviews and contemporaneous reporting show contractors and CMS did perform multiple tests (unit, component, integration and some user testing) on healthcare.gov prior to the October 2013 launch. The primary problem was that full end-to-end and real‑world load testing was inadequate, not that there was zero testing at all. Therefore the absolute claim that “no one beta-tested” is false.

claim: "Unemployment insurance kept more than 620,000 children out of poverty in 2012."
rationale: Contemporary analyses using the Census Bureau’s Supplemental Poverty Measure (as summarized by policy researchers such as the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities) estimated that unemployment insurance benefits kept roughly 620,000 children above the poverty line in 2012. The figure is reported as “more than 620,000” in those analyses, so the claim aligns with published estimates based on the SPM and UI benefit data for 2012.

claim: "In my home state, nearly one in five Floridians live in poverty."
rationale: Recent U.S. Census Bureau American Community Survey estimates place Florida's overall poverty rate in recent years around roughly 12–14%, well below 20%. Saying 'nearly one in five Floridians' therefore overstates the statewide poverty share, though some subgroups or counties have higher rates.

claim: "I was totally against the war in Iraq, saying for many years that it would destabilize the Middle East."
rationale: The claim cannot be verified as presented because the speaker is unspecified and no contemporaneous evidence is provided. Verifying such a personal political claim requires identifying the individual and checking public records (statements, votes, interviews) showing consistent opposition to the 2003 Iraq War and predictions of regional destabilization. While many public figures did oppose the war and predicted destabilization, this specific first‑person assertion is not confirmable without more detail.

claim: Says Bernie Sanders "was against the auto bailout" and "voted against the money that ended up saving the auto industry."
rationale: Bernie Sanders voted against the 2008 Emergency Economic Stabilization Act (the TARP bailout). Portions of TARP-authorized funds were later used in 2009 to provide loans and support that helped stabilize GM and Chrysler, so saying he "voted against the money that ended up saving the auto industry" is accurate in that sense.

claim: "The first so-called second hand information ‘Whistleblower’ got my phone conversation almost completely wrong."
rationale: This is a specific assertion about the accuracy of a particular secondary report of a phone call. I have no access to the underlying phone recording, transcript, or the referenced 'first so‑called second hand information' to independently verify the claim, and the phrase 'almost completely wrong' is subjective; under the instruction to prefer FALSE when uncertain, I judge it FALSE. Verification would require the primary audio/transcript and the original report for direct comparison.

claim: "Amazon accepts Dogecoin."
rationale: Amazon does not officially accept Dogecoin as a direct payment method on its platform. While there are third-party services that let customers convert Dogecoin (or other crypto) into Amazon gift cards or intermediary payment methods, that is not the same as Amazon itself accepting Dogecoin natively.

claim: "In many instances, (people's) health care costs are more than their mortgage costs or their rent, which, by the way, is a first in American history."
rationale: U.S. household spending data show housing is typically the single largest expense and average health-care outlays are substantially lower; while some households do face medical bills that exceed their mortgage or rent, that is not the norm. Claims that this is a "first in American history" are also unsupported—catastrophic medical expenses have caused severe financial strain for families in earlier eras as well. Therefore the broad, sweeping claim is false as stated.

claim: "Corporate entities are paying a lot less taxes this year than they have in the past. Part of that is from a loophole in a bill that was passed in 2015."
rationale: The claim is misleading and lacks necessary context. Major U.S. corporate tax reductions came from the 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act, not a 2015 law, and corporate tax payments vary year-to-year with profits, accounting, and one‑time items, so a blanket statement that corporations are paying “a lot less this year” due to a 2015 loophole is unsupported. Without a specified year or country the assertion cannot be verified and appears inaccurate.

claim: "Not a single person in the crowd on January 6 was found to be carrying a firearm. Not one."
rationale: This is false. Federal prosecutors and law-enforcement reporting from the Jan. 6 investigation show that multiple participants were found with or later charged for possessing firearms and other weapons in connection with the attack, and explosive devices (pipe bombs) were discovered near the Capitol complex. Therefore the absolute claim that 'not a single person' was carrying a firearm is contradicted by public records and prosecutions.

claim: Congressman Robert Hurt has a plan to cut education by 40 percent.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Rep. Robert Hurt proposed a standalone plan to cut education spending by 40 percent. While Hurt supported Republican budget proposals and spending limits that sought large reductions in non-defense discretionary spending, those proposals did not explicitly call for an immediate 40% cut to education and political ads have sometimes exaggerated those positions. The claim therefore overstates and mischaracterizes his record.

claim: Under President Barack Obama: 4 million jobs lost, unemployment rose from 7.8% to 9.9%, the S&P 500 was 1,115.1 and the GDP went down 2.8%.
rationale: The statement is inaccurate and misleading. Over Barack Obama’s presidency net payroll employment grew by roughly 11 million jobs (not a 4 million loss); unemployment did rise early in 2009 to about 10% but then steadily fell to about 4.7% by January 2017. The S&P 500 rose substantially during his terms (well above 1,115 by 2016), and while GDP contracted in the 2009 recession (roughly -2.5% for the year), that decline reflected the crisis he inherited and was followed by subsequent recovery. The claim mixes short-term early-2009 figures and inaccurate totals to misrepresent overall performance.

claim: "92 percent" of President Barack Obama's administration has "never worked outside government."
rationale: The specific claim that 92% of President Obama’s administration had never worked outside government is not supported by reliable data and was debunked by contemporary fact-checkers. Many senior Obama appointees and cabinet members (including officials with private-sector, business, legal, nonprofit, and academic experience) had prior non-government jobs, and the 92% figure appears to come from a misinterpretation or selective counting of a subset of personnel. Without a clear definition of which positions were counted and a transparent method, the assertion is false as stated.

claim: "SpongeBob’s license address is Jeffrey Epstein’s private island!"
rationale: This is false. SpongeBob SquarePants is a fictional character whose shown addresses are fictional Bikini Bottom locations, and there is no credible evidence that any in-show license or image corresponds to Jeffrey Epstein’s real private island (Little Saint James). Images claiming a match are viral memes or edits, not documentary proof.

claim: "Disney stock is down more than 70% and attendance is down more than 55%! 10.1 million people canceled their Disney+ subscription."
rationale: The claim bundles several exaggerated or misleading figures without a timeframe. Disney’s share price has fluctuated but has not been persistently down “more than 70%” from commonly cited recent peaks, theme-park attendance rebounded after pandemic lows and was not universally down >55% in recent reporting, and Disney+ never reported a single-period net cancellation of 10.1 million subscribers—quarterly net subscriber losses have been much smaller. Taken together the statement overstates and conflates disparate metrics.

claim: The COVID-19 vaccine could lead to prion diseases, Alzheimer’s, ALS and other neurodegenerative diseases.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that COVID-19 vaccines cause prion diseases, Alzheimer’s, ALS, or other neurodegenerative diseases. Biological mechanisms suggested online (for example, that vaccine mRNA or spike protein converts to persistent prion-forming proteins) are unsupported: mRNA vaccines are transient, do not integrate into DNA, and produce only limited protein expression. Large clinical trials and ongoing pharmacovigilance have not found increased incidence of these neurodegenerative conditions attributable to the vaccines.

claim: Says President Obama has cracked down "on employers who are attracting undocumented immigrants and hiring them more than any previous president."
rationale: The absolute claim that President Obama cracked down on employers who hire undocumented immigrants more than any previous president is not supported by clear comparative evidence. The Obama administration did increase worksite enforcement and prosecutions and oversaw high removal figures, but enforcement activity and metrics (raids, prosecutions, fines) vary across administrations and programs, and historical data do not unambiguously show he exceeded every prior president on employer-focused actions.

claim: Says his GOP challenger, Doug MacGinnitie, "hadn’t voted in a Republican primary for almost 20 years until 2008.
rationale: I could not find independent, publicly available evidence confirming that Doug MacGinnitie abstained from Republican primaries for nearly 20 years until 2008. Claims about an individual's primary voting history require specific voter-file records or credible reporting, neither of which are available to corroborate this statement. Given the lack of verifiable documentation, the claim cannot be treated as established fact.

claim: Stay-at-home orders "actually are the law of these states."
rationale: The statement is misleading. Stay‑at‑home directives issued during emergencies are typically executive or public‑health orders issued under state statutes and can be legally enforceable, but they are not identical to laws enacted by a legislature and their scope and enforceability vary by state and have been subject to judicial review.

claim: Says Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez said, "We must block Trump from stopping the return of the heroic Alabama mother from ISIS. In many ways she is more of a hero then our veterans. Welcome home sister!"
rationale: There is no credible record—tweets, press releases, or reputable news/fact-check reporting—showing Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez made this statement praising an Alabama woman who joined ISIS. Major fact-checkers have debunked social-media posts that attribute similar quotes to AOC; the wording and sentiment are inconsistent with her known public statements.

claim: West Virginia has "the nation’s lowest workforce participation rate, which hovers around 50 percent, when the national average is about 63 percent."
rationale: The statement exaggerates and slightly misstates current data. West Virginia does have one of the lower civilian labor force participation rates in the country, but recent BLS figures put it nearer the mid-50s percent rather than roughly 50%, and other states sometimes record similar or lower rates. The national participation rate being about 62–63% is roughly correct, but the claim that WV “hovers around 50%” and is definitively “the nation’s lowest” is inaccurate without a specific time reference.

claim: "Of those 850,000 (new Texas) jobs, most were public-sector jobs and minimum-wage jobs."
rationale: Available data on Texas payroll employment show that the bulk of recent job gains were in the private sector (e.g., professional and business services, trade/transportation, construction, leisure/hospitality), not government. While many low-wage positions were created in sectors like leisure and retail, they do not constitute a majority of the cited 850,000 jobs, nor are most of those jobs public-sector positions.

claim: "Only the fully vaccinated should fear the new ‘worst ever’ Covid-19 variant; data shows they already account for 4 in every 5 Covid deaths"
rationale: The claim is misleading. Whether a majority of reported Covid deaths are among the fully vaccinated depends on location, time period, age structure, and vaccination coverage (a base-rate effect) and does not mean only vaccinated people should fear a new variant; on a per-person basis unvaccinated people generally remain at substantially higher risk of severe disease and death. Without specific, contemporaneous denominator data the "4 in every 5" figure is not a generalizable fact.

claim: Says 89 members of Congress "hold dual citizenship with Israel."
rationale: There is no credible evidence or official record that 89 members of the U.S. Congress hold Israeli citizenship. Multiple independent fact-checkers and reporting have debunked viral claims of such a large number; while a handful of members might be Jewish or have family ties to Israel, claiming 89 hold dual Israeli citizenship is unsupported. The claim appears to conflate Jewish heritage, right-of-return eligibility, or speculation with actual Israeli citizenship.

claim: "As your Lieutenant Governor…I cut your taxes."
rationale: The statement is presented as a general claim but is ambiguous and likely untrue as stated: a lieutenant governor by themselves normally cannot unilaterally "cut" taxes. Tax law changes are passed by legislatures and typically require the governor's signature, so without naming the specific officeholder, state, and statute this claim cannot be verified.

claim: "Most of your serial killers, most of your people who commit domestic violence, they start off by abusing animals."
rationale: This is an overgeneralization. Although cruelty to animals appears in the histories of some serial killers and animal abuse is correlated with domestic violence in many households, research does not support the claim that a majority of serial killers or most domestic-violence perpetrators ‘start off’ by abusing animals; the so-called Macdonald triad is not a reliable predictor and prevalence estimates vary by study and sample. The claim thus overstates and simplifies a complex, mixed-evidence area.

claim: "Biden's plan is a 14% tax hike on middle class families."
rationale: This is false. Biden's stated tax proposals have focused on raising taxes primarily on corporations and households with annual income above $400,000, and independent analyses (e.g., Tax Policy Center, JCT) did not find a uniform 14% tax hike for middle‑class families. The 14% figure appears to come from partisan or narrowly scoped calculations or misunderstandings about which brackets, deductions, or definitions of “middle class” were being measured.

claim: Says U.S. Rep. Sean Casten has held numerous "invite-only" town halls.
rationale: Public reporting and Casten’s office record show he has held some small-group briefings, closed meetings, and virtual events requiring registration, but there is not clear evidence that he routinely held numerous strictly “invite-only” town halls. Critics have highlighted limited in-person open town halls, yet the available record mostly shows a mix of public virtual town halls, office hours, and targeted meetings rather than a pattern of many invite-only town halls.

claim: Says that under President Donald Trump, "not only have we not gone after al-Qaida ... our president is supporting al-Qaida."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that President Trump actively supported al-Qaida; the U.S. under his administration continued counterterrorism operations, maintained terrorist designations and sanctions, and conducted strikes against jihadist targets. While some Trump policies (for example troop withdrawals in Syria and reduced local pressure) may have indirectly benefited certain extremist groups, that is not the same as the president supporting al-Qaida.

claim: "More people without health care since George Bush took office; more children in poverty since George Bush took office."
rationale: Contemporary U.S. Census and health statistics show the number of people lacking health insurance rose during George W. Bush’s time in office, and child poverty rates/counts also increased in the early-to-mid 2000s compared with 2000. Thus the claim that there were more uninsured people and more children in poverty since he took office is supported by mainstream government data for that period.

claim: "Chinese lunar rover finds no evidence of American moon landings."
rationale: This is false. Chinese lunar rovers have not produced a credible, general finding that there is "no evidence" of U.S. Apollo landings — the Apollo sites are on the Moon's near side while some Chinese rovers landed elsewhere (e.g., Chang'e-4 on the far side) and have limited range, so they could not comprehensively search Apollo sites. Moreover, independent high-resolution images from NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter have photographed Apollo hardware at the landing sites, confirming their presence.

claim: Republicans included "the Akin amendment in the Republican Party platform, which bans abortion, even for rape victims."
rationale: Todd Akin did propose an amendment in 2012 to strip rape/incest exceptions and effectively ban abortion even for rape victims, but that amendment was defeated and was not adopted into the Republican Party’s official national platform. The final 2012 Republican platform did not include Akin’s language banning abortion in all cases.

claim: "68% error rate in Michigan Voting Machines. Should be, by law, a tiny percentage of one percent."
rationale: The claim is not supported by credible evidence — there is no documented 68% error rate for Michigan voting machines in official testing or post‑election audits. Voting systems used in Michigan are federally/state certified and subject to accuracy testing and audits that produce very low error rates; additionally, no law generically mandates an error rate described as a “tiny percentage of one percent.”

claim: "The states that have raised the minimum wage (this year) have had faster job growth than the states that haven’t raised the minimum wage."
rationale: The claim is too general and not verifiable as stated; cross‑state comparisons for “this year” depend on the specific year, which states are counted, timing of increases, and many confounding factors. Empirical evidence on minimum‑wage increases and job growth is mixed, and short‑term raw comparisons can be driven by preexisting economic trends and policy selection rather than the wage change itself. Without a specific year and controls for other influences, the blanket statement that states that raised the minimum wage had faster job growth is not supported.

claim: Say a "left wing extremist, chases down, rams car over Trump bumper sticker."
rationale: The statement as given is not verifiable: it provides no time, location, or source and I am not aware of any widely reported incident matching that precise description up to my 2024-06 knowledge cutoff. Allegations that someone “chases down, rams car” and labeling them a “left wing extremist” are specific factual and ideological claims that require contemporaneous police reports, video, or reliable news coverage, none of which are cited here. Without corroborating evidence the claim should be treated as unproven and thus classified as false.

claim: Emails show that Fauci knew "hydroxychloroquine worked [and] emailed friends about it being effective."
rationale: The released Fauci emails do not show him stating that hydroxychloroquine definitively worked or that he privately told friends it was effective. The emails mostly discuss early anecdotal reports, circulating studies, and express caution while urging randomized clinical trials; Fauci repeatedly warned against endorsing treatments without solid evidence. Subsequent high-quality clinical trials found no clear benefit and potential harms from hydroxychloroquine for COVID-19, contrary to the claim’s implication.

claim: Says Keanu Reeves gave a speech that began, "I cannot be part of a world where men dress their wives as prostitutes by showing everything that should be cherished ..."
rationale: There is no credible record or reliable news/source evidence that Keanu Reeves gave a speech beginning with that line. The quotation circulates on social media and in viral posts but has been traced by fact-checkers to misattribution or lacks any verifiable primary source. Keanu Reeves is not known to have made a public speech with that wording.

claim: In President Barack Obama’s 2015 State of the Union address, "the words ‘al-Qaida’ were never used, the first time those words have not been used in a State of the Union address since February 2001."
rationale: This claim is not accurate as a categorical statement. Contemporary transcripts and fact-checking coverage do not support the blanket assertion that the words ‘al-Qaida’ were never used in the 2015 State of the Union or that this was uniquely the first omission since February 2001; wording in presidential addresses and joint sessions varied and the ‘‘first omission since 2001’’ claim is not supported by the record. Because the statement mixes two precise claims (absence of the phrase in 2015 and a historical first), and that combination is contradicted by primary transcripts/fact checks, the overall claim is false.

claim: "The soda tax can make a difference by reducing consumption of unhealthy soda pop and sugary beverages."
rationale: Multiple peer-reviewed studies and real-world implementations show that excise taxes on sugar-sweetened beverages raise retail prices and lead to reduced purchases and consumption. Examples include national and local taxes (e.g., Mexico, Berkeley/US cities, and the UK levy) which produced measurable declines in soda purchases or reductions in sugar content, though magnitudes vary by design and context.

claim: The federal government "has $3 trillion in cash flow, so we can pay our bills" and won’t default.
rationale: The statement is misleading and likely false: the federal government does not carry a $3 trillion ‘cash on hand’ cushion that automatically prevents default. Treasury daily cash balances are typically in the low hundreds of billions (not trillions), and while annual revenues run in the multiple‑trillion range, timing of receipts and legal debt‑limit constraints mean inflows alone do not guarantee the ability to meet obligations. Without a debt‑ceiling increase or use of extraordinary measures, the government can still face a cash shortfall and potential default despite ongoing revenues.

claim: The Murray-Ryan deal "is the first divided-government budget agreement since 1986."
rationale: This is incorrect: there were several major budget agreements under divided government after 1986. Examples include the 1990 Omnibus Budget Reconciliation Act under President George H.W. Bush and the 1997 balanced-budget agreements under President Bill Clinton with a Republican Congress; the 2011 Budget Control Act is another post-1986 divided-government budget deal. Therefore the Murray-Ryan deal was not the first since 1986.

claim: Says "taxes were raised 115 times in the eight years before I became governor" and those increases were part of a "path that led to wealth and jobs and people leaving our state."
rationale: The numeric claim is misleading and not independently verifiable as stated: tallying '115 times' typically mixes different kinds of fee adjustments, local levies, and administrative raises rather than documented net tax rate hikes over eight years. The political claim that those increases were the clear 'path' causing wealth loss, job decline, and out‑migration is a causal assertion not supported by presented evidence — economic and population changes have multiple drivers and require rigorous analysis to attribute to tax actions alone.

claim: "In 2009, Yost spent 2.5 times more money than it took to run the (prosecutor’s) office before he got there."
rationale: There is no verifiable, widely reported evidence that in 2009 any official named Yost caused prosecutor’s office spending to jump to 2.5 times previous levels. The claim lacks a named jurisdiction, baseline numbers, or a primary source; without those details it cannot be substantiated and is implausible as stated. Absent specific budget records or contemporaneous reporting, the assertion should be treated as unverified/false.

claim: Says that "18 children died while in custody of Border Patrol" during the Obama administration.
rationale: Available public reporting and government records do not support the specific claim that 18 children died while physically in Border Patrol custody during the Obama administration. Investigations and news accounts identified far fewer deaths that occurred while a child was in CBP/Border Patrol custody; other child deaths in that period occurred after release, in HHS/ORR shelters, or elsewhere in the immigration system. The claim appears to conflate different categories and timeframes.

claim: Says Adam Putnam "was for amnesty."
rationale: Calling Adam Putnam “for amnesty” is misleading. During his 2017–2018 gubernatorial campaign and in prior public statements he opposed blanket amnesty and instead described support for limited, conditional measures (such as enforcement, E‑Verify, and an earned/legalization process with background checks, fines or taxes) rather than unconditional mass amnesty or immediate citizenship. Critics labeled these positions “amnesty,” but Putnam’s stated policy differed from a blanket amnesty.

claim: Federal regulations required the changes to Georgia's driver’s license renewal process.
rationale: Federal law (notably the Real ID Act and subsequent DHS rules) sets standards for what documentation is required for a Real ID-compliant credential, but it does not prescribe specific state-level renewal procedures. Georgia’s changes to how licenses are issued or renewed were implemented by the state to meet federal proof-of-identity requirements and its own administrative policies, not because a federal regulation explicitly dictated the exact renewal process. Therefore the blanket claim that federal regulations required the changes is misleading.

claim: "To give a sense of how families are struggling, a record four out of every 10 school kids in Ohio now qualifies for subsidized lunch."
rationale: The statement that a “record four out of every 10 school kids in Ohio now qualifies” (i.e. 40%) is misleading. Federal and state data show Ohio’s share of students eligible for free or reduced-price school meals has been at or above 40% for several years and recent counts are generally higher than 40%, so describing 40% as a new record is incorrect or unsupported without a specific date or definition. The claim conflates timing and omits that eligibility levels have varied and in many recent years exceeded 40%.

claim: Sen. Mark Kelly voted "for benefits to illegals."
rationale: The claim is vague and unsupported as stated: senators vote on specific bills, and there is no clear record of Sen. Mark Kelly casting a roll-call vote described unambiguously as "for benefits to illegals." Without naming a particular bill or benefit, the statement is misleading. Kelly has supported various immigration-related measures, but that does not equate to a documented vote to provide blanket public benefits to undocumented immigrants.

claim: Rhode Island's state pension system "underperformed the median three out of the four years that Mr. [Frank] Caprio was in office."
rationale: The claim cannot be verified as stated because it omits the exact four-year span and the benchmark 'median' being used. Public pension performance is reported annually and compared to different medians (peer public funds, Wilshire Trust Universe Comparison Service, etc.), and without specifying the years and benchmark the assertion is unsubstantiated. Available summaries of Rhode Island pension returns during periods when Frank Caprio served as treasurer do not clearly support a definitive "3 of 4 years underperforming" statement.

claim: The Senate Republican education plan is an unfunded mandate for local school districts.
rationale: The claim is too broad and cannot be verified without identifying which specific Senate Republican education plan is meant. 'Unfunded mandate' has a technical meaning (federal requirements imposed without accompanying funding), and Republican Senate proposals vary—some propose funding shifts or grants for programs, others attach conditions to federal funds—so it's incorrect to categorically label 'the' plan as an unfunded mandate. Without a specific bill text, there is insufficient evidence to state this as fact.

claim: "750 days since Bill Nelson & the Democrats in the Senate passed a budget. How can this be justified?"
rationale: The claim asserts that it has been “750 days since Bill Nelson & the Democrats in the Senate passed a budget,” which is not supported. Bill Nelson left the Senate on January 3, 2019, so he could not have been part of a Senate Democratic budget action within the past 750 days, and there is no clear, verifiable record that Senate Democrats alone passed a full budget resolution on a date 750 days prior to the claim. The statement also lacks a reference date, making the timeline unverifiable.

claim: Fewer Democrats were on the Georgia general election ballot in 2012 than in more than 100 years.
rationale: This claim is inaccurate and imprecise. In Georgia’s 2012 general election Democrats appeared on the ballot for presidential, multiple U.S. House seats, and numerous state and local contests, and there is no credible evidence that the total number of Democratic candidates that year was the lowest in more than a century. The statement also fails to specify whether it refers to statewide offices, legislative seats, or total candidates, which changes the meaning and makes the absolute claim unsupported.

claim: Says that PolitiFact Ohio confirms that Betty Sutton "maxed out federal debt"
rationale: This is false. PolitiFact Ohio would not 'confirm' that an individual like Betty Sutton literally 'maxed out federal debt' — fact-checkers assess specific claims and provide nuanced ratings and context rather than endorse hyperbolic language. While PolitiFact may have evaluated ads or statements about votes that increased the national debt, it did not validate the literal assertion that Sutton single-handedly 'maxed out' the federal debt.

claim: "We just don't want to get to be like Louisiana, where you have drive-up daiquiri shops."
rationale: The claim that Louisiana has drive-up/drive-thru daiquiri shops is accurate. Frozen daiquiri stands and drive-thru daiquiri windows are a well-known, widespread phenomenon in Louisiana, though some municipalities have enacted restrictions.

claim: "Barack Hussein Obama will ... force local authorities to allow Occupy protesters to live in parks."
rationale: There is no evidence President Obama announced or had the authority to "force" local governments to allow Occupy protesters to live in parks. Control over public parks and policing is primarily a state/local responsibility, and the federal executive branch cannot unilaterally compel local authorities to permit encampments without specific statutory authority or conditions on federal funding, none of which were enacted for this purpose.

claim: Says the state’s budget shortfall is "not that much different" than it was in 2003.
rationale: The claim is vague and likely misleading: budget shortfalls vary greatly by state and over time, and raw comparisons to 2003 without adjustments ignore inflation, population growth, and differences in revenue/expense bases. Many states experienced substantially larger shortfalls in later crises (e.g., 2009 recession, 2020 pandemic) when measured in inflation‑adjusted dollars or as a share of the budget. Without specifying the state and the metric used, the statement is not supported.

claim: The "top ten most unhealthy U.S. cities" are San Francisco; Seattle; Portland, Oregon; San Diego; Honolulu; Washington; Austin, Texas; Irving, Texas; Portland, Maine; and Denver.
rationale: This list is inconsistent with published city health rankings: most of the named places (San Francisco, Seattle, Portland OR, San Diego, Honolulu, Washington D.C., Austin, Denver, Portland ME) typically appear among healthier U.S. cities, not the unhealthiest. Independent studies and indexes that measure chronic disease, mortality, smoking, obesity, and access to care usually place different cities (often in Texas, the Rust Belt, or the South) at the bottom.

claim: "Suntrust Bank cancels account because company sells guns."
rationale: The statement is unsubstantiated as presented: there is no specific company, date, or source showing SunTrust canceled an account solely because the business sold guns. Banks do sometimes close accounts for legal, compliance, or reputational risk reasons, but that does not validate this broad, unsupported claim. Without verifiable details this assertion cannot be confirmed.

claim: Two federal government buses "stopped in front of a Mexican restaurant in the very small town of Green Cove Springs Florida… The passengers were illegal immigrants, straight from the southern border."
rationale: There is no credible, verifiable evidence that two federal government buses transporting migrants 'straight from the southern border' stopped in Green Cove Springs, Florida. Federal agencies do transport detainees under documented procedures, but local news and official sources do not corroborate this specific event and viral posts purporting to show it lack provenance and may misidentify vehicles or passengers.

claim: Barack Obama is the "First President to terminate America’s ability to put a man in space."
rationale: This is false. The United States previously lacked domestic crewed-launch capability after the end of Apollo in the mid-1970s until the first Space Shuttle flight in 1981 following program cancellations in the Nixon/Ford era, so Barack Obama was not the first president to end that ability. Although Obama's administration retired the Space Shuttle and cancelled the Constellation program (creating a gap until commercial crew launches resumed), those outcomes reflected multi-administration policy choices and congressional funding decisions rather than a unique first-ever termination by one president.

claim: Says the Obama Administration has fulfilled all of Texas’ requests for fire management assisting grants.
rationale: There is no basis to say the Obama Administration fulfilled every Texas request for fire-management assistance grants. FEMA's Fire Management Assistance Grant process approves aid only when incidents meet federal criteria, and public records and news coverage indicate some Texas requests were denied or only partially approved during major wildfire periods. Thus the blanket claim that all requests were fulfilled is inaccurate.

claim: "FREE HORSES!!!! 52 thoroughbred horses need homes. Will go to Sugarcreek this Sat. for slaughter. Gentleman died due to COVID-19 and his son wants nothing to do with them."
rationale: The post makes multiple specific, verifiable claims (exact number of horses, destination of 'Sugarcreek' this Saturday, owner died of COVID-19, son refusing them) but provides no names, dates, documentation, or credible sources. Without independent confirmation from local authorities, rescue groups, auction records, or news outlets, these particulars cannot be corroborated and are therefore treated as unverified and likely false.

claim: Dozens of artists, including Justin Timberlake, Jay Z and Rihanna, are canceling Florida shows like Stevie Wonder in protest of  "stand your ground."
rationale: Contemporary reporting and tour schedules do not support a widespread boycott in which dozens of major artists — including Justin Timberlake, Jay‑Z, and Rihanna — canceled Florida shows over 'stand your ground.' While some entertainers voiced opposition or a few individual concerts were canceled for various reasons, there was no mass cancellation campaign of the kind described and the named superstars did not collectively pull Florida dates as alleged.

claim: The stimulus bill "promised to keep unemployment under 8%."
rationale: No major U.S. stimulus law contains a clause that legally "promised" to keep the national unemployment rate below 8%. Stimulus bills (like the 2009 ARRA or 2020 CARES Act) included spending and tax measures and economic projections or estimates from agencies (CBO/OMB), but those are forecasts, not binding guarantees that unemployment would remain under a specified threshold.

claim: Says Miami-Dade Mayor Carlos Gimenez "approved a 67% pay raise for himself and increased his own pension. He makes $250,000 a year, more than almost every big-city Mayor in the country. He also kept his taxpayer-funded Mercedes-Benz after slashing $400 million in government jobs and spending."
rationale: The statement bundles several claims that are misleading or unsubstantiated. While Miami‑Dade’s mayoral pay has been reported around $240–$250K (so not far from the quoted $250,000), Gimenez did not unilaterally “approve a 67% pay raise for himself” — salary adjustments are subject to commission/charter processes and reporting shows no one‑time 67% self‑raise. The assertions about increasing his own pension, keeping a taxpayer‑funded Mercedes after slashing “$400 million in government jobs and spending,” and the comparative “more than almost every big‑city mayor” line are either inaccurate, lack context, or are exaggerated.

claim: "Austin is the largest city in the U.S. or Texas with no geographic representation" on its city council.
rationale: Austin currently elects city council members from single-member geographic districts (along with an at-large mayor), a change approved by voters in the 2010s. Because Austin has district-based geographic representation on its council, the claim that it is the largest city in Texas or the U.S. with no geographic representation is incorrect.

claim: A poll conducted in Egypt revealed that 80 percent of Egyptians oppose receiving foreign aid from the United States.
rationale: I am not aware of any credible, widely reported poll showing that 80% of Egyptians oppose receiving U.S. foreign aid. Major survey sources (e.g., Pew Research, Arab Barometer and other regional polls) have shown mixed and variable views of the U.S. and its influence in Egypt, but not an 80% opposition figure consistently. The claim appears to exaggerate or misstate typical poll results and likely omits key context such as question wording and timing.

claim: "To children and the vast majority of young and middle-aged adults and the vast majority of teachers, (the coronavirus) poses virtually zero threat."
rationale: This categorical statement is inaccurate. COVID-19 has caused hospitalizations, severe illness, multisystem inflammatory syndrome in children, long COVID, and deaths across age groups including young and middle-aged adults, and teachers have experienced occupational exposure and outbreaks; risks are not "virtually zero." While most people in those groups have lower absolute risk of death than the very old or medically vulnerable, nontrivial risks of severe outcomes and long-term effects remain.

claim: Norway decided "that (the coronavirus) should be treated like other respiratory diseases, such as the flu or cold, because… it is no more dangerous than those mentioned."
rationale: Norway did move to relax COVID-19 restrictions and to manage SARS-CoV-2 more like other endemic respiratory infections, but officials did not claim the virus is inherently "no more dangerous" than flu or common cold. Decisions were framed around high population immunity, vaccines, and health‑system capacity rather than a blanket statement of equal danger; authorities continued to note elevated risks for vulnerable groups. The quoted causal wording therefore misrepresents official reasoning and overstates what Norwegian authorities said.

claim: Says that guidance urging vaccinated people to avoid travel and continue wearing masks is "profoundly anti-science."
rationale: Labeling guidance that urges vaccinated people to avoid travel and continue wearing masks as “profoundly anti-science” is a value judgment, not an objective factual characterization, and is incorrect as a blanket statement. Public-health recommendations to limit travel and wear masks after vaccination have been based on evolving scientific evidence about breakthrough infections, variants, and transmission risk, so calling such guidance anti-science misstates its basis.

claim: Says Tony Thurmond was "Reprimanded by the Obama Administration for failing to address widespread sexual harassment and assault in district schools."
rationale: There is no reliable evidence that the Obama Administration formally reprimanded Tony Thurmond personally for failing to address sexual harassment or assault in district schools. Federal Office for Civil Rights actions during the Obama years were directed at school districts' Title IX compliance, not individual politicians, and contemporaneous reporting does not show a reprimand of Thurmond. The claim appears to misattribute or conflate district-level findings or criticisms with a personal federal reprimand of Thurmond.

claim: Seventy percent of Americans "don't have a college degree."
rationale: This claim overstates the share without a college degree. U.S. educational-attainment data show roughly 35–40% of adults 25+ hold a bachelor’s degree or higher, meaning about 60–65% do not — not 70%. The exact percentage varies by year and the age group or degree definition used, but 70% is higher than recent estimates.

claim: "We have laws on the books where people can walk right up to our ports of entry, say ‘I have a credible fear of persecution,’ and we bring them in. We don’t send them back."
rationale: This claim is misleading. U.S. law requires that noncitizens who express fear be screened with a "credible fear" interview; passing that screen places them into immigration court proceedings rather than automatically admitting them as lawful entrants. Individuals may be detained, paroled, or released on bond, and can be removed if they fail credible fear or lose their asylum case; those who fail credible fear are subject to expedited removal.

claim: Says Bill Gates said, "We need to develop a digital certificate that shows who has received all the vaccinations. Only those with all the required vaccinations may travel, visit churches, participate in sports and music events, get a job, etc."
rationale: There is no credible evidence Bill Gates ever made this exact statement; major fact-checkers and searches of his public remarks do not locate that quotation. While Gates has discussed digital verification of vaccination status in the abstract as a public-health tool, the attributed wording and the coercive list of restrictions appear fabricated and misattributed.

claim: "Your tellers were paid kickbacks for directing elderly consumers from ... safe deposits to risky ones."
rationale: The claim is an unsubstantiated allegation of criminal conduct with no specific actor, time, location, or cited evidence. Serious claims that tellers received kickbacks and steered elderly customers would typically generate regulatory investigations and news coverage; absent such corroboration the assertion is not supported. Because the statement is vague and lacks verifiable facts, it should be treated as false/unproven.

claim: Measures taken by my administration "have saved taxpayers $1 billion."
rationale: The statement is unverified as presented because it gives no specifics about which administration, which measures, the timeframe, or independent accounting. Claims of ‘$1 billion saved’ commonly rely on projected, avoided, or reclassified savings rather than audited, realized reductions in taxpayer outlays; without independent verification (CBO/GAO/OMB or audited financial statements) the assertion cannot be confirmed. Therefore I treat the unsupported claim as false pending evidence.

claim: "Black Lives Matter is a terrorist organization."
rationale: There is no credible evidence or official government designation that Black Lives Matter is a terrorist organization. BLM is a decentralized social movement and includes registered nonprofit groups; isolated criminal acts at protests do not legally or factually make the movement a terrorist organization.

claim: "The RI Board of Elections has heard official testimony from Providence residents who claim to have witnessed known illegal aliens voting in local elections."
rationale: There is no credible public record or contemporaneous reporting (through mid‑2024) showing the Rhode Island Board of Elections held official hearings in which Providence residents testified they had witnessed known illegal aliens voting in local elections. Board meetings and testimony are public and documented in minutes or news coverage; searches of those sources do not corroborate the claim. The statement appears to rest on unverified partisan assertions rather than documented official testimony.

claim: Republicans "went out of the way to praise (Eric) Holder's nomination. ... Not a single Republican senator opposed Eric Holder's nomination."
rationale: This is false. The Senate confirmation vote for Eric Holder was 75–21, and multiple Republican senators voted against his confirmation, so it is incorrect to say not a single Republican opposed him. While some Republicans offered measured praise during the nomination process, several ultimately voted no on confirmation.

claim: 60% of new COVID-19 patients are people who received the vaccine.
rationale: The claim is presented as a universal figure without specifying time, place, or whether it refers to cases, hospitalizations, or deaths. The proportion of new COVID-19 cases among vaccinated people varies widely by jurisdiction, vaccine coverage, time (waning immunity and boosters), and circulating variant, so a blanket statement that 60% of new patients are vaccinated is unsupported. Specific reports sometimes report shares above or below 60% in particular contexts, but that does not validate the universal claim.

claim: "As chairman of the City Colleges, I cut millions in waste and we cut property taxes."
rationale: The claim is unverified and implausible as stated. While a community college board chair can oversee campus budget reductions, they do not have unilateral authority to cut municipal property tax rates, which are set by city/county/state authorities; the assertion of having “cut millions in waste” is vague and unsupported without specific audit or budget evidence.

claim: Says the percentage of officers the Chicago Police Board fired after hearing their cases or who chose to resign prior to a board hearing roughly doubled during her tenure.
rationale: The statement is unverifiable as written because it does not identify who 'her' is or provide the timeframe or baseline percentages needed to confirm a doubling. Verifying such a claim requires reviewing Chicago Police Board personnel/hearing outcome statistics for the specified tenure; without those specifics and cited data the claim cannot be confirmed and is treated as false.

claim: "Oregon, once again, remains among the top five hungriest states in the nation."
rationale: Most reputable national measures of food insecurity (e.g., Feeding America/Map the Meal Gap and USDA food insecurity estimates) consistently list Southern states—Mississippi, Louisiana, New Mexico, Arkansas, Alabama—among the highest rates of hunger. Oregon is above the national average in some years but is not typically ranked in the top five hungriest states, so the claim is incorrect in general usage.

claim: "Making public colleges and universities tuition-free, that exists in countries all over the world, used to exist in the United States."
rationale: Many countries today offer tuition‑free public higher education, and the United States has had periods and programs that made public college effectively tuition‑free for certain groups or in certain places. In the 19th and early 20th centuries some state normal schools and land‑grant institutions charged little or no tuition for residents, and federal programs such as the GI Bill after WWII paid veterans’ tuition, making attendance effectively free for them. Thus the practice of tuition‑free public higher education has existed in parts of the U.S. historically, even if not as a permanent nationwide policy.

claim: Says Gov. Scott Walker "has caused Wisconsin to lose more jobs than any other state in the country."
rationale: This claim is false. BLS state employment data do not show Wisconsin losing more jobs than every other state, and the largest job declines in Wisconsin occurred during the 2008–09 recession before Scott Walker took office; moreover, attributing statewide job losses to a single governor requires direct causal evidence that is not provided.

claim: Brewpubs can't sell growlers of their beer to customers.
rationale: The claim is incorrect as an absolute statement: whether a brewpub can sell growlers depends on local and state alcohol laws. Many brewpubs in the U.S. and elsewhere routinely sell growlers or similar to-go containers, though some jurisdictions restrict take-away sales by on-premise licenses.

claim: The United States has "10,000 IRS agents making sure that you don't take an improper charity deduction," but to fight terrorism, it has "less than two dozen people focusing on countering violent extremism at home."
rationale: The claim is misleading. The IRS does not have 10,000 agents whose sole job is policing charitable deductions — IRS enforcement and the exempt-organizations functions are distributed across many job classifications and far fewer staff are dedicated specifically to charity audits. While it is true that federal countering-violent-extremism (CVE) offices were small (often a few dozen or fewer staff) in the mid-2010s, the statement juxtaposes non‑comparable counts and likely conflates different agencies, job titles, and time periods.

claim: Says Tony Evers "wants to cut Wisconsin's prison population in half, a dangerous plan that today would mean releasing thousands of violent criminals back into our communities."
rationale: This claim mischaracterizes Tony Evers' public criminal-justice proposals. Evers has advocated for sentencing reform, diversion, treatment, reentry and other measures intended to reduce incarceration and recidivism, but he has not put forward a policy to “cut the prison population in half” by indiscriminately releasing thousands of violent offenders; the assertion that thousands of violent criminals would be released is speculative and unsupported by his stated plans.

claim: Says Rick Scott "cut $700 million from water management."
rationale: There is no clear, documented record that Rick Scott single-handedly “cut $700 million from water management.” Public budget documents and independent fact-checks show his administration made some vetoes and reallocations affecting environmental programs, but the large $700 million figure appears to conflate multiple years, programs, and accounting categories rather than a single, identifiable $700 million cut to water management. Thus the precise claim as stated is not supported by available evidence.
cited_knowledge: General knowledge of Florida state budget reporting and prior fact-checking practices: budget cuts are tracked by line-item and year, reporting at the time noted smaller vetoes/reallocations and that headlines sometimes aggregated different programs/years leading to inflated totals.
safety_notes: The claim is ambiguous about timing, which programs are included, and whether it refers to vetoes versus transfers or withholding — specifying the year(s) and exact programs would be needed to verify precisely.

claim: In the weekend after the terrorist attacks in Paris, the White House said "this couldn't happen in the United States. ISIS couldn't reach us here."
rationale: Contemporaneous White House statements and press briefings after the November 2015 Paris attacks did not include the quoted line; instead officials, including the President and press secretary, acknowledged the threat of international terrorism and warned there are no guarantees against attacks. The alleged quote appears to be a misattribution or fabrication rather than a documented White House statement.

claim: "Fox News Sandra Smith: ‘Everybody could see from the United Airlines passenger’s behavior that he was not a genuine American.’ "
rationale: There is no credible evidence or Fox News transcript that attributes this exact statement to Sandra Smith. The line reads like an inflammatory misquote or paraphrase; major news archives and fact-checkers do not record her saying, “not a genuine American” about a United Airlines passenger. Without a specific date or clip, the claim appears to be fabricated or misattributed.

claim: The STAR Ohio fund "just received the highest possible credit rating one of these funds can receive."
rationale: There is no verifiable, date-specific evidence that STAR Ohio “just received” a new top credit rating; while STAR Ohio has historically held high short-term municipal/pool ratings (e.g., S&P’s AAAm), the claim’s timing and wording are ambiguous and unverified. Whether a rating is the “highest possible” also depends on the rating agency and product category, so the blanket statement is misleading without a clear source and date.

claim: The United States is "the oldest democracy" in the world.
rationale: The United States is not the oldest democracy in absolute terms. While the U.S. federal constitutional system dates from 1787–1789 and is one of the oldest continuous modern constitutional republics, much older representative or parliamentary assemblies and republican institutions exist (e.g., Iceland’s Althing dating to 930, claims by San Marino to very early republican origins, and ancient Athenian democracy). Whether the U.S. is “the oldest” depends on definitions (modern/continuous/constitutional), so the blanket claim is incorrect.

claim: "(Sen. Robert) Gordon cost us money, exempting the Newark sports arena from paying property taxes and sticking us with the bill."
rationale: There is no clear evidence that Sen. Robert M. Gordon single-handedly ‘‘exempted the Newark sports arena from paying property taxes’’ and thereby directly ‘‘stuck us with the bill.’’ Newark’s arena (Prudential Center) tax arrangements resulted from municipal/state financing and public–private agreements rather than a unilateral act by a senator who does not represent Newark’s district; statewide tax exemptions would require broader legislation and negotiation. Attributing the entire financial outcome to one senator is misleading.

claim: "More people, almost twice as many, pay the penalty or take the waiver than signed up for (Obamacare)."
rationale: This is not supported by available data: marketplace enrollment was in the multiple millions (roughly 8–12 million people selected plans in early ACA open-enrollment periods), while IRS and HHS reports showed only a few million people paid the individual mandate penalty or claimed exemptions. Those penalty/exemption counts were substantially lower, not almost twice the number who enrolled. The claim also fails to specify a year or precise definitions, which would be required to make a different determination.

claim: In 2010, uninsured voters made up "about 5 percent of the electorate."
rationale: The claim is inconsistent with 2010 data: roughly 44 million people (about 15–17% of the population) were uninsured in 2010. Even allowing for lower turnout among uninsured adults, multiple public-health and election analyses show their share of voters was substantially higher than 5%, so “about 5 percent of the electorate” is implausibly low.

claim: "Biden’s plan will immediately let in 25,000 asylum-seekers who’d been waiting in Mexico as their cases were judged."
rationale: The claim is inaccurate: Biden administration proposals have included limited, phased processing or parole programs with monthly caps, not an immediate admission of 25,000 asylum-seekers who had been waiting in Mexico. People subject to programs like the Migrant Protection Protocols (MPP) or other court-affected processes could not simply be admitted immediately; admissions require vetting, eligibility checks and operational ramp-up. Reporting around these plans typically described future or monthly processing capacities rather than an immediate mass entry of 25,000 pending asylum cases.

claim: Since being elected in 2002, Scott Walker has "given back over $370,000 of his salary to the county."
rationale: I cannot verify the specific figure. Public reporting shows Walker made some donations/forwent raises while Milwaukee County Executive, but I find no clear, authoritative documentation that he returned over $370,000 of salary to the county since 2002. Without primary payroll or county-adopted accounting confirming that exact cumulative amount, the claim is unproven and likely inaccurate.

claim: "States with the most gun laws tend to have the fewest gun deaths."
rationale: Multiple public-health analyses and state-level data show that U.S. states rated as having more comprehensive gun-safety laws (for example Massachusetts, New York, Hawaii) generally have lower firearm death rates, so the claim is supported as a broad correlation. However, this is observational evidence and does not prove causation because other factors (demographics, urbanization, enforcement, cross-border flows) also influence death rates.

claim: Planned Parenthood clinics are "closing down all over the country" because Roe v. Wade was overturned.
rationale: The Dobbs decision led some Planned Parenthood centers in states with immediate abortion bans or restrictions to stop providing abortion care or temporarily close those sites, but Planned Parenthood health centers nationwide have not been "closing down all over the country." Many centers remain open for a wide range of non‑abortion services, and Planned Parenthood has shifted services or expanded capacity in states where abortion remains legal. The impact is real but geographically concentrated rather than a nationwide shutdown of clinics.

claim: Says of MS-13 gang members, "We are getting them out of our country by the thousands."
rationale: The claim asserts that MS-13 members are being removed “by the thousands,” but public law‑enforcement and immigration records do not document deportations or removals of MS‑13 members at that scale in a short timeframe. Reported arrests, prosecutions, and deportations tied to MS‑13 have been substantial but number in the hundreds per year or fewer in documented cases, not thousands verified as removals of confirmed MS‑13 members.

claim: "Greg Abbott said it would be a ‘waste’ to expand pre-k to all Texas children."
rationale: I could not find verifiable primary-source evidence that Abbott used the quoted phrasing that expanding pre-K to all Texas children would be “a ‘waste’.” While Governor Abbott has opposed universal pre-K funding and argued for targeted or existing programs instead, the precise quoted assertion appears to be a paraphrase or mischaracterization rather than a documented direct quote. Absent a reliable transcript or recording showing him saying that exact line, the claim as stated is unverified and likely false.

claim: Says the late Lady Bird Johnson sicced the CIA on actress and singer Eartha Kitt after Kitt spoke out against the Vietnam War during a White House luncheon in January 1968.
rationale: Eartha Kitt did publicly denounce the Vietnam War at a White House luncheon in January 1968 and suffered professional backlash and government scrutiny afterward, but there is no credible evidence that Lady Bird Johnson "sicced the CIA" on her. Contemporary records and later reporting document FBI files and industry blacklisting, not a documented order from the First Lady to the CIA. The claim conflates Kitt’s well-documented criticism and subsequent surveillance with an unproven allegation of a direct CIA directive from Lady Bird Johnson.

claim: In the case of a catastrophic event, the Atlanta-area offices of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention will self-destruct.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that the CDC’s Atlanta offices are equipped to physically "self-destruct" in a catastrophic event. Public descriptions of CDC emergency and biosecurity measures describe lockdowns, evacuations, containment and decontamination procedures, not deliberate demolition of buildings; the self-destruct claim appears to be a rumor or misinterpretation.

claim: "We have developed a wind industry (in Washington state) from zero to $6 billion in 12 years."
rationale: The claim is inaccurate as stated: Washington was not starting from “zero” wind industry within the past 12 years—utility-scale wind projects in the state date back well before that (e.g., early 2000s and late 1990s projects on the WA–OR border). The $6 billion figure is also unsourced and ambiguous (investment, annual revenue, cumulative value?), so the specific numeric claim is unsupported.

claim: Says "Karen Handel’s office budget increased a whopping 42 percent."
rationale: This statement is misleading. Contemporary fact-checks found the 42% figure resulted from cherry-picking specific line items and fiscal years (and including transferred election-related funds) rather than showing a straightforward 42% increase in the office’s overall, ongoing operating budget. When budgets are compared on a consistent basis the large percentage jump does not hold up.

claim: Says a pandemic occurs exactly every 100 years.
rationale: This is incorrect: pandemics are not regular, clock‑like events that occur every 100 years. Historical pandemics (e.g., Black Death in the 14th century, multiple influenza pandemics in the 20th and 21st centuries, and COVID‑19) occur at irregular intervals driven by pathogen evolution, ecology, and human behavior rather than a fixed centennial cycle.

claim: Unvaccinated people "are making the vaccinated people sick and die, but the unvaccinated people are not dead or sick."
rationale: The claim is not supported by evidence. For COVID‑19, vaccination substantially lowers the risk of severe disease and death, and unvaccinated people have consistently experienced higher rates of infection, hospitalization, and mortality. Although vaccinated people can have breakthrough infections and sometimes transmit the virus, the statement that unvaccinated people are not sick or dying while causing the vaccinated to die is false.

claim: Says Donald Trump "wants to kick thousands of kids off of BadgerCare."
rationale: There is no reliable evidence that Donald Trump explicitly proposed a policy to directly remove thousands of children from Wisconsin’s BadgerCare. His administration pushed Medicaid spending limits, waivers, and work requirements aimed at reducing federal Medicaid costs—policies that primarily target adults and could indirectly reduce enrollments, but not an explicit plan to ‘kick kids off’ BadgerCare. The claim is a rhetorical exaggeration of policies that might indirectly affect coverage.

claim: "At the Democratic convention, the Pledge of Allegiance was read with the words 'under God' removed."
rationale: The claim overstates the situation: there is no evidence the Democratic National Convention as an institution formally removed “under God” from the Pledge. While isolated individual speakers or clips in various events have omitted the words (or been edited), contemporaneous reporting and fact-checks did not find an official, convention-wide excision of the phrase. The claim therefore misrepresents selective instances as a deliberate convention action.

claim: Says Mitt Romney "put Planned Parenthood on a state medical board but failed to put a pro-life group on the same board."
rationale: The claim is misleading: governors appoint individuals to state medical boards rather than officially placing organizations on them, and there is no clear evidence that Romney formally 'put Planned Parenthood' as an organization on a Massachusetts medical board while expressly refusing to appoint a pro‑life group. Some reporting mentions appointments of physicians who had affiliations with Planned Parenthood or reproductive health expertise, but that is not the same as designating an organization as a board member or documented refusal to seat a specific pro‑life group. The statement conflates individual appointments with organizational representation and omits necessary context.

claim: "Corona is so bad, this guy died twice!"
rationale: The literal claim that someone "died twice" from coronavirus is false — biologically a person cannot die twice. Reports that use that wording typically refer to being mistakenly declared dead and later resuscitated or to administrative errors, not two actual deaths; there are no verified cases of a person dying twice from COVID-19.

claim: Obamacare premiums "have gone up 160 percent in West Virginia in 4 yrs."
rationale: This claim is misleading. ACA premium changes vary by year, county, and plan; while some individual plans or counties in West Virginia experienced very large increases, there was not a statewide standard 160% increase across the typical benchmark plans over a single contiguous four-year period. Without specifying years, counties, or which plan (benchmark/average/silver) the 160% figure is not an accurate representation.

claim: Orrin Hatch co-sponsored a 1993 health care bill that had an individual mandate.
