rationale: This is false. Billie Eilish does not have a younger sister — her known sibling is her older brother Finneas O'Connell — and there are no credible reports or evidence of any sister of hers having an OnlyFans account. The claim appears to be a misidentification or misinformation.

claim: This is the first time since World War II that five nuclear-powered aircraft carriers were docked together.
rationale: The claim is false or misleading. Nuclear-powered aircraft carriers did not exist during World War II (the first U.S. nuclear carrier, USS Enterprise CVN-65, was commissioned in 1961), so the phrasing “first time since World War II” is nonsensical, and contemporary reports and photo-claims of five carriers together have been disputed or miscaptioned rather than documenting a unique first-ever occurrence. There is no verifiable record that five nuclear-powered carriers had never been co-located prior to the cited event.

claim: The federal government is sending refugees to states with governors who are "Republicans, not to the Democrats."
rationale: There is no evidence of a federal policy that sends refugees only to states with Republican governors and not to Democratic ones. Refugee placements are organized by federal agencies and local resettlement agencies based on capacity, housing, services, and sponsors, and refugees have been resettled in states governed by both parties; governors do not direct placements by party affiliation.

claim: "All of the records, as far as I know, about what we did with health care, those are already available."
rationale: The statement asserts that literally all records about what was done with health care are already available. While many public items (legislation, votes, press releases, official reports) are accessible, internal communications, drafts, privileged legal documents, personnel records, and certain health or proprietary data are typically not publicly available, so the absolute claim is incorrect. The qualifier “as far as I know” does not make the universal claim true in practice.

claim: Since 2009, the Ohio Republican Party has made more contacts with voters — nearly 6.6 million — than any other GOP state organization in the nation.
rationale: I could not verify the comparative claim: there is no publicly available, independent nationwide record showing every GOP state committee's total voter contacts since 2009. The specific figure of 'nearly 6.6 million' appears to originate from internal party reporting or press releases, and without audited, comparable data the assertion that Ohio has made more contacts than any other state party is unproven. Therefore the claim should be treated as false unless corroborated by independent data.

claim: "We have pay equity. When you think about that wage gap, we all know it's 78 cents to the dollar. Well, in New York state it's 90 cents to the dollar."
rationale: The claim mixes imprecise, context-dependent figures and implies pay equity exists; it is misleading. The often-cited “78 cents” figure is a specific, historically dated estimate that varies by year and by how earnings are measured, and New York’s female-to-male earnings ratio is not uniformly 90 cents across standard data sources and definitions. Depending on the year and whether you use median annual, full-time hourly, or age-adjusted measures, both the national and New York gaps differ from the blanket numbers asserted.

claim: Says West Virginia is "down to around 50 percent of the adult workers who are actually working now because of addiction or conviction."
rationale: The statement mixes facts and a causal claim. While West Virginia’s employment‑to‑population/labor‑force participation rates have been unusually low (in the low‑50s percentage range in recent years), there is no evidence that addiction and criminal convictions alone are the primary reasons that the rate is “around 50 percent.” Multiple factors (aging population, disability rates, economic structure, long‑term health issues, and local labor demand) contribute, and published data do not attribute the shortfall mostly or solely to addiction/conviction.

claim: "Our most important work has been creating and retaining almost 55,000 Ohio jobs."
rationale: The statement is unverifiable as presented because it does not identify who “Our” refers to or specify a timeframe or data source. Independent employment data from BLS and Ohio state reports do not corroborate a single, clearly attributable "almost 55,000" jobs claim without additional context, so the assertion cannot be confirmed and is assessed as false.

claim: "If Joe Manchin had his way, Judge Gorsuch never would have been able to get a vote."
rationale: False. Manchin did not have the power to unilaterally prevent a floor vote, Republicans invoked the Senate "nuclear option" in 2017 to change cloture rules and proceed to a confirmation vote, and Manchin himself voted in favor of Judge Gorsuch’s confirmation. Thus it is incorrect to claim that Gorsuch "never would have been able to get a vote" if Manchin had his way.

claim: "We're experiencing a net outflow of illegal, undocumented workers from America back to Mexico."
rationale: Contemporary migration data and reporting show high numbers of migrants encountered at the U.S. border and substantial net arrivals in recent years, not a net outflow back to Mexico. While Mexican migration to the U.S. slowed and even reversed for a period in the 2010s, overall undocumented flows recently have been into the U.S., often from Mexico and many other countries, and returns/deportations do not exceed arrivals.

claim: Says Gov. Greg Abbott offered the uncle of a Uvalde shooting victim money to say "we don’t need stronger gun laws."
rationale: Contemporaneous reporting and fact-checkers found no evidence that Gov. Greg Abbott or his office offered money to an uncle of a Uvalde victim to say "we don’t need stronger gun laws." Media accounts documented the uncle’s remarks but did not corroborate any payment or offer from Abbott, and Abbott’s office denied making such an offer. The claim appears to be a mischaracterization or amplification of unverified social-media posts.

claim: Quotes Kamala Harris as saying: "After we impeach, we round up the Trump supporters."
rationale: There is no credible record—no transcript, video, or reputable news/fact-check report—showing Kamala Harris ever saying “After we impeach, we round up the Trump supporters.” Major fact‑checking organizations investigated this claim and found it fabricated or the result of manipulated/edited content. The wording is inconsistent with her public statements about accountability and due process.

claim: "Two Iraqis came here to this country, were radicalized and they were the masterminds behind the Bowling Green massacre. … It didn't get covered"
rationale: There was no "Bowling Green massacre." In 2011 two Iraqi nationals were arrested in Kentucky for attempting to provide material support to al‑Qaeda in Iraq and later pleaded guilty; they were not masterminds of any massacre. The claim conflates those arrests with a non‑existent attack and is factually incorrect.

claim: "Simply being in this country without documentation is not a crime"
rationale: Under U.S. federal law, mere unlawful presence (being in the country without valid immigration status) is generally a civil immigration violation handled through removal proceedings, not a criminal offense. However, separate federal statutes criminalize unlawful entry at the border and reentry after removal, and other offenses (fraud, certain state crimes) can apply in particular situations.

claim: "This is the only state in the country that bypassed the General Assembly to authorize [in-state tuition for undocumented immigrants]."
rationale: The assertion that a single state is uniquely the only one to have bypassed its legislature to authorize in-state tuition for undocumented immigrants is not supported. Multiple states have used administrative actions, board-of-regents decisions, executive directives, or court rulings at various times to enable in-state tuition without a new legislative statute, so it is unlikely any one state is uniquely the sole example.

claim: "Our country's got this huge debt, and (President Barack) Obama says raise taxes and keep spending more."
rationale: This statement misrepresents President Obama’s positions. While Obama supported some tax increases (notably on higher-income earners) and backed stimulus spending early in his term, he also proposed deficit-reduction plans, spending caps, and entitlement reforms rather than an open-ended policy of “keep spending more.” The claim overgeneralizes and combines separate policies into an inaccurate slogan-like assertion.

claim: "Before Congress, (Tom) Cotton got paid handsomely working for insurance companies and corporate interests."
rationale: Public biographical information shows Tom Cotton's pre‑Congress career was dominated by military service (infantry deployments to Iraq and Afghanistan), a Harvard Law degree and judicial clerkship, and practicing law — not a documented period of being paid as an insurance‑company executive or corporate lobbyist. While as a lawyer he may have done private‑sector legal work that involved corporate clients, there is no clear evidence he ‘got paid handsomely working for insurance companies and corporate interests’ as the claim asserts.

claim: "Under Gov. Kasich, Ohio wages have increased by $10.3 billion."
rationale: The claim is not verifiable as stated and appears to rely on an ambiguous aggregation. While Ohio wages did rise during John Kasich’s governorship, sources differ on whether comparisons refer to annual payroll, cumulative payroll, private-sector wages, or inflation-adjusted figures, and no authoritative dataset unambiguously supports the precise $10.3 billion increase for the entire term. Without a clear timeframe and data definition the claim is misleading.

claim: House Republicans required the use of Styrofoam cups in House cafeterias that are "part of Koch Industries."
rationale: There is no evidence that House Republicans instituted a rule requiring Styrofoam cups in House cafeterias, nor are the cafeterias part of Koch Industries. House dining facilities are managed by the federal Architect of the Capitol, not a private company, and no authoritative reports show a GOP mandate tying cup use to a Koch-owned supplier. The claim appears to conflate supplier ownership with a supposed House requirement, which is unsupported.

claim: "If there were not derivatives, there would be no bank loans at all today."
rationale: This is false. Bank lending existed for centuries before modern derivatives markets and banks can and do make loans funded by deposits, capital, and interbank/central bank facilities without using derivatives. While derivatives (swaps, options, credit derivatives) are important modern tools for hedging interest-rate, currency and credit risks and can increase the scale and flexibility of lending, they are not a necessary precondition for loans to exist.

claim: "One of the first nurses to receive the vaccine in AL is now dead."
rationale: There is no credible evidence or official report that one of the first nurses vaccinated in Alabama died as a result of receiving the COVID-19 vaccine. Media fact-checkers and local health authorities investigated similar social-media claims and found them to be misattributions or unproven assertions rather than confirmed vaccine-related deaths.

claim: Say Bernie Sanders "won Nevada after all."
rationale: The claim as stated is ambiguous because it gives no year or context. Bernie Sanders did win the Nevada Democratic caucus in 2020, but he lost Nevada in 2016 to Hillary Clinton, so the blanket statement without a timeframe cannot be verified as true.

claim: "COVID19 PCR tests are scientifically meaningless."
rationale: The claim is false. PCR (polymerase chain reaction) tests detect SARS‑CoV‑2 genetic material and have been widely validated as sensitive and specific tools for diagnosis and surveillance; they are not "scientifically meaningless." That said, PCR detects viral RNA rather than directly proving infectious virus, and results must be interpreted with attention to timing, sampling quality, and cycle‑threshold limitations.

claim: "Due to ... tax cuts and lower (property) values, 2009 property taxes were almost $3 billion below 2007 property taxes."
rationale: The claim cannot be verified as stated because it gives no jurisdiction or data source; aggregate property-tax receipts are determined at local/state levels and require specific budget figures. Although the 2007–2009 recession did lower property values and some jurisdictions enacted tax cuts, I found no substantiating evidence that 2009 property taxes were nearly $3 billion below 2007 in any unspecified aggregate. Without a named state, city, or dataset the assertion is unsubstantiated.

claim: If Wisconsin Gov. Tony Evers "had passed his (gas) tax increases ... fuel prices would be at least a dime higher.
rationale: The statement is unverified and likely misleading because whether retail pump prices would be “at least a dime higher” depends on the exact size of the proposed excise increase and on how much of any tax is passed through to consumers. Public descriptions of Gov. Evers’ fuel-tax proposals do not unambiguously show a guaranteed +$0.10/gal increase, and market factors can offset or amplify tax pass-through. Without a specific legislative proposal and empirical pass-through evidence the categorical claim cannot be supported.

claim: Agriculture contributes $71 billion to Georgia’s economy annually, making it the state’s largest industry.
rationale: State economic-impact studies and Georgia Department of Agriculture/University of Georgia summaries have reported that agriculture and related industries generate roughly $70–75 billion annually in Georgia, and these reports commonly describe agriculture as the state’s largest industry by economic contribution. The figure $71 billion falls within that commonly cited range, though it reflects total economic impact (including agribusiness and multiplier effects) rather than only farm cash receipts.

claim: Barack Obama is the "first president to file lawsuits against the states he swore an oath to protect."
rationale: This claim is false. The Department of Justice and prior presidential administrations have long brought suits against state governments to enforce federal laws (for example many civil‑rights and voting‑rights enforcement suits in the 1950s–1960s and other regulatory suits in later administrations), so Obama was not the first president whose executive branch sued states. The phrasing also conflates the president personally filing lawsuits with the executive branch (DOJ) acting on the United States' behalf.

claim: Says no one from the Bush family attended the 2012 Republican National Convention and "there was no President Bush" at the 2008 convention.
rationale: The claim is an absolute statement of non‑attendance but is contradicted by contemporary reporting and photographic records showing members of the Bush family and/or a President Bush present at those Republican conventions. Historical coverage indicates at least some Bush representation at the 2008 and 2012 RNCs, so the blanket claim that “no one from the Bush family” attended 2012 and “there was no President Bush” at 2008 is incorrect.

claim: "In New York State, Democrats blocked a Bill expanding College Tuition for Gold Star families after approving aid for illegal immigrants."
rationale: I could not find reliable evidence that New York Democrats blocked a specific bill to expand college tuition benefits for Gold Star families immediately after approving aid for undocumented migrants. New York has approved various migrant relief funds and there have been disputes over tuition and benefits, but the claim ties together a specific blocking action and a chronological cause that is not supported by public legislative records or credible reporting. The statement appears to conflate separate votes and political rhetoric rather than reflect a verifiable single legislative event.

claim: Barack Obama "is the first ex-president to ever speak against his successor."
rationale: This is false. Multiple ex-presidents publicly criticized their successors long before Obama — for example Theodore Roosevelt actively attacked and then ran against his successor William Howard Taft in 1912, Herbert Hoover openly opposed Franklin D. Roosevelt’s New Deal policies, and Jimmy Carter criticized Ronald Reagan’s policies after leaving office. Thus Obama is not the first ex-president to speak against his successor.

claim: Says the Obama administration approved a major disaster declaration for Oklahoma in 2009, when nine of the state’s 77 counties burned for "about three days," while Texas wildfires have been burning for longer without such a declaration.
rationale: This claim mixes a kernel of truth with misleading and unverifiable elements. The Obama administration did approve at least one major disaster declaration related to Oklahoma wildfires in 2009, but the specific phrasing about “nine of the state’s 77 counties burned for about three days” is a selective, imprecise characterization and the comparison to Texas is vague and time‑dependent. Whether Texas did or did not have a comparable declaration depends on particular fires and dates and is not supported by the blanket assertion in the claim.

claim: "Military take over on May 11 confirmed!"
rationale: The statement asserts a confirmed military takeover on May 11 but gives no country, year, or source; such an event would require corroboration from multiple credible news outlets or official statements. Without verifiable reporting or contextual details, the claim cannot be treated as confirmed and therefore is judged false.

claim: As Florida secretary of state, Kurt Browning "allowed 1,800 illegal voters to register in Florida."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Kurt Browning personally "allowed 1,800 illegal voters to register." Public reporting and official reviews of alleged non‑citizen or otherwise ineligible registrations in Florida have produced much smaller confirmed counts or have reflected data‑matching/administrative errors, and the claim conflates raw flags with confirmed illegal registrations. Additionally, a secretary of state administers processes and databases rather than individually approving thousands of registrations.

claim: The newly drawn congressional district map in Arkansas "keeps communities together."
rationale: The claim is misleading: independent observers, civil-rights groups, and news coverage of Arkansas's recently redrawn congressional map have concluded the plan fractures key population centers and concentrates minority voters into a single district rather than broadly preserving communities of interest. The map was drawn by a Republican-controlled legislature with the practical effect of protecting a 4–1 GOP delegation, which critics say required slicing some cities and neighborhoods across districts instead of keeping them whole.

claim: Says no elections protest was filed, McCready conceded and "every" county board certified its results from the Mark Harris, Dan McCready race.
rationale: This is incorrect. Dan McCready did not concede and Democrats filed formal complaints and requested an investigation into absentee-ballot irregularities; in December 2018 the North Carolina State Board of Elections unanimously refused to certify the congressional result and ordered a new election after finding evidence of fraud tied to a campaign operative. While many county boards had completed local canvasses, the State Board withheld final certification for the race, so the claim that no protest was filed, McCready conceded, and 'every' county board certified is misleading and false.

claim: "In 2009, Mitch McConnell was the person that’s saying, 'Hey, we should get all the ethics information in before we do the hearings.' "
rationale: I am not aware of any contemporaneous record or widely reported attribution from 2009 showing Senate Republican leader Mitch McConnell saying that line; it appears to be a misattribution. Key 2009 confirmation-discussion quotes and media coverage from that year do not contain this informal phrasing attributed to McConnell, and similar procedural comments were more commonly voiced by committee chairs or Democrats seeking paperwork. Without corroborating contemporaneous reporting or a primary source, the claim is likely false or misattributed.

claim: Says Rep. Matt Gaetz and Sen. Ted Cruz took two weeks paid sick leave to self-quarantine. Gaetz "voted in 2013 to make it illegal for any city in Florida to enact paid sick leave," and Cruz "voted in 2015 in the U.S. Senate against paid sick leave."
rationale: The claim bundles multiple assertions, and key elements are unverified or misleading. While both Gaetz and Cruz publicly entered self‑quarantine at times during the COVID‑19 pandemic, there is no clear evidence they each took a distinct two‑week “paid sick leave” in the way the claim implies; members of Congress continue to receive salary and routine leave rules differ from typical employer sick‑leave benefits. The voting assertions are also imprecise: records do not cleanly support the blanket statement that Gaetz in 2013 voted to make it illegal for any Florida city to enact paid sick leave, nor that Cruz cast a single explicit 2015 Senate vote plainly described as “against paid sick leave” without identifying the specific bill or amendment.

claim: "Wisconsin took a break, and when they returned, Biden coincidentally came back ahead by 100k."
rationale: This is false as stated. In the 2020 Wisconsin presidential count there was a temporary pause in reporting in some jurisdictions and late-counted absentee ballots helped Biden overtake Trump, but the change was on the order of tens of thousands — his final Wisconsin margin was about 20,000 votes — not a 100,000-vote swing when counting resumed.

claim: Scott Walker "couldn’t get his own party" to back more than a 500-student increase in Milwaukee’s school choice program, but in Indiana, "Mitch Daniels’ voucher program is approaching 30,000 students two years after opening."
rationale: The claim combines two verifiable points that align with contemporary reporting: Wisconsin Republicans balked at a large expansion of Milwaukee’s voucher program and approved only a modest increase (roughly on the order of a few hundred students), and Indiana’s school voucher program under Gov. Mitch Daniels expanded very rapidly after its launch and reached the neighborhood of 30,000 participants within about two years. Both statements match widely reported descriptions comparing Walker’s constrained expansion to Indiana’s fast-growing program.

claim: "Same little boy died of COVID-19 in three different countries. Still don’t believe the media is #fakenews?"
rationale: The claim is false. Independent fact-checkers have shown that viral posts reused or miscaptioned the same photo across different reports, but there is no credible evidence that one boy died of COVID-19 in three different countries. The situation reflects recycled imagery and misattribution, not a single child dying multiple times.

claim: "Of all cities in the United States with more than 100,000 people, Providence is the 183rd safest."
rationale: The claim gives a precise national rank but provides no source or year, and there is no widely accepted federal or academic list that names Providence exactly the 183rd safest city among U.S. cities over 100,000. Safety rankings vary by methodology (violent vs. property crime, per-capita adjustments, year) and change annually; Providence more commonly appears with higher-than-median violent crime rates, so this specific rank is unsupported without a cited report.

claim: "59 people die as pastor gives them dettol to drink in church to prevent coronavirus."
rationale: This specific claim circulated on social media but could not be corroborated by credible contemporary news reports or health authorities reporting 59 deaths from a pastor giving Dettol to congregants. It matches a known pattern of viral misinformation about ingesting disinfectants to prevent COVID-19; while accidental poisonings from corrosive cleaning products have occurred, there is no reliable evidence for this exact event and death toll.

claim: "Violent crime is now going down for the first time in a long while."
rationale: The statement is too general and therefore misleading. Violent-crime trends differ by country, city, and specific crime type; some places have recently seen declines while others have not, and the U.S. saw long declines from the 1990s into the 2010s followed by increases in parts of the 2015–2020 period and mixed changes thereafter. Saying "now going down for the first time in a long while" asserts a uniform, novel reversal that is not supported by available, heterogeneous data.

claim: A Colgate toothpaste is subject to "recall."
rationale: The statement is too vague and lacks any identifying details (brand variant, lot number, date, or source) so it cannot be verified as currently true. While specific Colgate products have been subject to recalls at various times in the past, without a named product or official recall notice this blanket claim is unsubstantiated.

claim: Four (maybe five) Latinos have served on the Austin City Council.
rationale: The claim is unlikely to be accurate as stated — historical records and broad knowledge of Austin politics indicate more than four individuals of Latino heritage have served on the Austin City Council over the decades. The claimant’s hedged “maybe five” and lack of timeframe suggests uncertainty; without specifying years or definitions the number as presented appears too low.

claim: "Not only is there no scientific evidence that CO2 is a pollutant, higher CO2 concentrations actually help ecosystems support more plant and animal life."
rationale: The claim is false. Atmospheric CO2 is a well-established greenhouse gas and abundant scientific evidence links rising CO2 to global warming and harmful climate impacts; CO2 is also treated as a pollutant for regulatory purposes. While elevated CO2 can stimulate plant growth in some controlled or nutrient-rich contexts (the CO2 fertilization effect), those benefits are limited by nutrients, water, pests and can reduce plant nutritive value, and they do not offset widespread negative ecosystem effects of climate change, ocean acidification and extreme events driven by higher CO2.

claim: Says remdesivir is responsible for killing patients hospitalized with COVID-19.
rationale: Randomized controlled trials and large WHO-led studies did not find that remdesivir causes increased mortality in hospitalized COVID-19 patients; instead they showed mixed benefit on recovery time and no consistent signal of harm causing deaths. While remdesivir can have adverse effects (eg, liver enzyme elevations, kidney concerns) there is no credible evidence that it is generally 'responsible for killing' hospitalized COVID-19 patients. Claims of causation ignore trial data, confounding by indication, and the absence of a demonstrated increase in mortality in controlled studies.

claim: "Since I took office, Michigan has added more than 25,000 auto jobs."
rationale: I cannot verify this precise numeric claim from available knowledge; while Michigan has seen job gains in auto-related sectors since recent governors took office, publicly reported counts for 'auto jobs' vary by definition (manufacturing only vs. broader supply chain) and available data do not conclusively confirm an increase of more than 25,000 tied exactly to the stated tenure. Without a cited source and a clear start date and definition, the claim is not reliably substantiated.

claim: Four state Assembly Democrats "scored a death blow to northeast Wisconsin’s economy" by killing hundreds of jobs at a potential Bass Pro Shops near Green Bay.
rationale: The statement is a partisan, causal claim that is not supported by clear public evidence. Large retail projects like a Bass Pro proposal involve developers, local councils, financing and market decisions, and reporting does not credibly attribute the project's cancellation or the loss of “hundreds of jobs” solely to four state Assembly Democrats. The phrase “scored a death blow” is rhetorical and overstates causation beyond verifiable facts.

claim: "California has more kids in poverty ... than virtually any other state."
rationale: Interpreted as a statement about the absolute number of children in poverty, the claim is accurate: because California is the most populous state, recent U.S. Census/ACS and child-poverty estimates consistently show it has the largest count of children living in poverty among states. The claim does not refer to child poverty rate (percentage), where California is not necessarily the highest. This makes the statement true in the usual sense people mean by “more kids in poverty.”

claim: "The Red Cross sells your donated blood to hospitals for $150 and then that hospital charges you thousands for a blood transfusion."
rationale: The statement mixes a factual practice with inaccurate specifics. Donors are unpaid and organizations like the Red Cross charge hospitals fees to cover collection, testing, and distribution of blood, but the fee is not a universal fixed $150 and varies by product and region. Hospitals may bill patients (including large facility and procedure fees) that can far exceed the blood product fee, but it’s misleading to claim the Red Cross simply "sells your donated blood for $150" and that hospitals always charge "thousands" for the blood itself.

claim: Tax increases under Michigan Gov. Jennifer Granholm led to state unemployment going from 6.8 percent to 15.3 percent.
rationale: While Michigan unemployment did rise sharply during Jennifer Granholm's tenure, the state’s unemployment rate peaked around roughly 14.9% in 2009 during the Great Recession, not definitively from 6.8% to 15.3% solely because of tax increases. The large jump was driven primarily by the national recession and the collapse of the auto industry in Michigan; attributing that rise to state tax increases is unsupported and ignores major macroeconomic causes.

claim: "There are no tax increases in this debt limit bill. Period."
rationale: The claim is unverifiable as an absolute statement because it does not specify which debt limit bill and many such bills have included tax-related provisions, offsets, or revenue changes even if they do not raise headline tax rates. Without naming the specific legislation, one cannot responsibly assert “no tax increases” with certainty; historically some debt-limit or budget compromise measures have contained revenue-raising or tax-code changes. Because the claim is categorical (“Period”) and lacks context, it is judged false as stated.

claim: "At John Lewis funeral Obama told a room full of people that rooms full of people is too dangerous so we must mail in vote."
rationale: This specific claim is false. Public records and contemporaneous news coverage of John Lewis's memorial services in 2020 do not show Barack Obama telling attendees at the funeral that "rooms full of people is too dangerous so we must mail in vote." While public figures (including Obama) did encourage voting by mail and cautioned about COVID-era gatherings generally in 2020, there is no evidence he made that statement at Lewis's funeral.

claim: Says Paul Ryan’s budget plan "ends Medicare."
rationale: This is misleading rather than literally true. Paul Ryan’s budget proposals did not immediately terminate Medicare for current beneficiaries; they proposed restructuring future Medicare into a premium-support/voucher-style system or converting it to block grants for people who become eligible later, which critics call an “end” to traditional Medicare but is not an immediate program shutdown. Whether that restructuring amounts to ‘ending Medicare’ is a political interpretation, not a factual description of an immediate termination.

claim: Says he didn't cancel a political rally because after Sept. 11, "the New York Stock Exchange was open the following day."
rationale: The statement is false because the New York Stock Exchange did not reopen the day after the Sept. 11 attacks; it remained closed for several days and reopened on Sept. 17, 2001. Because the factual premise is incorrect, any claim that someone justified not cancelling a political rally by saying “the New York Stock Exchange was open the following day” is inaccurate or misleading unless quoting a person who misstated the historical fact.

claim: Wisconsin is "run by Democrats right now," so they should address election social distancing concerns.
rationale: The claim that Wisconsin is “run by Democrats right now” is misleading. While the governor (Tony Evers) and some statewide offices are held by Democrats, the state legislature has been Republican-controlled, and election administration is carried out largely by local clerks and constrained by state law and courts, so responsibility for election social-distancing measures is shared and not solely a Democratic prerogative.

claim: "A clear majority of Americans support removing the cost-sharing requirement for prescription contraceptive coverage."
rationale: Multiple national polls over the past decade have consistently found that a majority of Americans support insurance coverage of prescription contraception without cost-sharing (i.e., no copay), not removing that requirement. Public opinion generally favors preserving or expanding no-cost contraceptive coverage, so the claim that a clear majority support removing the cost-sharing requirement is inconsistent with typical survey results.

claim: Says recent polls show Americans agree with Republicans that the federal debt ceiling should not be raised and the debt and deficit should be dealt with mostly by cutting spending.
rationale: This claim is misleading. Multiple recent national polls have generally found that a majority of voters prefer raising the debt ceiling to avoid default and that Americans’ preferences on deficit reduction are mixed (many favor a blend of spending cuts and revenue increases and protect popular programs), not a clear consensus in favor of refusing to raise the ceiling and relying mostly on spending cuts as Republican leaders often propose.

claim: John McCain's health care plan "leaves you on your own to pay McCain’s health insurance tax."
rationale: There was no provision in John McCain’s major health proposals that created a specific "health insurance tax" individuals were forced to pay. McCain’s 2008 platform emphasized refundable tax credits, market reforms (e.g., buying across state lines) and opposed universal mandates; critics sometimes framed changes to tax treatment as a new burden, but the literal claim is inaccurate or misleading. No widely recognized McCain plan imposed a named individual "health insurance tax."

claim: Says "Canada has one-tenth of our population—yet it issues far more high-skilled visas (more than 150,000) yearly than we do (65,000)."
rationale: The first part (Canada ≈ one-tenth the U.S. population) is approximately correct, but the visa comparison is misleading and therefore false. Canada does admit well over 150,000 economic-class/worker entries in recent years, but the U.S. issues many more high-skilled authorizations overall when you count H‑1B (65,000 cap plus 20,000 master’s cap), employment‑based green cards, L/TN visas and other categories. Comparing a single U.S. visa cap figure to aggregated Canadian admissions is an apples-to-oranges contrast and gives a false impression.

claim: "More black babies are aborted in NYC than born."
rationale: The claim is not supported by available vital-statistics patterns: while Black women in NYC have a disproportionately high share of induced abortion relative to their population, citywide counts of live births to Black mothers generally exceed induced terminations. The statement also conflates categories (race of fetus vs mother, year, residency) that can distort comparisons.

claim: Says Texas schools have had "massive increases" in class sizes with Rick Perry as governor.
rationale: There is not clear evidence that class sizes across Texas experienced “massive increases” during Rick Perry’s tenure as governor. Statewide pupil-to-teacher ratios and enrollment/teacher trends changed modestly and varied by district; some districts saw increases while others kept sizes stable or reduced them. The claim overstates the statewide effect without specifying years or metrics.

claim: "In Ohio, we invested in our children, raising school funding by 5.5 percent in the last budget."
rationale: The claim cannot be confirmed as stated because it lacks a specific budget year and the 5.5% figure does not match a clearly documented, across-the-board increase in Ohio K–12 funding in the most recent biennial budgets. Ohio budget increases vary by measure (total appropriation, state share, per‑pupil, or formula support), and public budget summaries for recent cycles report different percentage changes depending on which measure is used. Without a precise biennium and funding metric, the 5.5% claim is unverified and likely misleading.

claim: New and proposed state laws on voting mean "if you are going to be standing in that line for all those hours, you can’t have any water or any food."
rationale: This is not universally true. Some recent state laws and proposals restrict third parties from distributing food or water within a specified buffer zone around polling places or bar gifts intended to influence voters, but they do not enact a blanket prohibition on voters bringing or consuming their own food or water while waiting in line across all states. Rules vary by jurisdiction and many laws include exceptions or target paid/distributed refreshments rather than personal use.

claim: Says Tallahassee mayor Andrew Gillum "wants to make Florida not a sanctuary city but a sanctuary state."
rationale: I cannot find a clear, reliable record that Gillum used the exact phrasing “wants to make Florida not a sanctuary city but a sanctuary state.” During the 2018 campaign he spoke about protecting immigrants and cited support for local noncooperation with federal immigration enforcement, but those remarks were often paraphrased or taken out of context. As Tallahassee mayor he had no authority to make statewide policy, and fact-check coverage at the time treated the precise quote as disputed or misleading.

claim: Says Supreme Court nominee Merrick Garland "voted, so the folks know, in Washington, D.C., to keep guns away from private citizens."
rationale: The claim is misleading. Merrick Garland was a federal judge on the D.C. Circuit and therefore participated in judicial rulings in specific cases—he did not cast legislative votes in Washington, D.C. There is no clear single vote showing he simply voted to "keep guns away from private citizens" as a broad policy; judicial decisions are case‑specific and his record does not support that blanket characterization.

claim: Data show that more white people than Black people are shot and killed by police.
rationale: Most large databases of U.S. police shootings (e.g., Washington Post, Mapping Police Violence) report higher absolute numbers of white victims than Black victims in recent years. However this statement omits the important caveat that Black people are killed at a higher rate per capita, and year-to-year counts and classifications can vary by data source.

claim: "The president and vice president can't be from the same state."
rationale: The U.S. Constitution does not prohibit the president and vice president from being from the same state. The 12th Amendment only restricts electors from casting both of their votes for two candidates who are inhabitants of the elector's own state, which can reduce that state's available electoral votes for a same‑state ticket but does not make such a ticket illegal.

claim: "If we keep the minimum wage at the current level, then single-parent families earning the minimum wage at a full-time job will live in poverty in New Jersey."
rationale: The claim is too general and therefore incorrect. Whether a full‑time minimum‑wage single parent lives in poverty depends on family size and the exact wage: annual pay = hourly wage × 2,080 hours, and 2023 federal poverty thresholds imply a two‑person household needs about $9.50/hr, three people about $12/hr, and four people about $14.40/hr to exceed the poverty line. New Jersey’s recent minimum wage has been well above the two‑person threshold (and around or above the three/four‑person thresholds depending on year and employer size), so some single‑parent households (e.g., with one child) would typically be above the poverty line while larger families could still be below. The blanket “will live in poverty” statement is therefore false.

claim: Video shows a child who tested positive for COVID-19 "being separated from their parents."
rationale: There is insufficient verifiable information to confirm that the referenced video actually shows a child who tested positive for COVID-19 being separated from their parents. Without an identified video, date, location, or corroborating reporting, the claim cannot be substantiated and could reflect miscaptioning or missing context. Given the uncertainty, the claim is treated as false pending reliable evidence.

claim: "Illinois suffered 1,652 overdose deaths in 2014 ... of which 40 percent were associated with heroin. Illinois is ranked number one in the nation for a decline in treatment capacity between 2007 and 2012, and is now ranked the third worst in the country for state-funded treatment capacity."
rationale: The claim bundles precise counts and national rankings that I cannot confirm from authoritative public data without a cited source. While Illinois did see substantial overdose and heroin-involved deaths mid-decade and some reports documented reductions in publicly funded treatment slots, the specific figure of 1,652 deaths with '40% heroin-associated' and the asserted #1 decline (2007–2012) and 'third worst' current ranking depend on particular data definitions and sources and are not verifiably true as stated. Because key numeric and ranking assertions lack a clear, authoritative citation and hinge on varying definitions of 'treatment capacity,' the composite claim is not supported as presented.

claim: "It takes almost a year for a refugee to be processed in the United States."
rationale: The time to process a refugee application for the U.S. is highly variable and there is no single standard of "almost a year." Some cases are completed in a few months but many take longer than a year due to security vetting, medical checks, interviews, and resettlement logistics; others are expedited. Saying it takes almost a year as a blanket statement is therefore misleading.

claim: Cher "is moving to Canada because of President Trump."
rationale: The claim that Cher is moving to Canada because of President Trump is false. While Cher tweeted and joked in 2016 about moving to Canada if Donald Trump won, there is no credible evidence she ever actually relocated and she later characterized the remarks as hyperbole/expressions of frustration. Current public records and coverage do not show she moved to Canada for that reason.

claim: Says the U.S. Postal Service has taken no taxpayer aid since 1971, funds operations entirely from the sale of stamps and related products and makes an "operational profit year after year."
rationale: This is inaccurate. While the Postal Service was reorganized in 1971 to fund core operations largely from postage and service revenue, Congress has provided targeted appropriations, credit lines and Treasury loans (notably emergency borrowing authority and pandemic-era assistance), and USPS has not produced an ‘‘operational profit year after year’’ — it has reported repeated annual losses in many years since the 2006 retiree-health prefunding mandate. Thus the blanket statement that it took no taxpayer aid since 1971 and consistently makes operational profits is false.

claim: "Obama's Environmental Protection Agency sent emails for Hispanic Heritage Month with a photo of Che Guevara."
rationale: Multiple news reports documented that during the Obama administration the EPA circulated Hispanic Heritage Month materials that included an image of Che Guevara, prompting complaints and an agency apology. The imagery was widely reported as part of an internal Hispanic employee group’s outreach and was characterized as inappropriate by EPA officials at the time.

claim: Says Ron Johnson voted to turn Medicare "into a voucher program."
rationale: This is misleading. Ron Johnson has supported and voted for budget measures and proposals that advocated converting Medicare to a “premium support” or voucher-like system, but no law has actually turned Medicare into a voucher program and there is no single Senate vote by Johnson that enacted such a change. The claim conflates support or votes for proposals with having voted to actually convert Medicare into a voucher program.

claim: Says U.S. Rep. Steve Southerland "voted to keep the shutdown going."
rationale: There is no specific, universally identified vote that by itself proves Southerland “voted to keep the shutdown going” without a bill and date; members often voted for alternative measures or amendments tied to policy riders rather than a simple ‘keep shutdown’ motion. Because the claim lacks a cited vote, I cannot verify that he cast a definitive vote solely intended to prolong a shutdown.

claim: Says Sens. Joe Manchin and Kyrsten Sinema "are Republicans … Just look at the way they vote."
rationale: Neither senator is a Republican. Joe Manchin is a member of the Democratic Party in the Senate, and Kyrsten Sinema was elected as a Democrat but left the party in 2022 to register as an independent; voting records that sometimes align with Republicans do not make them Republicans. The claim conflates occasional conservative votes with formal party affiliation.

claim: "More than 9,000 Rhode Island voters used the Moderate Party master lever mechanism and they didn't have a single Moderate on their ballot."
rationale: I could not find corroborating evidence for the specific numeric claim and it is implausible as stated. Rhode Island's "master lever" (party-column) voting is recorded in official tallies and there are no public election reports showing more than 9,000 voters selecting the Moderate Party while that party had zero candidates on the ballot; the claim appears to conflate or misstate reported figures. Without a cited election year or official precinct-level data the assertion is unverified and likely inaccurate.

claim: "Romney signed government-mandated health care with taxpayer-funded abortions."
rationale: Mitt Romney did sign the 2006 Massachusetts health reform that included an individual mandate, but the law included provisions to prevent state (taxpayer) funding of abortion except in narrow circumstances and required separate accounting so subsidies would not directly pay for abortions. While some insurance plans available in the marketplace could cover abortion as part of a private premium, that is not the same as the state using taxpayer funds to pay for abortions. Thus the claim that he signed “government‑mandated health care with taxpayer‑funded abortions” is misleading and incorrect.

claim: In the wake of the Republican-backed tax bill, "more than 100,000 American workers have already been laid off in 2018."
rationale: There is no reliable evidence that more than 100,000 U.S. workers were laid off in 2018 as a direct consequence of the Republican-backed tax bill. Labor statistics and contemporaneous reporting do not document an aggregated, causal total of that size tied to the law; many announced workforce changes that year were unrelated or far smaller, and overall employment remained strong. Claims summing disparate announcements to reach >100,000 rely on selective counting and do not establish causation.

claim: Mental health provisions related to mass shootings "got over 90 votes in the Senate."
rationale: The statement is vague and no well-known Senate vote specifically described as "mental health provisions related to mass shootings" received more than 90 votes. Major post-mass-shooting gun-policy efforts (for example, background-check amendments) failed to reach cloture or the 60-vote threshold and did not approach 90; while some standalone mental-health bills have passed with large margins, they are not generally framed as mass-shooting provisions. Without a specific bill or date the claim is misleading.

claim: The Obama administration "went to court to keep one of these five in jail at Guantanamo just three years ago because he was such a huge risk."
rationale: The claim is misleading and not supported as stated. While five Guantanamo detainees were transferred in a 2014 prisoner swap for Bowe Bergdahl and there were prior government legal proceedings and detention reviews concerning some detainees, there is no clear, simple record that the Obama administration 'went to court to keep one of these five in jail just three years ago' as a singular, dispositive action — the situation involved ongoing habeas litigation and periodic review board assessments over many years. The statement compresses complex legal history and timing into an inaccurate one-line claim.

claim: "In the last 29 months, our economy has produced about 4.5 million private-sector jobs."
rationale: The claim is misleading because it lacks a clear reference period and does not match Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) payroll trends for comparable 29‑month spans. For example, from Jan 2021 through mid‑2023 private‑sector payrolls increased by substantially more than 4.5 million (on the order of roughly 8–9 million), so stating “about 4.5 million” is inconsistent with official BLS monthly job‑count data for likely 29‑month windows. Without a precise start/end date the figure cannot be verified and appears understated for the most plausible periods referenced.

claim: Says 2012 was the "first year in American history that more minorities are being born than people in the majority."
rationale: This is accurate as commonly reported: in 2012 U.S. vital statistics showed that births to minorities (combined non‑Hispanic racial/ethnic minority groups and Hispanics) exceeded births to non‑Hispanic white mothers for the first time, making minority births a slight majority that year. The finding is based on national birth data rather than overall population counts.

claim: Says Denmark’s suicide rate has been about twice as high as the United States’ over the past five decades.
rationale: International data do not support a consistent twofold higher suicide rate in Denmark versus the United States over the last fifty years. WHO/OECD and national statistics show Denmark’s suicide rate has generally been similar to or lower than the U.S. in many periods (Denmark peaked mid-20th century then declined, while U.S. rates rose in recent decades), so a sustained ~2x gap is inaccurate.

claim: "Wendy Davis has already taken more $ from teacher unions than the past 3 Democrat gubernatorial candidates combined."
rationale: There is no clear evidence that Wendy Davis had taken more money from teacher unions than the prior three Democratic gubernatorial nominees combined. Past Democratic nominees (e.g., Tony Sanchez 2002, Chris Bell 2006, Bill White 2010) received substantial union support across multiple cycles, and combining those totals is likely larger than the reported teacher‑union contributions to Davis. The claim also fails to define which organizations count as “teacher unions” or the exact time window for “already.”

claim: Says Stefani Carter "repeatedly used her campaign contributors’ donations to rent margarita machines for our state house office."
rationale: I found no reliable evidence or official records showing Stefani Carter repeatedly charged campaign contributions to rent margarita machines for a state house office. Such expenditures would normally appear in campaign finance filings or news reporting, and credible sources do not corroborate the repeated conduct described. The claim appears to be anecdotal or from partisan rhetoric without documentary proof.

claim: "A year ago, in March 2007, I called for immediate action to address abuses in the subprime market, and I laid out detailed concrete proposals for how to do so."
rationale: The statement is presented in first person but does not identify who 'I' is, and no specific citation or record from March 2007 is provided to verify the claim. Although many public figures raised concerns about subprime lending in 2007, without the speaker's identity and a contemporaneous speech or document showing concrete proposals the assertion cannot be confirmed. Given the missing context and evidence, the claim is treated as false (unverified).

claim: "More suicide deaths than coronavirus death past two months."
rationale: The claim as written is ambiguous and unsupported because it gives no location or exact two‑month period. In many countries and during COVID surges, deaths from COVID‑19 in a two‑month span have exceeded the number of suicides in that same span; without precise context the blanket statement is unreliable. Because the statement could be true in some specific locales or months but is not generally true as presented, it is judged false.

claim: "We sell 40 percent of our guns without a background check."
rationale: If “we” means a licensed firearms dealer, federal law requires dealers to document sales and run background checks for most retail transfers, so claiming they sell 40% of their guns without checks would describe widespread illegal behavior and is implausible. If the speaker meant all U.S. gun transfers (including private-party and gun‑show sales), estimates vary by survey and state and are context‑dependent, but that does not validate a blanket 40% claim for a seller’s inventory.

claim: Says Nancy Pelosi tweeted that she was disgusted with Donald Trump over taxes
rationale: There is no reliable record that Nancy Pelosi tweeted the specific claim that she was “disgusted” with Donald Trump over his taxes. While Pelosi and other Democrats publicly criticized Trump’s tax practices after media reports, available archives and contemporaneous coverage show statements and tweets that criticized or called for transparency rather than a tweet using the quoted wording. The claim appears to be a misattribution or paraphrase rather than an exact tweet.

claim: "Many of the countries in question (in Trump’s travel ban) don't even have a U.S. embassy there to help us vet."
rationale: The original Trump travel ban targeted several countries where the U.S. had no functioning embassy or had suspended operations (for example Iran, Syria, Libya, Somalia and Yemen), meaning there was no on‑the‑ground U.S. post available to assist with local vetting. Later iterations added other countries with limited or closed U.S. missions (e.g., North Korea, Venezuela), so it is accurate to say many of the listed countries lacked a U.S. embassy to help vet applicants.

claim: "Barack Obama had 150 days in the U.S. Senate where he was able to vote quite often 'present.' "
rationale: This claim is not supported by Senate roll-call records or reputable fact-checking: Barack Obama cast only a small number of explicit “present” votes during his Senate tenure, not enough to amount to 150 days of frequently voting “present.” The statement likely conflates being physically present for votes or committee activity with formally recording many “present” votes, which is inaccurate.

claim: "Medicaid expansion isn’t necessarily a very popular issue on the street."
rationale: The claim is a vague generalization but asserts Medicaid expansion is not necessarily popular ‘on the street.’ Public-opinion data and multiple statewide ballot results show that Medicaid expansion typically receives majority support across a range of electorates, so the blanket negative statement is not supported. While intensity and salience vary by place and partisan group, the overall pattern is one of measurable public favor rather than clear unpopularity.

claim: Photo shows "people coming from California to Washington DC" to protest election results.
rationale: A standalone photograph cannot reliably demonstrate that the pictured people came from California or that their purpose was to travel to Washington, D.C. to protest election results. Determining origin or intent requires corroborating evidence such as image metadata, reliable reporting, participant testimony, travel records, or context that the photo alone does not provide, so the claim is not supported as stated.

claim: Says Russ Feingold said that with Obamacare, "we could keep our doctors and our plans, it was rated as the Lie of the Year."
rationale: The claim attributes a specific quote to former Senator Russ Feingold saying the Obamacare promise that 'we could keep our doctors and our plans' 'was rated as the Lie of the Year.' While PolitiFact did name the 'you can keep your health care plan/doctor' promise its 2013 "Lie of the Year," there is no credible public record that Feingold made that exact statement; the quote appears to be misattributed. Thus the attribution is not supported.

claim: Says Texas has more than 80,000 abortions each year.
rationale: Authoritative state-level estimates (CDC surveillance and the Guttmacher Institute) do not support an annual total over 80,000 for Texas in recent years; pre-2022 totals were generally in the ~40,000–70,000 range and declined further after major restrictions. The claim gives no timeframe or source and therefore conflicts with available data-based estimates.

claim: Says Russ Feingold supported a stimulus plan that allowed a company to create 3,000 jobs in China.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Sen. Russ Feingold specifically supported a stimulus provision that ‘‘allowed’’ a company to create 3,000 jobs in China. The major 2009 stimulus (ARRA) comprised broad domestic spending and tax measures; corporate decisions to hire offshore are private business actions and not direct, documented outcomes traceable to a single senator's vote. Without a named company, bill provision, or verifiable link, the claim is unsubstantiated and misleading.

claim: The "president of Drag Queen Story Hour" was "arrested, charged with child pornography."
rationale: There is no credible evidence or reporting that an individual serving as a named “president of Drag Queen Story Hour” was arrested and charged with child pornography. The claim appears to be a social-media misattribution or conflation and has been raised previously without substantiation; moreover, Drag Queen Story Hour is a decentralized program without a single national “president.” Without a specific name, date, or jurisdiction the allegation cannot be verified and has been debunked in similar past claims.

claim: "More Americans receive food aid than work in (the) private sector."
rationale: U.S. private‑sector employment is much larger than the population served by major food assistance programs. Private‑sector payrolls typically exceed 120 million people, while SNAP (food stamps) covers roughly 40–45 million people and other programs (school meals, WIC, food banks) add tens of millions but with substantial overlap. Even aggregating programs, the unique number of people receiving food aid is unlikely to exceed private‑sector employment.

claim: I spent only $36.29 on my campaign for governor.
rationale: I cannot verify this assertion from the information given and spending only $36.29 on a gubernatorial campaign is extremely unlikely given usual costs and legal reporting requirements. Without seeing the candidate name, jurisdiction, election year, and official campaign finance filings to substantiate the amount, the claim should be treated as unsupported and therefore false.

claim: "I went to the Olympics that was out of balance, and we got it on balance."
rationale: The sentence is ambiguous and lacks any specific, verifiable facts (no identified speaker, which Olympics, or what ‘out of balance’ means). Without attribution or independent corroboration this claim cannot be verified as true, so it is judged false for fact-checking purposes. If the user supplies context (who said it and when) the statement could be re-evaluated.

claim: "There are parks in Southeast Raleigh that still don’t have air conditioning in the gym"
rationale: I cannot confirm the specific claim with available information. While older community centers and park gyms in many cities sometimes lack modern HVAC, I have no verified, up-to-date evidence that multiple parks in Southeast Raleigh currently lack air conditioning. Without local facility inventories or recent reporting, the assertion remains unverified and thus treated as false for this fact-check.

claim: "They voted for (a border wall) in 2006. Then-Senator Obama voted for it. Sen. Schumer voted for it. Sen. Clinton voted for it."
rationale: In 2006 Congress passed the Secure Fence Act, which authorized construction of hundreds of miles of fencing along the U.S.–Mexico border; the measure passed with strong bipartisan support. Roll-call records show then-Senator Barack Obama, Senator Chuck Schumer and Senator Hillary Clinton voted in favor of the legislation. The claim accurately attributes votes for that 2006 border-fencing bill to those three senators.

claim: Says "Bruce Starr voted to throw 6,000 Oregonians off unemployment."
rationale: There is no clear, verifiable record that Bruce Starr cast a vote that directly and literally “threw 6,000 Oregonians off unemployment.” Legislative votes can change eligibility and agencies sometimes estimate how many claimants will be affected, but attributing a precise, immediate removal of 6,000 people to a single legislator’s vote is an oversimplification and likely an exaggeration used in political messaging. Without a specific bill and official post‑enactment count tying his vote to that exact number, the claim is unsubstantiated.

claim: "The most likely triggering cause of (microcephaly)" is the "DTaP shot, a vaccine that had been recently mandated by the Brazilian government to be injected into pregnant women."
rationale: High-quality epidemiological and laboratory evidence established Zika virus infection during pregnancy as the primary cause of the 2015–2016 increase in microcephaly in Brazil; studies found Zika in fetal and infant brain tissue and showed a strong temporal and geographic correlation. There is no credible evidence that the DTaP vaccine (or Tdap boosters) caused those birth defects, and the claim also misstates vaccine policy (DTaP is the childhood series; Tdap is the adult/pregnancy booster). The assertion that a recently mandated maternal DTaP shot was the most likely trigger contradicts the scientific consensus.

claim: "While the initial increase in oil prices resulted in a near instantaneous increase in gas prices for consumers, the subsequent decrease in crude oil prices has failed to meaningfully provide relief for Georgia's families at the pump."
rationale: The statement describes a well-documented asymmetric pass-through: retail gasoline prices commonly rise quickly when crude oil prices jump but decline more slowly when crude falls, so consumers often see delayed or muted relief. Georgia pump prices generally track national/regional trends and are subject to the same refining, distribution, inventory and retail-margin frictions that produce this lag, making the claim credible for Georgia families.

claim: Newt Gingrich "co-sponsored a bill with Nancy Pelosi that would have given $60 million a year to a U.N. program supporting China’s brutal one-child policy."
rationale: This claim is not supported by the legislative record. The $60 million figure refers to Clinton-era requests to fund the U.N. Population Fund (UNFPA), and Nancy Pelosi did press to restore UNFPA funding in the 1990s, but there is no credible evidence that Newt Gingrich co-sponsored a bill with Pelosi to give $60 million a year to a U.N. program that explicitly funded China’s one‑child policy. Congress also had longstanding restrictions against U.S. funding for organizations that support coercive family‑planning practices, and fact‑checks have found the claim conflates and misstates separate events.

claim: Rhode Island's unemployment insurance system "is the most expensive such system in the country."
rationale: The claim is not supported as an unqualified statement: there is no single, consistent metric that identifies Rhode Island as definitively "the most expensive" unemployment insurance system nationwide. States differ by how you measure cost (employer payroll tax rates, benefits per recipient, cost per covered worker, or total program outlays), and other states (e.g., Massachusetts, New Jersey, Washington, Alaska in various years) often rank as more costly on different measures. Rhode Island may be relatively costly by some measures or at particular times, but it is not universally the most expensive across the country.

claim: Said President Barack Obama "said he was going to stop (signature strikes)."
rationale: There is no clear record of President Obama publicly declaring that he would stop the use of “signature strikes” outright. The Obama administration did tighten and clarify drone-targeting policies and emphasized limits and oversight, but officials (including CIA director John Brennan) acknowledged signature strikes had been used and Obama did not make an explicit, unqualified public promise to end them. The claim overstates what was said.

claim: Bath and Body Works products are not recommended during pregnancy because they are suspected of "damaging fertility or the unborn child."
rationale: This is not a correct blanket statement: Bath & Body Works has not issued a company-wide recommendation that all its products be avoided in pregnancy, and public-health guidance does not single out the entire brand as ‘suspected of damaging fertility or the unborn child.’ Some individual ingredients commonly used in fragranced personal-care products (for example certain phthalates) have been linked in studies to reproductive effects and may trigger region-specific warnings, but that concern applies to specific chemicals and exposures, not an automatic prohibition of the whole product line.

claim: Ketanji Brown Jackson "says she gave pedophiles lighter sentences (because) it’s different when they use computers vs mail to get volumes of child porn. This makes ‘total sense’ according to Jackson."
rationale: The quoted assertion misstates and strips context from Jackson’s record. As a federal district judge she applied federal sentencing guidelines and in court documents and hearings discussed how guidelines treat offenses involving digital distribution differently than older mail-based schemes; she did not say she gave “pedophiles lighter sentences” as a policy or endorse leniency because crimes involved computers. Fact-checkers and the sentencing records show she imposed substantial prison terms in many cases and explained guideline-driven distinctions rather than expressing blanket sympathy for offenders.

claim: Says "Bill Pascrell voted to eliminate all estate taxes for billionaires, and I voted no."
rationale: This is false based on Pascrell’s public voting record: he has not voted to eliminate the estate tax for billionaires and has opposed Republican proposals to repeal or gut the estate tax. Major GOP tax bills either raised the exemption or made other changes but Pascrell voted against those measures rather than in favor of eliminating the estate tax entirely.
